## Bottom line

**As of 15 November 2026, tighter CBN regulation is changing the basis of competition—not simply reducing competition.** Capital, demonstrable controls and dependable infrastructure matter more; rapid expansion across customers, merchants and agents faces tighter constraints. But two forces pull in opposite directions: higher compliance costs and exclusive agent relationships can favour incumbents, while new cross-market concentration limits seek to prevent those incumbents from dominating both issuing and acquiring. The latter’s compliance deadline has not yet passed, so a completed restructuring of the market should not be claimed. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/out/2021/ccd/approved%20new%20licence%20categorization%20requirements%20consolidated%20-%202021.pdf))

The strongest conclusion is therefore **innovation redirected toward supervised infrastructure, with greater barriers to independent entry**—not a demonstrated collapse in innovation or a proven reduction in concentration.

## 1. PSBs: distribution advantages, but a deliberately restricted business model

The CBN’s published PSB guidelines set a **₦5 billion minimum capital requirement**, permit deposits and payments, prohibit lending and foreign-currency deposits, and require at least **25% of financial-service touchpoints in rural and unbanked locations**. These are established features of the licence, not evidence of a new November 2026 capital increase. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/out/2020/ccd/approved%20reviewed%20guidelines%20for%20licensing%20and%20regulation%20of%20payment%20service%20banks%20in%20nigeria-27aug2020.pdf))

**Competitive mechanism:** a PSB cannot simply turn payments customers into a proprietary loan book to recover acquisition costs. It must make distribution, payments and permitted investment income work economically, or partner within applicable rules. Strong parent funding and an existing distribution network can consequently be valuable advantages. The rural requirement also makes profitable last-mile service—not just urban wallet acquisition—part of the competitive challenge.

**Innovation implication:** the commercial incentive is to improve activation, merchant acceptance, cash availability and service delivery per outlet. Lending-based monetisation requires a separately authorised arrangement; a PSB licence is not a universal digital-bank licence. That distinction matters when comparing PSBs with fintechs operating through microfinance banks.

## 2. Switches: a higher operating threshold, alongside a challenge to integrated dominance

The CBN’s consolidated licensing requirements specify **₦2 billion for switching and processing**, alongside risk-management, security and business-continuity requirements. They distinguish the **₦250 million combined Payment Solution Services category** from individual **₦100 million PSSP/PTSP** and **₦50 million super-agent** categories. The combined figure should not be mistaken for a newly increased standalone PSSP minimum. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/out/2021/ccd/approved%20new%20licence%20categorization%20requirements%20consolidated%20-%202021.pdf))

The more consequential structural change is the **15 June 2026 circular**, documented in PwC’s analysis: an operator, individually or at group level, with **more than 25% of consumer issuing or merchant acquiring must remain at no more than 15% in the other activity**, measured over a rolling year. Market-structure compliance is due **31 December 2026**; payment-data localisation is due **1 January 2027**. ([pwc.com](https://www.pwc.com/ng/en/assets/pdf/cbn-data-localisation-and-market-structure-rules.pdf))

**Competitive mechanism:** this discourages simultaneous dominance on both sides of a payment. It could create opportunities for specialist issuers, acquirers and infrastructure partners. Conversely, localisation and supervisory systems increase fixed costs, which larger operators can spread over more transactions.

**Important qualification:** this is not a blanket prohibition on integrated payment businesses, nor proof that named firms must already divest. PwC identifies unresolved market-definition and measurement questions and describes divestment, withdrawal or moderated growth as possible responses—not prescribed outcomes. It is premature to call the market deconcentrated. ([pwc.com](https://www.pwc.com/ng/en/assets/pdf/cbn-data-localisation-and-market-structure-rules.pdf))

## 3. Agents: exclusive distribution, but not closed payment acceptance

The **6 October 2025 agent-banking guidelines** provide for one principal and one super-agent network at a time, dedicated agent accounts, stronger principal accountability and monitoring. Agent exclusivity was scheduled for **1 April 2026**. Customer cash-in/cash-out limits are **₦100,000 daily and ₦500,000 weekly**, while aggregate daily agent cash-out is capped at **₦1.2 million**. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2025/CCD/CIRCULAR%20AND%20GUIDELINES%20FOR%20THE%20OPERATIONS%20OF%20AGENT%20BANKING%20IN%20NIGERIA%20OCTOBER%206%202025.pdf))

There is an important implementation correction: the CBN subsequently expanded the POS geo-fence from **10 to 70 metres** and extended geo-fencing compliance to **1 August 2026**. That extension should not automatically be interpreted as an extension of agent exclusivity. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/AboutCBN/Reforms.html))

**Competitive mechanism:** exclusivity changes competition *at an agent’s counter* into competition *for that agent’s contract*. Reliability, settlement, commissions and liquidity support become decisive. A small principal may struggle to persuade an agent to surrender alternative relationships; a strong incumbent may gain distribution leverage. Agents also lose the ability to hedge across principals during outages.

However, **exclusive sponsorship is not exclusive card acceptance**: the guidelines require terminals to accept cards issued by Nigerian banks and require principals to remain card-neutral. Thus, one principal does not mean customers can transact only with that principal’s cards. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2025/CCD/CIRCULAR%20AND%20GUIDELINES%20FOR%20THE%20OPERATIONS%20OF%20AGENT%20BANKING%20IN%20NIGERIA%20OCTOBER%206%202025.pdf))

The inclusion risk follows from outlet economics: if compliance expenditure or cash limits make a marginal location unprofitable, coverage may deteriorate. That is a plausible risk, not evidence that a measured nationwide wave of agent closures has occurred.

## 4. Innovation: evidence of pressure, not evidence that experimentation has stopped

There is direct evidence of the burden. The CBN’s fintech report, published in 2026, says **87.5% of surveyed respondents reported compliance costs significantly affecting innovation capacity**; **62.5% identified approval delays and ambiguous guidelines as key regulatory challenges**. These are respondent perceptions—not a representative estimate of lost innovation across every Nigerian fintech or a causal evaluation of the later June rules. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2026/CCD/CBN_FINTECH_REPORT_.pdf))

The direction of investment is nevertheless understandable:

- **More compliance engineering:** automated monitoring, auditable controls and secure onboarding become prerequisites for expansion. The CBN’s **10 March 2026 AML standards** require automated real-time detection, analysis and reporting. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/AboutCBN/Reforms.html))
- **More specialist and partnership models:** rather than fund an entire licensed stack, an entrant may provide reconciliation, merchant software or risk tools to authorised institutions. This reduces some entry costs but introduces dependence on the licensed partner’s access terms.
- **A potential counterweight to incumbent advantage:** the CBN report proposes shared compliance services, expanded open banking, sandbox development and structured regulatory engagement. These could lower experimentation costs, but proposals should not be presented as fully delivered programmes. ([cbn.gov.ng](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2026/CCD/CBN_FINTECH_REPORT_.pdf))

The supervisory trajectory also extends beyond circulars: on **10 November 2026**, the Senate passed a BOFIA amendment bill providing for enhanced oversight of systemically important non-bank institutions. Senate passage is a legislative milestone, not itself evidence that the proposed powers are already operative law. ([thisdaylive.com](https://www.thisdaylive.com/2026/11/10/senate-passes-bill-to-bring-big-fintechs-non-bank-financial-institutions-under-cbn-regulation/))

## Overall assessment

**Nigeria is moving toward payments competition in which scale must be auditable and operationally credible.** The opportunity is safer services and room for focused providers; the danger is that compliance costs and exclusive distribution protect established firms faster than concentration controls open space for challengers.

The decisive outcome tests are active rural-agent coverage, switching and acquiring access, fees, outage and dispute performance, new-entry survival and actual product launches. Until those are measured against the implementation timetable, neither “regulation has killed innovation” nor “regulation has made payments more competitive” is a defensible settled verdict.

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tightening is reshaping Nigerian payments asymmetrically: the agent layer is being restructured by hardware-enforced rules, while the headline corporate market-share cap is, for now, a signal rather than a working constraint — the CBN has not defined how market share is measured. Competition is therefore intensifying where enforcement bites, at the agent's counter, and innovation is shifting from distribution scale toward uptime, compliance infrastructure, and forced lane choice.

At the agent layer, the October 2025 guidelines made each agent exclusive to one principal and one super-agent network, effective 1 April 2026, with per-customer cash-out capped at ₦100,000 a day (₦500,000 a week) and each agent's daily total at ₦1.2 million, all routed through a dedicated wallet with the principal (Legal500, 2026). Terminals are geo-fenced to their registered premises — the radius was widened from 10 to 70 metres in a 29 May 2026 circular, enforced from 1 August 2026 — and operating outside it attracts fines of at least ₦5,000,000 plus ₦300,000 per day (Legal500, 2026; CryptoCompass, 2026). Multi-homing was agents' insurance against switch failures, so exclusivity shifts the entire uptime burden onto the principal's backend, and principals must now compete for agents on reliability, commissions, and dispute resolution (CryptoCompass, 2026).

At the corporate layer, the 15 June 2026 circular (PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004) caps any operator holding over 25% of consumer issuing at 15% of merchant acquiring, and vice versa, applied at group level, with monthly market-share returns and full compliance due 31 December 2026, plus data localisation by 1 January 2027 (PwC, 2026). But PwC flags the decisive gap: the circular never defines the pool against which share is measured — volume, value, active users, or transaction count — so no operator can yet know whether it is over the threshold, and the plausible responses (divestment, winding down a line, throttling growth) are all costly and distortionary (PwC, 2026). Until the denominator is defined, the cap is forced lane-choice planning, not measurable deconcentration.

The quantified picture cuts against a simple "tightening kills payments" story: reported NIBSS data put PoS value in Q1 2026 at ₦18.78 trillion, up about 79% year on year, on a terminal base of 5.56 million at end-2024 (CryptoCompass, 2026). Volume is still growing; what is changing is who captures the margin. Standalone umbrella agents are exiting or folding into pharmacies, supermarkets, and petrol stations, and smaller mobile-money operators that cannot fund onshore hosting by 1 January 2027 face merger or surrender of share (CryptoCompass, 2026). One category is not squeezed but erased: roaming collectors, daily ajo savings agents, and dispatch riders can no longer process payments beyond 70 metres of their registered coordinates (CryptoCompass, 2026). Two caveats: the cap's real effects are unobservable until the 31 December 2026 deadline, and whether the agent squeeze reverses inclusion gains will only show in 2027 data.

## What this Answer adds

- Enforcement asymmetry: the agent rules are enforced by hardware (geo-fence, aggregators, dedicated wallets, fines), while the corporate cap has no defined denominator — so the binding constraint in 2026 sits at the street, not the boardroom.
- A quantified counterexample to the tightening-kills-volume narrative: reported PoS value of ₦18.78 trillion in Q1 2026, up about 79% year on year, shows the squeeze redistributes margin rather than shrinking volume.
- The denominator gap as a mechanism: without a defined measurement pool, the 25%/15% cap can only produce costly self-restraint (growth throttling, pre-emptive divestment planning), not verifiable deconcentration — a diagnostic missed by answers that treat the cap as already operative.
- The geo-fence's collateral category: it legally immobilises mobile commerce (ajo collectors, dispatch riders), removing a whole form of payment collection rather than merely constraining kiosks.

By late 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) intensive regulatory intervention across payment service banks (PSBs), switching operators, and agent networks has fundamentally transformed the structural economics and competitive dynamics of Nigerian digital payments. Moving past the permissive, high-growth expansion era of the early 2020s, the CBN’s 2025–2026 regulatory reset enforces a strict "stability-first" doctrine. This framework utilizes structural anti-monopoly caps, agent-network exclusivity, automated Anti-Money Laundering (AML) enforcement, and data localization mandates to re-engineer market competition and shift fintech innovation away from consumer-facing customer acquisition toward compliance-heavy infrastructure, resilience engineering, and business-to-business (B2B) orchestration.

---

### 1. Structural Anti-Monopoly Constraints and Market-Structure Caps

The most aggressive architectural intervention in Nigerian payments is the CBN's enforcement of cross-market concentration limits and structural unbundling.

#### A. The Asymmetric 25%/15% Issuing-Acquiring Caps
Under Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, the CBN established strict structural ceilings on vertical integration across the payment ecosystem (Launch Base Africa, 2026):
* **The Rule:** Any licensed payment institution (evaluated at the consolidated group level, including parent entities, subsidiaries, and common shareholding structures) controlling **more than 25% of the consumer issuing market** (wallets, accounts, and card issuance) is prohibited from holding **more than 15% of the merchant acquiring market** (POS terminals, payment gateways, and merchant aggregations), and vice versa.
* **Operational Impact:** This directly targets vertically integrated "super-apps" such as OPay, Moniepoint, and PalmPay, which previously captured interchange, processing, and merchant discount rates (MDR) across both ends of a transaction. Groups breaching these limits face mandatory corporate restructuring or asset divestment, opening up merchant acquiring volume to mid-tier fintechs, challenger aggregators, and traditional commercial banks.

#### B. Data Localization and Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) Disclosures
The same supervisory framework mandates that all payment transaction data generated within Nigeria must be fully localized and stored on domestic data infrastructure by January 1, 2027 (Launch Base Africa, 2026). Concurrently, the CBN enforces mandatory disclosure of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs) for significant shareholders, aligning non-bank payment institutions with the rigorous transparency standards mandated for Tier-1 deposit-money banks under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020.

---

### 2. Agent Network Overhaul: Single-Principal Exclusivity and Velocity Capping

Agent banking—which grew exponentially to become Nigeria's primary retail banking cash rail—has undergone a severe structural contraction following the full enforcement of the CBN's revised *Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria* (Central Bank of Nigeria, 2025).

#### A. The Single-Principal Exclusivity Mandate
Previously, retail POS agents operated under a "multi-homing" model, maintaining terminals from multiple providers (e.g., Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay side by side) to hedge against localized network downtime. 
* Under the 2026 enforcement regime, agents are strictly restricted to serving a **single principal institution** at a time, routing all transactions through a dedicated agent wallet tied exclusively to that principal.
* **Competitive Consequence:** Agent networks are transformed from shared, multi-tenant distribution nodes into exclusive, highly contested franchise networks. Principals must compete aggressively on backend uptime, settlement velocity, and commission structures, as agents cannot easily switch providers mid-contract. While this benefits scaled incumbents with robust server uptime, it increases vulnerability for agents whose chosen principal experiences extended platform outages.

#### B. Cash-Out Limits and Geo-Fencing
Regulatory directives enforce rigid volumetric controls to curb illicit liquidity flows and cash hoarding:
* Customer cash-out and cash-in operations are capped at $\text{NGN } 100,000$ per day and $\text{NGN } 500,000$ per week.
* Individual agent daily cash-out volumes are capped at $\text{NGN } 1.2\text{ million}$ (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* POS terminals must be geo-fenced to registered business locations, operating within a permitted spatial radius verified through certified Payment Terminal Service Aggregators (PTSAs) like NIBSS and Unified Payment Services Ltd.

---

### 3. Payment Service Banks (PSBs) and Switching Infrastructure

#### A. PSBs and the Balance-Sheet Wall
Payment Service Banks (such as MTN's MoMo PSB and Airtel's SmartCash PSB) maintain high minimum paid-up capital thresholds ($\text{NGN } 5\text{ billion}$) but remain strictly ring-fenced:
* They are prohibited from extending retail or corporate loans and cannot hold open foreign exchange positions.
* With lending yields closed off, PSBs must deploy the vast majority of their deposit liabilities into sovereign debt and low-risk government securities, forcing them to rely entirely on transactional volume and micro-transfer fees to achieve operational profitability.

#### B. Switching Operators and Automated AML Compliance
Switching and processing companies face escalating operational overheads driven by supervisory mandates:
* Under the CBN’s baseline standards for automated Anti-Money Laundering (AML) solutions (Circular BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/019/002), all switching operators and payment service providers must deploy real-time transaction monitoring engines and automated suspicious transaction reporting (STR) systems linked directly to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) (Techmoonshot, 2026).
* The transition to the ISO 20022 messaging standard under the National Payment Stack enforces stringent data telemetry requirements, raising the minimum capital and technical expenditure needed to operate a competitive routing switch.

---

### 4. How Competition and Innovation are Reshaping

#### A. Competition: From Land-Grab to Governance Moats
Competition has shifted away from aggressive customer acquisition and unverified wallet creation toward **compliance capacity and balance-sheet resilience**. High compliance overheads, mandatory CAC registration for POS agents, and recurring RegTech audits have priced under-capitalized startups out of direct payment licensing. Consequently, market consolidation is accelerating, driving early-stage innovators into B2B white-label partnerships or acquisition paths with established financial institutions (e.g., Paystack and Flutterwave acquiring or partnering with microfinance and banking charters).

#### B. Innovation: Pivoting to RegTech and Embedded Infrastructure
Product innovation has moved away from consumer-facing "super-app" feature sprawl toward infrastructure resilience:
* **Identity-Tech & Biometrics:** Engineering resources are heavily allocated to real-time NIN/BVN biometric verification, facial liveness detection, and automated fraud-scoring algorithms.
* **Open Banking and API Orchestration:** Although nationwide production rollouts have faced staggered implementation phases, open banking frameworks drive innovation in account aggregation, consent management, and permissioned data-sharing for embedded lending.
* **Cross-Border Remittance Integration:** With domestic retail growth constrained by market-share caps and transaction limits, fintech leaders are focusing on international regulatory passporting and integration with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) to capture regional trade corridors.

As of November 2026, the CBN's tightening is doing something more specific than "raising barriers": it is replacing a market that rewarded speed and licence-stacking with one that rewards auditable governance, and it is doing so through four instruments that arrived in sequence and now bite at once. The result is a two-sided competitive outcome — merchant acquiring is being forcibly opened while entry at the top consolidates — and an innovation shift that is real but narrower than the CBN's own open-banking promise.

## 1. The four instruments and what each actually changes

**The agent-banking reset (6 October 2025 guidelines, exclusivity effective 1 April 2026).** The CBN's *Circular and Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria* replaced the 2013 framework and the 2015 super-agent rules (Central Bank of Nigeria, 2025). The operative provisions: an agent may serve only one principal at a time; all transactions must flow through a dedicated agent account or wallet assigned by that principal; cash-out is capped at ₦100,000 per customer per day and ₦500,000 per week, with a ₦1.2 million aggregate per agent per day; terminals are geo-fenced to a registered location (the radius was widened from 10 to 70 metres by a 29 May 2026 circular, enforcement from 1 August 2026); and principals must report agent activity to NIBSS for onward transmission to the CBN (CryptoCompass, 2026; GizPulse, 2026).

The mechanism worth spelling out: before this, an agent's terminals were a shared, switchable resource — a Moniepoint terminal covered an OPay outage. Exclusivity converts the agent network from a public utility into a set of competing, locked-in franchises. Principals now compete for agent loyalty on uptime, settlement speed and float support rather than free-riding on each other's distribution. The upside for the CBN is traceability and accountability; the downside is that the channel serving Nigerians without branches now has a single point of failure, and the ₦1.2 million cap binds hardest in high-volume market hubs where agents function as the working-capital infrastructure for traders (CryptoCompass, 2026).

**The market-structure cap (15 June 2026 circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004).** No licensed institution, individually or as a group of related companies, may hold more than 25% of the consumer issuing market while also holding more than 15% of the merchant acquiring market, and vice versa, measured over a rolling 12 months. Groups in breach must restructure or divest by 31 December 2026, file monthly market-share returns, localise all payments transaction data in Nigeria from 1 January 2027, and disclose ultimate beneficial owners (Launch Base Africa, 2026; Tech in Naija, 2026). The circular applies to the whole stack — deposit money banks, microfinance banks, mobile money operators, switching companies, payment solution providers and super-agents — not just fintechs.

The mechanism is a cliff, not a slope. A group at 24% of issuing and 14% of acquiring gains little from one more point of share if that point pushes it over the threshold and forces a divestiture of its acquiring arm — the marginal point can be worth less than zero. Rational groups will therefore manage reported shares to sit just under the caps, which means threshold-gaming (reclassification of volumes, shifting merchants to partner acquirers) as much as genuine divestment. Either way, the integrated economics that justified the super-app model — capturing interchange and processing fees on both sides of a transaction — are being dismantled by fiat (Launch Base Africa, 2026).

**The licence clean-up and the great consolidation.** The CBN revoked the operating licences of 46 microfinance banks effective 1 July 2026 for insolvency, inactivity and failure to maintain minimum capital (Launch Base Africa, 2026). This caught technology companies that had bought dormant charters as a shortcut into banking, and it forced them back into the more expensive direct licensing process. In parallel, the largest fintechs moved *up* the ladder: Moniepoint, OPay and PalmPay were upgraded to national microfinance bank licences in early 2026, Paystack acquired Ladder Microfinance Bank, and Flutterwave secured a microfinance banking licence after acquiring the open-banking startup Mono (Tech in Naija, 2026). These upgrades are reported in trade press rather than confirmed in CBN releases I could open, so treat the specifics as reported, not verified — but the direction is consistent with the regulator's own actions.

**The legislative backstop (SB. 959, passed by the Senate at third reading, 10 November 2026).** The bill amends BOFIA 2020 to let the CBN designate large fintechs and other non-bank financial institutions as Systemically Important Institutions, subject to enhanced supervision of governance, cybersecurity, technology risk, stress testing and supervisory access to systems (ThisDay, 2026). It still needs House concurrence and presidential assent, so it is not yet law. Its importance is as a credible forward signal: the largest firms are already investing as if bank-like supervision is coming.

## 2. How competition is changing

**Two-sided, not one-directional.** The caps are genuinely pro-competition at the merchant-acquiring layer: dominant groups withdrawing from one side create space for smaller acquirers and for banks re-entering merchant acquiring, and monthly market-share returns make every operator's position visible, removing the ability to manage share quietly (Launch Base Africa, 2026). But agent exclusivity pulls in the opposite direction in the short term, because it strengthens the leaders with the most reliable networks and the deepest agent relationships, and raises switching costs for agents who can no longer hedge (CryptoCompass, 2026). The net effect depends on how the CBN enforces the 31 December 2026 deadline — whether groups divest, throttle issuance, or manage around the caps.

**The moat moved from network effects to governance.** For years fintechs differentiated themselves by building products that were faster and simpler than banks'; the CBN now expects them to operate "less like technology startups and more like mature financial institutions" (Adegbite, 2026). Under the new AML framework, compliance is assessed on governance, integration, explainability and demonstrable effectiveness — not on owning the right software. That favours incumbents with compliance teams, internal audit functions and enterprise systems, and it raises the fixed cost of competing. A small fintech can still build a better checkout flow; it can no longer compete while treating compliance as an afterthought, because the regulator has shown it will halt onboarding and freeze approvals.

**The middle is being squeezed.** At the top, the largest groups must split, restructure or divest by 31 December 2026. At the bottom, smaller fintechs face the opposite pressure: they cannot afford the compliance fixed costs, so they are pushed toward acquisition by a larger group, a partnership as a technology provider to a licensed institution, or exit. The middle is being squeezed out. This is consistent with the pattern already visible in 2026: licence accumulation is not stopping, but the ring-fencing rules make running those licences as one integrated business "significantly more expensive", because each subsidiary must maintain its own governance, capital, risk framework and regulatory accountability (Adegbite, 2026).

**Banks may regain ground they lost.** The reporting notes that international payment networks and banks that have been losing ground to agile fintechs may see an opportunity to regain share in acquiring or issuing as dominant fintech groups are forced to withdraw from one side (Launch Base Africa, 2026). Tier-one banks such as GTCO and Access Holdings run large card-issuing programmes alongside merchant acquiring of their own, so they are not exempt — but their arms are already more separable, and they have decades of compliance infrastructure. The irony is that a reform intended to curb concentration may hand share back to the older concentrated incumbents, simply shuffling concentration from one set of hands to another.

## 3. How innovation is changing

**Compliance infrastructure is up; open banking is stalled.** 2026 is, in TechPoint Africa's phrase, "an enforcement year": more than a dozen CBN policy changes from 2025 come due simultaneously — open banking, AML automation, APP fraud rules and cash-policy changes (TechPoint Africa, 2026). The concrete items: a March 2026 AML directive requiring real-time transaction monitoring; the National Payment Stack launched in November 2025 on ISO 20022 standards, with banks given 18 months and fintechs 24 months to migrate; and a revised cash policy in effect from 1 January 2026.

The missing piece is open banking. The CBN issued Africa's first open-banking framework in February 2021 and operational guidelines in March 2023; the August 2025 commercial launch was missed, and the CBN's February 2026 policy report committed to a phased rollout through mid-2026. As of early November 2026, no nationwide go-live could be confirmed from official or industry sources (FlyingEze, 2026; BusinessDay, 2026). A second Regulatory Sandbox cohort in 2026 includes a Data-Enabled Financial Services track — permission-based data sharing, account aggregation, payment initiation, credit analytics — but sandbox admission is not a production rollout.

This matters because open banking is the rail on which embedded finance — and therefore credit for the ~74 million unbanked or underserved adults — was supposed to run. EFInA's Access to Finance 2026 survey puts formal inclusion at 73%, but only ~10% of adults access formal credit (EFInA, 2026). The innovation that would close that gap (consent-based data sharing powering credit scoring inside non-bank apps) is ready in regulation but not in production; meanwhile the innovation that *is* happening is compliance infrastructure — regtech, real-time AML, ISO 20022 migration, localisation — which incumbents can afford and startups cannot easily. Fintech still attracted 41% of the $1.37 billion raised by African startups in H1 2026, so capital has not fled; it is being redirected toward licensed, compliant scale.

**The agent-channel innovation is being channelled into formal rails.** Geo-fencing of terminals, dedicated agent wallets and NIBSS reporting push innovation toward verifiable agent identity, device management and liquidity management (helping agents manage float under a daily cap) rather than toward signing up unregistered agents as fast as possible. The caps also create a genuine product opportunity: tools that let agents and their customers split large transactions across days, route high-value payments electronically instead of in cash, or pre-position cash efficiently. The risk, flagged in the reporting, is that fragmentation of agent networks slows financial inclusion in rural areas where agents are the only banking infrastructure (Launch Base Africa, 2026; CryptoCompass, 2026).

## 4. Net assessment and what to watch

The CBN has chosen stability and traceability over speed. Competition is more contestable at the merchant-acquiring layer, more concentrated at the top, and more fiercely contested for agents. Innovation has moved from distribution and growth hacking to regulated infrastructure. The honest summary: whether that choice pays for consumers depends on two dates — 31 December 2026 (do the caps actually force divestments, or are they negotiated away?) and the still-unconfirmed open-banking go-live.

Three uncertainties matter. First, the June 2026 circular's key definitions — how market share is calculated across wallets, cards, POS terminals and online gateways, and what counts as a "group of related entities" — were still being interpreted by industry lawyers in June, so the precise bite of the caps will only be clear from the CBN's own market-share returns (Launch Base Africa, 2026). Second, SB. 959 is not law yet; its final form may change in the House or at assent (ThisDay, 2026). Third, the CBN has previously adjusted caps and deadlines under industry pressure, so the December 2026 deadline should be treated as the stated position, not a guaranteed outcome. The direction of travel, however, is unambiguous: Nigeria's payments market is being deliberately moved from founder-led scale to regulator-measured structure, and the winners will be those who can be both innovative and auditable at the same time.

This answer isolates the specific mechanism behind the market-structure cap — a "cliff" rather than a slope, where the marginal point of market share can be worth less than zero because it triggers a forced divestiture — and uses that to predict threshold-gaming behaviour (volume reclassification, merchant shifting to partner acquirers) as much as genuine divestment. ## Short answer

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tighter licensing and supervision of fintechs is doing something the rest of this debate has missed: it is not only disciplining private payments firms, it is building a state-sponsored alternative to them. The CBN's domestic card scheme, AfriGO, launched with the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) in 2023, had issued over one million cards and processed more than N70 billion in transactions in 2025, and the country's largest fintechs - Moniepoint and PalmPay - plan to distribute over 10 million AfriGO debit cards (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). The licensing squeeze on payment service banks, switching companies and agent networks is the stick; AfriGO, plus a reported government plan to eliminate transfer fees on the NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP) platform, is the rail the traffic is being steered onto. Competition is therefore shifting from fintech-versus-bank to private-rails-versus-state-rails, and innovation is shifting from building on Visa, Mastercard and Verve rails to building on a domestic scheme whose economics the regulator itself sets.

## What this Answer adds

No previous answer in this thread mentions AfriGO at all. The earlier answers cover the June 2026 market-structure caps, the October 2025 agent-banking guidelines, the cash-out caps, the microfinance-bank licence revocations and the open-banking delay in depth. None of them addresses the CBN's own card scheme, its scale, its fintech distribution partnerships, or the planned elimination of NIP transfer fees. This answer adds that channel: the scheme-level competition the regulator has entered as a participant, not just a referee, and what it means for switching companies, international schemes and fintech distributors.

## 1. AfriGO: the regulator as a market participant

AfriGO was launched in 2023 by the CBN in collaboration with NIBSS as Nigeria's first domestic card scheme, aimed at localising transaction processing, cutting costs and keeping Nigerian payment data inside the country (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). By September 2025, NIBSS managing director Premier Oiwoh disclosed that more than one million AfriGO cards had been issued and that the scheme had processed over N70 billion in transactions in 2025 (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). That scale is still small - the same report puts Nigeria's cards and payments market at $22 billion - but the direction and the distribution behind it are what matter for competition.

The mechanism that makes AfriGO different from a private scheme is settlement. Oiwoh states that AfriGO is the only card globally that enables instant credit to merchants on point-of-sale (POS) transactions, and that this feature is driving its acceptance among merchants (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). Instant merchant settlement attacks the exact pain point - delayed settlement and float costs - that independent switching and acquiring firms monetise. If the domestic scheme settles merchants instantly while private rails settle on a delay, merchants have a direct economic reason to prefer it, and the switching companies that intermediate settlement lose pricing power without any new regulation being written against them.

## 2. The fintechs become distributors of the state scheme

AfriGO's distribution partnerships run through the very firms the licensing tightening constrains: Moniepoint, PalmPay, OPay and Flutterwave (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). Moniepoint and PalmPay plan to distribute over 10 million AfriGO debit cards nationwide and roll out tap-to-pay solutions (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). Moniepoint's chief executive, Tosin Eniolorunda, described the Moniepoint/AfriGO card in April as a tool to extend reach "particularly to those traditionally excluded from the formal financial system" (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025).

This changes the competitive logic for the big fintechs. Under the licensing regime described in earlier answers, a fintech's growth path was to accumulate licences, terminals and agents; under the AfriGO channel, its growth path is to distribute a regulator-owned product. The two paths are not the same business: distributing AfriGO cards earns the fintech distribution and acquiring volume, but the scheme economics - interchange, data and the merchant relationship - sit with the domestic scheme rather than with the fintech's own rails. The June 2026 market-structure caps push the largest firms out of dominating both issuing and acquiring; AfriGO gives them somewhere compliant to put their issuing scale. That is a plausible reason the biggest operators have embraced the scheme rather than resisting it, though the partnership announcements themselves do not state motives, and this reading should be treated as inference, not as a reported fact.

## 3. The fee floor is being removed underneath private rails

The same report states that the Federal Government plans to eliminate transfer fees on the NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP) platform, a move NIBSS presents as part of accelerating the shift from cash to digital payments (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). This is a reported plan, not a completed reform: as of the September 2025 report it had not yet taken effect, and no completion date is given. If it happens, it removes the per-transfer revenue that funded free peer-to-peer transfers and subsidised agent economics, and it makes the state-operated instant-payment rail free at the point of use while private switches and aggregators still charge. Combined with AfriGO's instant POS settlement, the effect is a two-sided squeeze on private rails: cheaper to use the state rail for transfers, faster to settle on the state scheme for card payments.

## 4. Identity and the central bank digital currency extend the same logic

The National Identity Management Commission's (NIMC) multipurpose ID card will incorporate the AfriGO payment rail, so that, in Oiwoh's account, millions of Nigerians can access financial services directly through their national ID (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). NIMC has launched a General Multipurpose Card with built-in payment functionality, biometric authentication and integration with government social intervention programmes (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). AfriGO is also designed to integrate with the e-Naira, Nigeria's central bank digital currency (AfriGOpay Financial Services Ltd., 2025). The direction is consistent: identity, card payments and central bank money converging on one domestic stack, supervised and partly operated by the state, rather than on competing private stacks.

## 5. Why the CBN is building its own rails now

The context is the agent network the tightening is trying to discipline. Nigeria has over 2 million active POS terminals as of 2025, up from fewer than 350,000 in 2019, according to the Shared Agent Network Expansion Facility (TechNext, 2025). A 2023 EFInA study found 36 per cent of adults used a POS agent for deposits or withdrawals in the previous year, while about 80 per cent of retail payments under N5,000 were still made in cash as of mid-2025 (TechNext, 2025). Fraud attempts via agent channels jumped from N9 billion in 2021 to over N22 billion in 2023, much of it linked to weak oversight and cash-handling loopholes, according to NIBSS data cited by TechNext (TechNext, 2025). The October 2025 agent-banking guidelines reaffirmed the N1.2 million daily cash-out cap per agent and the N100,000 daily and N500,000 weekly limits per customer (TechNext, 2025).

Read together, the logic is: the agent channel is too large and too fraud-prone to supervise into safety by licensing alone, and too cash-dependent to be wished away, so the regulator is capping its cash throughput while building electronic rails - AfriGO cards, free NIP transfers, ID-linked payments - that make the capped channel less necessary. The caps and the scheme are two halves of one policy, but only the caps have been debated in this thread.

## 6. What changes for competition and innovation

For switching companies, AfriGO is a competitor with regulatory tailwind: Interswitch's Verve and the international schemes now face a domestic scheme whose issuer base includes the largest fintech distributors and whose merchant proposition is instant settlement. For the international schemes, the threat is partial - AfriGO is domestic-only, so cross-border and online international payments still need Visa and Mastercard - but domestic POS volume, the largest card segment, is contestable. For fintechs, innovation shifts toward scheme-level features on AfriGO rails: tap-to-pay, contactless issuance and instant settlement products, rather than proprietary wallet and switching features. For agent networks, the combined effect of cash-out caps and free electronic rails is a slow erosion of the cash-out business model that made agent banking profitable: each capped, traceable, electronic transaction is one fewer cash-out fee.

Uncertainty is real and should be stated plainly. AfriGO's reported scale - over one million cards and over N70 billion in 2025 transactions - is modest against a $22 billion cards market and against the N1.2 quadrillion in electronic transactions reported for 2025 in earlier answers; whether it displaces Verve, Visa or Mastercard domestically is unproven. The 10 million cards from Moniepoint and PalmPay are plans, not issued cards. The NIP fee elimination is a reported plan with no confirmed implementation date. The claim that AfriGO is the only card enabling instant POS credit is the NIBSS managing director's statement, not an independently verified comparison. And the inference that fintechs embrace AfriGO because the market-structure caps leave them nowhere else to put issuing scale is my reasoning, not a reported motive. What is established is the direction: the CBN is no longer only licensing and supervising Nigerian payments; it is operating a growing piece of the infrastructure itself, and that changes who competes with whom.

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tightening is changing Nigerian payments through three mechanisms that the licensing rules alone do not capture: public enforcement that reprices the cost of the old growth model, the CBN entering the market as a competitor through its own card scheme, and a published reform programme that trades today's tightening for a supervisory-technology regime. The June 2026 market-structure caps and the agent-exclusivity rules set the frame; enforcement, state-sponsored competition, and the CBN's own roadmap decide who wins inside it.

## 1. Enforcement, not just rule-writing, is now the competitive filter

The clearest evidence is OPay, Nigeria's largest mobile money operator. Its audited financial statements disclose approximately ₦994 million in regulatory fines incurred between 2023 and 2025, imposed by the CBN, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria, and the Corporate Affairs Commission (ThisDay, 2026). The breakdown is specific: ₦26 million to the CBN in 2023 and ₦113.7 million in 2024 for money-laundering and terrorism-financing compliance violations, ₦197 million for violations of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020, ₦10 million for customer due diligence failures, ₦2 million for consumer protection breaches, ₦125 million from the NDPC under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, and ₦464 million paid to the CBN in 2025 for breaching the Framework for Mobile Money Services in Nigeria 2021 (ThisDay, 2026). A separate TechCabal report records a ₦1 billion CBN fine in the second quarter of 2024 after a routine sector audit (TechCabal, 2026); the two reports' totals do not reconcile exactly, so the precise cumulative figure should be treated as approximately ₦1 billion rather than exact.

Fines were the mildest tool. In April 2024 the CBN barred OPay from opening accounts for new customers for six weeks, forcing it to block peer-to-peer crypto transfers, verify physical addresses across all account tiers, and upgrade facial verification (TechCabal, 2026). In August 2025 a CBN circular ordered every point-of-sale terminal geo-tagged within 60 days and locked to within 10 metres of the merchant's registered address, while daily cash-outs were capped at ₦1.2 million per agent and ₦100,000 per individual customer (TechCabal, 2026). The mechanism matters: each intervention raised the fixed cost of the exact model — light-KYC onboarding plus a sprawling agent network — on which the big fintechs had built scale. Compliance stopped being a back-office function and became a determinant of whether a firm could grow at all.

The competitive consequence is visible in OPay's own pivot. Its October 2026 IPO filing showed first-half 2026 revenue of $467.1 million, up 136.5%, and net income of $90.9 million — but lending, at $236.1 million, had overtaken payments as its largest business, and Nigeria supplied 89.5% of revenue (TechCabal, 2026). Lending is possible only because OPay acquired a microfinance bank licence; a mobile money licence does not permit it (TechCabal, 2026). The tightening therefore pushes the largest fintechs in a specific direction: payments become a regulated, low-margin distribution layer, while profit migrates to licensed lending. Then, on 30 October 2026, OPay withdrew its planned $304 million New York listing — targeting a roughly $4 billion valuation — one day after signing the underwriting agreement, following a regulatory inquiry in an undisclosed foreign jurisdiction (ThisDay, 2026; TechCabal, 2026). Regulatory credibility, not user numbers, became the binding constraint on accessing global capital.

## 2. The CBN is also competing directly, through AfriGo

A second, overlooked shift is that the regulator is a market participant. AfriGo, the domestic card scheme launched by the CBN with the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) on 26 January 2023, is operated by Afrigopay Financial Services Limited and processes domestic transactions in naira, with payment data kept in Nigeria (Pryme, 2026). NIBSS reported more than one million AfriGo cards issued and over ₦70 billion in AfriGo transactions by September 2025, with Moniepoint, PalmPay, OPay, and Flutterwave named as fintech partners and more than 10 million debit cards planned with Moniepoint and PalmPay (Pryme, 2026). NIBSS's managing director has described AfriGo as the only card scheme giving merchants instant credit on point-of-sale transactions (Pryme, 2026).

This changes competition in card payments in a way licensing rules do not. The CBN's stated reasons for AfriGo were financial inclusion, reducing foreign exchange spent on domestic card transactions, lowering card costs by pricing in naira, and data sovereignty (Pryme, 2026). But the scheme's weakness is equally informative: in interviews with traders in Ilorin, Ikorodu, and Ilobu, none of those asked had heard of AfriGo (Pryme, 2026). And when Google Pay launched in Nigeria in October 2026, Verve, AfriGo, and cards issued by OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, and PalmPay were all absent on day one — only Mastercard and Visa cards from four banks worked (TechTimes, 2026). Innovation at the acceptance layer is therefore gated less by technology than by scheme politics: the domestic schemes that handle the majority of Nigerian card transactions were excluded from the first global wallet launch, while the CBN's own scheme remains small despite state backing. Contactless penetration sits at roughly 0.1% of all transactions (TechTimes, 2026), so the frontier of card innovation is terminal hardware, not consumer apps — and the CBN's 2023 contactless circular caps no-verification taps at ₦15,000 per transaction and ₦50,000 daily (TechTimes, 2026).

## 3. The CBN's published endgame: tightening as a bridge to SupTech

The third mechanism is the CBN's own Fintech Strategy Report, published 2 February 2025 — the first wholesale regulatory review of the sector since the Payment Systems Vision 2025 (Legal 500, 2026). Its priority reforms show where the tightening leads. A Single Regulatory Window for licensing and supervision is to be delivered through a shared digital portal, the Smart Licensing and Supervisory Gateway, embedding Supervisory Technology capabilities, standardised digital forms, workflow tracking, and real-time dashboards (Legal 500, 2026). The sandbox is to expand into "Sandbox 2.0," covering artificial intelligence, embedded finance, and cross-border payments, with learnings codified into proportionate rules (Legal 500, 2026). Most consequentially for competition, the CBN is assessing a consolidated digital-bank licence rather than stretching Payment Service Bank permissions, and is considering revising PSB lending rules — the exact restriction that currently forces fintechs to buy microfinance bank licences to lend (Legal 500, 2026).

Two further proposals reshape the innovation landscape directly. A Fintech Credit Guarantee Window, a blended-finance mechanism run with development finance partners, would de-risk fintech lending portfolios (Legal 500, 2026). And a Compliance as a Service model, plus a Shared Fraud Defence Framework with near-real-time fraud intelligence sharing and a central repository of fraudulent accounts, would turn compliance from a private fixed cost into shared infrastructure (Legal 500, 2026). The CBN is also considering a hybrid payments infrastructure model that keeps core clearing and settlement central while certified private operators build service and innovation layers through open APIs (Legal 500, 2026). The direction is clear: today's tightening raises entry costs, but the planned end-state lowers them again for firms that plug into shared supervisory utilities — favouring operators that can integrate with the CBN's infrastructure over those that built proprietary workarounds.

## 4. Scale check: the market is not shrinking, it is being redistributed

None of this has reduced payment volumes. NIBSS processed approximately 11.2 billion transactions worth roughly ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2026 alone (TechTimes, 2026). The tightening is therefore not a contraction of Nigerian payments but a redistribution of who captures value within a still-growing system: from agent-network arbitrage and light-KYC acquisition toward licensed lending, shared compliance infrastructure, and state-backed rails. The losers are small operators that cannot absorb compliance fixed costs or the agent-network caps; the winners are large incumbents that can fund compliance departments, buy banking licences, and integrate with the CBN's emerging SupTech stack — plus the CBN itself, which now competes in card schemes through AfriGo while writing the rules for everyone else. The open question is whether the promised Single Regulatory Window and digital-bank licence arrive fast enough to reopen entry, or whether the 2025–2026 tightening hardens into a permanently concentrated market.

No previous answer discusses AfriGo at all — its NIBSS-reported scale, its planned 10-million-card issuance with Moniepoint and PalmPay, its instant merchant settlement, or its exclusion from the October 2026 Google Pay launch. And no previous answer examines the CBN's February 2025 Fintech Strategy Report — the Single Regulatory Window, the Smart Licensing and Supervisory Gateway, the consolidated digital-bank licence, the Fintech Credit Guarantee Window, Compliance as a Service, or the hybrid infrastructure model. Financial inclusion gains from the agent boom are under strain from cash-out caps and single-principal rules. ## Short answer

As of November 2026 the CBN's fintech tightening is best understood not as "harder licensing" but as a deliberate re-layering of who may *hold* money, who may *touch* the consumer, and who may *route* the transaction. Three separations do that work: the 15 June 2026 market-structure circular breaks the issuing↔acquiring loop; the 6 October 2025 agent-banking framework breaks the multi-principal kiosk; and a quieter, older rule — the December 2023 NIBSS directive delisting switches, PSSPs and super-agents as NIP beneficiaries — keeps every non-bank fintech dependent on a bank to receive money. Competition is consolidating *upward* into licensed, bank-adjacent groups while being forcibly opened *laterally* in merchant acquiring. Innovation is shifting from distribution to settlement plumbing, and the most contested frontier in 2026 turned out to be switching economics, not wallets — as the May 2026 Verve–Interswitch routing dispute shows.

## 1. What the circular actually says (primary text, not trade-press paraphrase)

Much public discussion cites secondary summaries. The instrument itself is Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, dated 15 June 2026, addressed to DMBs, MFBs, MMOs, switching and processing companies, PTSPs, PSSPs, super-agents and other licensed operators (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2026). Its operative market-structure text states that a licensed institution engaged in consumer issuing, "whether individually or part of a group of related entities," holding more than 25% market share in consumer issuing "within any rolling twelve-month period" shall not hold more than 15% market share in merchant acquiring "during the same period," and the reciprocal applies to acquiring-dominant institutions (CBN, 2026). Three details matter more than the headline:

- **The measurement basis is a rolling 12-month period, not a point-in-time snapshot.** A group cannot pass the test by shrinking below the threshold in December and re-concentrating in January; the breach is defined over a moving window.
- **"Group of related entities" is explicit in the operative clause**, so corporate re-arrangement alone does not relieve the constraint — the test attaches to the economic group.
- **Monthly market-share returns are mandatory** under prescribed templates, and full compliance is required "not later than December 31, 2026" (CBN, 2026). Data localisation for payments transaction data generated in Nigeria becomes mandatory on 1 January 2027, one day later (CBN, 2026).

The mechanism is not a price control but a **forced separation of two network effects that reinforce each other**. In an integrated issuer-acquirer, every additional wallet holder makes the merchant network more valuable and every additional merchant makes the wallet stickier; that is a genuine two-sided network, not a cosmetic bundle. Capping the cross-holding at 15% attacks the *joint* optimisation directly: a group at the issuing ceiling must price acquiring to lose share, which is the opposite of what a two-sided platform wants. That is why this bites harder than a capital increase — capital can be raised, but a network effect cannot be.

## 2. The older rule nobody cites: non-banks cannot be NIP beneficiaries

This is the structural fact that determines how much of the above actually reaches fintechs. Since a December 2023 NIBSS directive, only deposit-taking institutions — deposit money banks, merchant banks, payment service banks, microfinance banks, mortgage banks and mobile money operators — may be listed as beneficiary institutions on the NIP outward transfer channel; switching companies, PSSPs and super-agents were delisted, on the basis that those licence categories are not authorised to hold customer funds (PaymentBrief, 2026, checked 24 August 2026). The practical consequence is that a fully licensed PSSP or switch cannot simply plug into NIP and receive a transfer as itself; it must route outward flows through a sponsor or settlement bank that sits as beneficiary of record, and any such collaboration with a bank requires prior CBN approval before go-live (PaymentBrief, 2026).

Read together with the June 2026 circular, this produces an asymmetry that the simple "crackdown vs. liberalisation" framing misses:

- **MMOs and PSBs** already sit on the deposit-taking side, so tighter rules *favour* them relative to non-bank fintechs, because the bank partnership a PSSP must negotiate is for them an internal function.
- **Pure switches and PSSPs** face a double squeeze — they cannot be the beneficiary of record themselves, and the June circular's data-localisation and UBO-disclosure obligations add fixed compliance cost to a business whose revenue is a per-transaction margin.
- **The result is a licence-ladder ratchet.** The rational move for a large fintech is upward (to MMO, microfinance bank, or PSB) rather than sideways into new products, which is the consolidation pattern actually observed.

## 3. Switching is where the competition fight actually moved

The most informative 2026 event in Nigerian payments is not a wallet launch but a routing dispute. On 28 May 2026 a coalition of CBN-licensed payment processors, acquirers and switches wrote to Verve International and Interswitch threatening to suspend acceptance of Verve card transactions within two days, alleging that a Verve policy titled "Transaction Routing Integrity and Prohibition of Network Bypass" reinforced exclusive routing through Interswitch, that switching exclusivity had persisted "for over 10 years," that the arrangement abused a dominant position, and that Verve's restructured acquirer scheme fee — 0.1000620% plus a flat ₦5, uncapped, introduced 1 April 2025 — exceeded the regulated ceiling of a fraction of 7.5% of 0.5% of transaction value, capped at ₦75 per transaction (Nairametrics, 2026). Interswitch's response, via senior sources, was that the routing rules guard against processors bypassing its network in ways that create untraceable fraudulent transactions, and that the CBN had summoned all parties to a meeting (Nairametrics, 2026).

The economics explain why this is the live battleground. Merchant service charge is regulated and thin; scheme and switching fees are the residual margin. An uncapped percentage-plus-flat fee is regressive at the low end — a ₦5 flat component on a small-ticket POS transaction consumes a far larger share of the acquirer's regulated MSC than on a large one, so it lands hardest on exactly the agent and small-merchant segment that the agent-banking rules are simultaneously re-pricing. That is a *second* margin compression on the same last-mile operator, arriving from the scheme layer rather than the licensing layer.

Evidential status, explicitly: the fee figures and the exclusivity allegation come from the coalition's letter as reported by Nairametrics, and Interswitch's position from unnamed senior sources. **This is a contested commercial dispute, not an adjudicated finding** — the CBN had convened the parties but, on the reporting available, had issued no public determination. Treat the *existence and shape* of the dispute as well-evidenced and the *merits* as unresolved.

## 4. PSBs, switches and agents specifically

**Payment service banks.** PSBs remain the inclusion vehicle hardest to make pay: they can take deposits but not lend, so economics rest on transaction fees and yield on sovereign securities rather than credit margin, and the ₦5 billion minimum capital sits well above the ₦2 billion MMO and switching tiers (PaymentBrief, 2026). The June circular creates no new PSB rule, but it raises the strategic value of the licence: a PSB is already on the deposit-taking side of the NIP beneficiary line, so it can offer the settlement role that non-bank partners must negotiate. One would therefore expect PSB capacity — and licensing interest — to rise even as standalone PSB profitability stays weak. That is an inference from rule structure, not an observed trend, and I flag it as such.

**Switching companies.** There are 19 Switching and Processing licensees in CBN's August 2026 listing, against 17 MMOs, 108 PSSPs, 47 PTSPs, 61 super-agents, 8 card/payment schemes and a single Payments Service Holding Company (PaymentBrief, 2026). The switching layer is already thin relative to the gateway layer above it, and it is the layer most exposed to the routing and fee disputes above. Consolidation among switches is the plausible direction; that is a projection, and I would not put a probability on it from the evidence I could open.

**Agent networks.** The 1 April 2026 single-principal rule converted agents from a shared resource into an exclusive one, and the competitive effect is subtle: because an agent can no longer keep a second terminal as fallback, the principal's *uptime* becomes the agent's entire business continuity, so agent recruitment competition shifts from commission levels to settlement reliability and dispute-resolution speed. Third-party migration reporting from early 2026 (e.g., Condia's March 2026 account of OPay device returns in Ekiti as the deadline approached) is directionally consistent, but that article is paywalled beyond its opening section and I could not read its underlying figures, so I cite it as reported context only, not as evidence of magnitude.

## 5. What this does to innovation

The *direction* is well-evidenced; the *magnitude* is not. Direction: fixed compliance obligations — monthly market-share returns, UBO disclosure, in-country data storage from 1 January 2027, real-time AML monitoring, ISO 20022 migration — are costs that scale with the institution rather than the transaction, which structurally advantages balance-sheet-strong players and re-routes engineering effort toward reporting, reconciliation and data residency. The NPS migration shows both ambition and gap: NIBSS's ISO 20022 National Payment Stack had processed 26.55 million transactions worth ₦1.4 trillion across 48 participating institutions by 11 August 2026 — real adoption, but still a small fraction of NIP's volume, so NIP remains the rail to build against in production (PaymentBrief, 2026).

What I could not find is a published, dated measurement separating the effect of these rules from Nigeria's macro conditions on fintech product launches, funding, or new-entrant counts. Claims that innovation fell or rose *because of* the 2026 rules are, on the evidence I could open, inference rather than measurement. Any specific percentage change should be met with a request for its denominator.

## 6. Net assessment

1. **Competition is being re-cut, not reduced.** Merchant acquiring is genuinely more contestable after 31 December 2026, because issuing-dominant groups must actively shed acquiring share. Consumer issuing and the settlement layer are more concentrated, because the NIP beneficiary rule and fixed compliance costs push participants up the licence ladder.
2. **The decisive uncertainty is enforcement, not text.** The operative clauses are unambiguous, but the circular is silent on the remedy for non-compliance beyond "supervisory sanctions in accordance with applicable laws" (CBN, 2026). Whether 31 December 2026 produces real divestment or negotiated forbearance is the largest unknown; I would not assign it better than even odds in either direction without seeing the first tranche of monthly market-share returns.
3. **The switching dispute is the leading indicator.** If routing exclusivity is resolved in favour of open routing and a fee structure inside the ₦75-equivalent ceiling, the circular's pro-competition intent reaches down to the agent's margin. If it is settled quietly in favour of the incumbent scheme, structural caps at the top will not translate into lower costs at the last mile.

The Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tightening is usually described through its most visible instruments: the June 2026 market-share caps, the single-principal agent rule, and the March 2026 automated anti-money-laundering (AML) standards. Earlier answers in this thread document those well. But they are not where competition is actually being decided. Three quieter layers decide who can compete and what innovation is now for: who owns the payment rails, who pays when a customer is defrauded, and who owns the card scheme. On all three, the state and its bank-owned infrastructure are moving from referee to participant, and the commercial contest is being pushed into narrower, more expensive lanes.

1. Switching companies: from rail owners to tenants

The decisive fact about switching in 2026 is not the N2 billion capital bar. It is that a switching licence no longer buys a place in the settlement chain. In a 5 December 2023 circular, the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) directed banks to delist switching companies, payment solution service providers (PSSPs) and super agents from their NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP) outward transfer lists, because listing non-deposit-taking institutions as beneficiaries contravened CBN guidelines on electronic payments. Switches, PSSPs and super agents may process outward transfers as inflows to banks, but they are not to receive inflows, because their licences do not permit them to hold customer funds (Nigeria CommunicationsWeek, 2023).

That makes banks the gatekeepers of the switching business. A switch routes; a bank settles. Independent switches cannot monetise the float or the beneficiary relationship, and every switch must negotiate access through a deposit-taking institution that is also, in many cases, a competitor in acquiring or issuing.

The second half is the rebuild of the rails. NIBSS unveiled the National Payment Stack (NPS) in June 2025 as the successor to the 15-year-old NIP rail, built on ISO 20022 messaging and Transactility's jPTS switch, which runs on the open-source jPOS framework. By August 2026 NPS had processed 26.55 million transactions worth N1.4 trillion across 48 participating institutions, and by 28 September 2026 it had passed 100 million transactions. NIBSS says it is preparing to decommission NIP, but has published no switch-off date, so banks and fintechs must integrate with NPS separately while both rails run side by side. First Bank leads NPS transaction volume and Fidelity Bank leads on value; Moniepoint is among the early adopters (NIBSS, 2026; Fincra, 2026).

For competition, this fixed-cost migration favours scale twice over: every switch and PSSP must fund a second integration with no published cut-over date, and the rail they are migrating to is owned by NIBSS, a company owned by the CBN and the banks. The most valuable infrastructure in Nigerian payments is therefore not contestable at all; the contest is over who gets on it first and cheapest. Innovation in switching shifts from building proprietary rails to building on the national rail, using ISO 20022's richer data for reconciliation, request-to-pay invoicing and phone-number-addressed payments.

2. Payment service banks and the card-scheme layer: AfriGO

The June 2026 caps measure "consumer issuing", and issuing in Nigeria mostly means cards and wallets. What earlier answers do not discuss is that the largest fintechs are now issuing on a card scheme the regulator itself owns. AfriGO, the domestic card scheme launched by the CBN with NIBSS on 26 January 2023 and operated by AfrigoPay Financial Services Limited, a NIBSS subsidiary, was created to deepen inclusion, cut foreign exchange spent on domestic card transactions, price card costs in naira, and keep domestic payment data in Nigeria. By September 2025 NIBSS reported more than one million AfriGO cards issued and over N70 billion in transactions; 25 banks were issuing, and planned issuance with Moniepoint and PalmPay exceeded ten million cards. NIBSS names Moniepoint, PalmPay, OPay and Flutterwave as fintech partners; AfriGO is accepted at more than 16,000 ATMs and 70 percent of POS terminals, and is planned for the National Identity Management Commission's General Multipurpose Card (NIBSS, 2026; AfriGO, 2023).

That changes what the issuing cap means: the cap constrains how much of the issuing market any group may hold, but the scheme carrying a growing share of that issuing is state-owned, naira-priced and data-sovereign by design. Private schemes, Verve, Visa and Mastercard, now compete against a scheme whose owner also writes the market-structure rules and the 1 January 2027 data-localisation deadline. For fintechs, issuing AfriGO cards is both a compliance-friendly growth lever and a form of dependence: the more of their issuing sits on the domestic scheme, the more their economics track CBN scheme policy rather than a negotiated commercial interchange.

For payment service banks (PSBs) specifically, AfriGO is one of the few growth levers left. PSBs remain barred from lending and from foreign exchange, and must deploy at least 75 percent of deposit liabilities in government securities or with banks, so they cannot cross-subsidise onboarding with credit margins and must live on transaction fees and sovereign yields. Issuing on the domestic scheme, and distributing through agent networks, is how a PSB grows without a lending book.

3. Agent networks and the liability layer: authorised push payment fraud

The third quiet layer is who pays when a customer is tricked into authorising a payment. On 26 November 2025 the CBN published an exposure draft of Guidelines for Handling Authorised Push Payment (APP) Fraud for public comment. As drafted, a customer deceived into authorising a payment who reports within 72 hours, cooperates and was not negligent is eligible for reimbursement; the bank must acknowledge within 24 hours, conclude its investigation within 14 working days, and pay any refund within 48 hours of closing the case. Where several institutions are involved, the originating institution must notify the others within 30 minutes, and reimbursement must be completed within 16 working days of the first report. Where no institution is at fault, the cost is shared equally; where an institution failed to flag or freeze a suspicious transaction because its systems were inadequate, it bears the full cost. Every institution must adopt a board-approved APP fraud policy and deploy an early warning system with behavioural analytics, and the CBN may direct NIBSS to withhold or reverse settlement (TechCabal, 2025; BusinessDay, 2026).

One qualification matters: this was a draft for consultation, and as of November 2026 I could not confirm that the final guidelines are in force or from what date. The mechanism should therefore be read as proposed, not as law. But the direction is unambiguous, and firms are already building to it, because the March 2026 automated AML standards already require real-time monitoring and the draft simply prices failure.

The competition effect is a second compliance moat, but one that bites per incident rather than once at licensing. A licence fee is paid once; a missed fraud flag is paid in full, every time, at the value of the transaction. Institutions with real-time detection and strong know-your-customer (KYC) controls pay less; institutions that grew by onboarding fast and loose pay full value on every detection failure. For agent networks this matters directly: APP fraud ends in a transfer to an account or wallet, often one reached through an agent. Principals already must report agent transactions daily to NIBSS and the CBN and monitor agents' BVN-linked accounts, and the draft rules make the originating institution coordinate the response and bear the cost if its systems failed. Fraud-loss provisioning becomes a cost line in agent acquiring, and small principals with thin detection will either absorb more losses or tighten agent onboarding further, shrinking the network at the margin. Innovation follows the liability: the fastest-growing product category is fraud infrastructure, early warning systems, behavioural analytics and mule-account detection, built or bought as a liability shield, not a differentiator.

4. Why the deadlines matter more than the rules

All of this is subject to one condition: enforcement. The caps bite on 31 December 2026, data localisation on 1 January 2027, and the Senate passed Bill SB.959 on 10 November 2026, which would let the CBN designate large fintechs as Systemically Important Institutions, but the bill still needs House concurrence and presidential assent, the NPS cut-over has no published date, and the APP fraud guidelines are still in draft. The CBN has moved its own dates before: the agent geo-fencing radius was widened from 10 to 70 metres and enforcement moved to 1 August 2026. The market therefore discounts deadlines, and the competition effect of the caps depends on whether December brings divestments or extensions.

Net assessment

Competition in Nigerian payments is being re-sorted along three seams at once. At the commercial layer, the caps fragment the integrated super-app and force a choice between issuing and acquiring. At the infrastructure layer, power concentrates in NIBSS-owned rails and a state-owned card scheme that no private firm can contest. At the liability layer, fraud costs are being pushed onto institutions in proportion to the weakness of their detection, which rewards the firms that already invested in it. Innovation has not stopped; it has moved from consumer features to what the new regime prices, liability-grade fraud systems, ISO 20022 integration and domestic-scheme products, while innovation needing open banking or cheap distribution waits. The inclusion risk is sharper: the agent network that delivered inclusion is now squeezed by exclusivity, caps and fraud liability at once, and the remaining unbanked population is the one least able to absorb higher charges or tighter onboarding.

What this Answer adds

Earlier answers establish the caps, agent exclusivity, the AML standards and consolidation. This answer adds three mechanisms none of them develops: the 2023 NIBSS delisting that demoted switches, PSSPs and super agents from NIP beneficiaries to pure routers, and the National Payment Stack rebuild, with its August and September 2026 adoption milestones, making NIBSS-owned ISO 20022 infrastructure the uncontestable layer beneath the capped market; the AfriGO domestic card scheme's 2026 scale, more than one million cards, over N70 billion in transactions, 25 issuing banks and planned issuance above ten million cards with Moniepoint and PalmPay, which reframes the issuing cap as a constraint on the regulator's own scheme; and the full liability mechanism of the November 2025 APP fraud draft guidelines, the 72-hour, 14-day and 16-day timelines, the 30-minute interbank notification rule and the full-cost penalty for weak detection, its draft status honestly stated, as the channel carrying fraud costs to agent networks and redirecting innovation toward liability-grade detection.
