As of November 2026, three developments no previous answer on this question has covered change the picture of how Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) supervision is reshaping Nigerian payments. First, on 5 November 2026 the CBN brought stablecoins and virtual-asset payment services under a full licensing regime, extending the capital-barrier logic of the 2026 payments rules to the one channel that had escaped CBN licensing (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). Second, the telco-backed payment service banks (PSBs) have now published 2026 results: they are growing fast on thin economics, competing on price rather than distribution (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). Third, OPay priced a roughly $4 billion New York IPO on 29 October 2026 and abandoned it the next day after disclosing a regulatory inquiry, showing that regulatory risk now reprices even the largest and most profitable Nigerian fintech (Global Private Intelligence, 2026, https://gpi.4bin.ai/country/ng/fintechdisruption/). Previous answers documented the June 2026 market-share caps, the agent-exclusivity rules, automated anti-money-laundering (AML) standards and the Senate's systemically important institutions bill; this answer adds the newest licensing frontier, the first 2026 PSB financial results, and the capital-markets consequence of the supervisory reset.

## 1. A new licensing frontier: stablecoins and virtual-asset payments

The Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria, dated 5 November 2026, create five CBN approval routes for virtual-asset activity, and they matter for payments because they explicitly cover stablecoins used for payments, transfers, remittances, foreign-exchange conversion and settlement (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). A Class 1 licence for naira-referenced tokens requires at least ₦10 billion in paid-up capital; a Class 2 licence for foreign-currency-referenced tokens requires ₦15 billion and a Nigerian-incorporated entity; other virtual-asset service providers face a ₦1 billion bar (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). Issuers must hold eligible reserves on a one-to-one basis plus a 2% overcollateralisation buffer, give holders an enforceable right to redeem at par generally by the end of the business day after a valid request, and are barred from paying interest or yield to holders; algorithmic stablecoins are banned outright (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/; TechRegard, 2026, https://techregard.com/cbn-tightens-grip-on-crypto-bans-algorithmic-stablecoins-in-nigeria/).

The mechanism is the same one previous answers identified in the payments caps, applied to a new perimeter. Before November 2026, stablecoin peer-to-peer (P2P) desks and remittance channels operated without a dedicated CBN licensing framework; now platform-facilitated P2P transactions require express CBN approval, transfers of USD/EUR 1,000 or more trigger Financial Action Task Force Travel Rule information-sharing, and issuers must build freeze, burn and deny-list controls into token smart contracts (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). Existing operators must register within 30 days, begin supervisory reporting within 60 days and file a full licence application within 180 days; operating without approval carries a minimum fine of ₦100 million plus ₦1 million per day, and using reserves as leverage draws ₦250–500 million per breach (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/).

The competition effect is a sorting of the crypto-payments channel by balance sheet. Only firms able to post ₦10–15 billion can issue; smaller P2P desks must obtain approval or exit; and CBN-regulated institutions can seek approval to extend their permitted activities into virtual-asset payments, which hands an advantage to already-licensed banks and fintechs over crypto-native entrants (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). The innovation effect is equally direct: compliance is engineered into the product itself, since the token contract must be freezable and the transfer must carry identity data. That is the same shift previous answers described for AML automation, but now embedded at the asset layer rather than the monitoring layer. One boundary matters: the CBN regulates non-security virtual assets and payment activity while the Securities and Exchange Commission retains securities, and an SEC licence alone does not authorise payment services (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/).

## 2. Payment service banks: the gap previous answers left open, now filled by 2026 results

One verified answer on this question stated frankly that it found nothing 2026-specific on payment service banks. The 2026 half-year results now fill that gap, and they show a distinct competitive model. Airtel Nigeria's SmartCash PSB generated $10 million in revenue in the six months ended September 2026, up 176.4% from $4 million a year earlier, and its customer base more than doubled to 4.2 million from 2 million (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). MTN Nigeria's MoMo PSB grew core mobile money revenue by 102.2% in the nine months ended September 2026, and its wallet balances more than quadrupled to ₦43.8 billion from ₦9.8 billion at the end of December 2025, after migrating to a platform powered by Alipay+ in August 2026 (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). MTN reported 3.2 million monthly active users on the new platform at the end of September, with third-quarter transaction volumes up 69.1% (The Condia, 2026, https://thecondia.com/smartcash-vs-momo-2026/).

The reasoning chain behind these numbers is that PSBs compete on price and yield, not on distribution. SmartCash introduced zero charges on transfers and bill payments alongside a savings product paying 15% annual interest, and reported nearly three million active users in March 2026 on that model (The Condia, 2026, https://thecondia.com/smartcash-vs-momo-2026/). MoMo's growth, by contrast, came mainly from income on customer wallet balances, which quadrupled (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). Because PSBs are barred from lending, they cannot monetise customers through credit; instead they monetise balances — float income and sovereign-security yields — and buy customers with free transfers and above-market savings rates. That is a different innovation path from the microfinance-bank-licensed fintechs, which can lend: OPay reported $467.06 million in revenue for the first half of 2026, against SmartCash's $10 million, and recorded a $72.47 million net profit for 2025 on $536.25 million of revenue (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). OPay processed $358 billion in gross transaction value in 2025, more than double the $166.2 billion of 2024, with monthly active users rising from 25.1 million to 39.3 million (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/).

The scale gap — roughly 47-to-1 in half-year revenue between OPay and SmartCash — quantifies the binding constraint previous answers described in principle: the PSB licence's lending and foreign-exchange prohibitions cap the revenue a telco-backed bank can earn per customer, so even 110% customer growth leaves it far behind a licensed fintech that can lend. The implication for competition is that the agent-exclusivity rules and the PSB model pull in opposite directions: exclusivity hands distribution leverage to the largest principals, while the PSBs' price war (zero fees, 15% savings) is the one competitive weapon the smaller, telco-backed players can still wield. Whether that weapon is sustainable is doubtful on the numbers alone: SmartCash's $10 million half-year revenue must fund a zero-fee model for 4.2 million customers, and Airtel has not disclosed a detailed revenue breakdown that would show the underlying unit economics (The Condia, 2026, https://thecondia.com/smartcash-vs-momo-2026/).

## 3. The capital-markets consequence: OPay's IPO was priced, then pulled

OPay prepared a United States IPO with Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan Chase targeting roughly a $4 billion valuation, and on 27 August 2026 signalled a possible parallel domestic listing (Global Private Intelligence, 2026, https://gpi.4bin.ai/country/ng/fintechdisruption/). It priced the offering on 29 October 2026 — 16 million American depositary shares at $19, a roughly $4 billion valuation, ticker OPAY — but on 30 October, before trading began, it disclosed a regulatory inquiry relating to a foreign jurisdiction and agreed with its underwriters to terminate the underwriting agreement, so the offering was not completed and no IPO valuation was set (Global Private Intelligence, 2026, https://gpi.4bin.ai/country/ng/fintechdisruption/). An early investor, Opera Ltd, which holds 9.5% of OPay, carried its stake at $294.6 million at 31 December 2025 and $300.9 million at 30 June 2026, with a probability-weighted equity value for OPay of $3.4 billion at the end of 2025 (Global Private Intelligence, 2026, https://gpi.4bin.ai/country/ng/fintechdisruption/).

The mechanism here is regulatory risk repricing the whole sector's cost of capital. Nigeria's nine largest fintechs were worth a combined $10.6 billion as of January 2026, with Flutterwave at $3 billion, OPay at $2.75 billion, Moniepoint and Interswitch at about $1 billion each, and PalmPay at $0.85 billion (Techpoint Africa, 2026, http://techpoint.africa/guide/best-fintech-companies-in-nigeria/). A successful OPay listing would have set a public-market benchmark for all of them and opened an exit route for venture investors; its collapse days after pricing removes that benchmark and signals that even a profitable, scaled fintech — $72.47 million net profit in 2025 — cannot convert scale into public capital while a regulatory inquiry is outstanding (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/; Global Private Intelligence, 2026, https://gpi.4bin.ai/country/ng/fintechdisruption/). That raises the cost of capital for the sector, reinforces the consolidation previous answers described (only the largest can absorb the compliance load and the funding drought), and narrows exit options for smaller firms — which makes acquisition by a licensed group, rather than independent growth, the more likely path. I must calibrate this carefully: the inquiry was disclosed as relating to a foreign jurisdiction, and its subject has not been made public, so it would be wrong to attribute the IPO's failure to the CBN or to any specific Nigerian rule. The lesson is narrower but still material: regulatory overhang in any jurisdiction now reprices Nigerian fintech.

## 4. What this means for switching companies

The stablecoin regulations also change the switching and infrastructure layer, which previous answers treated mainly through capital requirements. Because Travel Rule data must accompany qualifying transfers, P2P matching needs approval, and tokens must be freezable on instruction, enforcement now happens at the infrastructure layer — the switches, aggregators and payment rails that move value between institutions (AELEX, 2026, https://aelex.com/cbn-introduces-new-regulatory-framework-for-non-security-virtual-assets/). That turns compliance capability into a product that switching companies can sell: identity matching, sanctions screening, transaction monitoring and token-control tooling are now mandatory features of the rail, not optional add-ons. The same logic applies to the Alipay+ migration at MoMo PSB: the competitive edge in 2026 is increasingly the quality of the platform underneath the wallet, not the number of agents in front of it (Korede, 2026, https://www.theoctopusnews.com/smartcash-momo-trail-in-fintech-revenue/). I could not verify any 2026-specific licensing or enforcement action against a named switching company, so the switching claim here is a mechanism argument from the verified rules, not an observed market outcome.

## Net assessment

As of November 2026, CBN supervision is changing Nigerian payments along three axes previous answers had not yet documented. First, the licensing perimeter has widened again: stablecoins and virtual-asset payments now face ₦10–15 billion capital bars and contract-level compliance duties, closing the last large unlicensed payments channel. Second, the PSB experiment is now measurable, and the measurement is sobering: triple-digit growth on a revenue base 47 times smaller than the leading fintech's, funded by zero-fee pricing and float income because the licence forbids lending. Third, the supervisory reset has a capital-markets cost: the largest fintech's $4 billion listing was priced and then withdrawn within a day on a regulatory disclosure. Competition is therefore intensifying on price at the wallet layer while concentrating on distribution at the agent layer and on capital at the licensing layer — and innovation is moving from acquiring customers to engineering compliant infrastructure, yield on balances, and platform reliability. The open questions are whether the CBN enforces the stablecoin 180-day licensing window, whether SmartCash's zero-fee model survives contact with its own unit economics, and whether any Nigerian fintech can set a public valuation while regulatory inquiries remain unresolved.

### Bottom-Line Answer

The Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) intensified licensing thresholds and supervisory interventions—anchored by the *New Licence Categorisations for the Nigerian Payments System* (Circular PSM/CIR/GEN/CIR/01/022), the *Supervisory Framework for Payment Service Banks* (2020), and aggressive anti-money laundering/know-your-customer (AML/KYC) enforcement—have driven market consolidation, raised entry barriers, and redirected innovation away from aggressive retail customer acquisition toward institutional compliance, B2B infrastructure, and cross-border settlement. Rather than democratizing retail acquiring, these tighter controls have reinforced an oligopolistic core dominated by deep-pocketed telecom-backed Payment Service Banks (PSBs), legacy switches, and heavily capitalized fintechs (notably OPay, Moniepoint, and Interswitch), while squeezing independent super-agents and early-stage payment startups out of core rails.

### 1. Structural Mechanisms: The Regulatory Instruments and Market Transmission

The operational environment for Nigerian payment entities is bounded by four distinct regulatory mechanisms enacted by the CBN:

1. **Licensing Segmentation and Balance-Sheet Ring-Fencing**:
   Under the consolidated framework, fintech activities are partitioned into four discrete tiers:
   - **Switching and Processing** (minimum paid-up capital: ₦2.0 billion);
   - **Mobile Money Operations (MMO)** (minimum paid-up capital: ₦2.0 billion);
   - **Payment Solution Services (PSS)** (incorporating Payment Solution Service Providers [PSSP] at ₦100 million, Payment Terminal Service Providers [PTSP] at ₦100 million, and Super-Agents at ₦50 million; or ₦250 million for a consolidated PSS license);
   - **Payment Service Banks (PSBs)** (minimum paid-up capital: ₦5.0 billion, maintained under a dedicated prudential regime).

   Crucially, the CBN strictly prohibits horizontal integration across certain tiers. Specifically, switching companies are barred from merchant acquiring and direct retail wallet issuance to prevent routing self-preferencing and anti-competitive fee structures. This restriction forces fintechs pursuing full-stack ecosystems to maintain siloed, independently capitalized corporate subsidiaries, substantially inflating recurring compliance and governance overhead.

2. **Capital Adequacy and Liquidity Sequestration**:
   For PSBs, the supervisory framework requires holding at least 75% of their deposit liabilities in liquid Central Bank of Nigeria securities (Treasury bills, OMO bills) and government bonds, with direct lending to retail or corporate borrowers strictly prohibited (permissible credit is limited solely to staff loans within tight ceilings). While this eliminates fractional-reserve credit risk, it permanently alters unit economics: PSBs cannot cross-subsidize payment processing margins with net interest margins (NIM) from high-yield retail credit, forcing them to compete purely on transaction volume, float yield, and fee-based distribution.

3. **Supervisory Onboarding Freezes and Traceability Directives**:
   Beginning in Q2 2024, the CBN demonstrated its willingness to invoke Section 45 of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA 2020) to freeze retail customer onboarding across major mobile money and non-bank payment institutions (including OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay, and Kuda). This enforcement wave mandated:
   - Mandatory Bank Verification Number (BVN) and National Identity Number (NIN) biometric identity linking for all account tiers (Tier 1 to Tier 3);
   - Strict physical address verification for agent networks;
   - Real-time transaction reporting pipelines interfacing with the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) anti-fraud portals.

4. **Agent Network Formalization**:
   Joint mandates from the CBN and the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) ended unregulated sub-agent proliferation by requiring point-of-sale (PoS) operators and merchant aggregators to undergo formal CAC business registration and dedicated KYC verification. This eliminated informal sub-agency arbitrage and forced super-agents to absorb compliance overheads or offboard non-compliant terminals.

### 2. Competitive Impacts Across Verticals

#### A. Payment Service Banks (PSBs): The Telecom Float Monopoly
The PSB vertical is defined by high minimum capital requirements (₦5.0 billion) and mandatory financial inclusion directives (requiring at least 25% of operational points of presence in financially excluded or rural zones). 

As a result, independent standalone applicants have been largely priced out, leaving the sector dominated by telco subsidiaries:
- **MoMo PSB** (MTN Nigeria Communications Plc)
- **SmartCash PSB** (Airtel Africa)
- **Moneymaster PSB** (Globacom)
- **9PSB** (9mobile)
- **Hope PSB**

Telco-backed PSBs leverage massive pre-existing subscriber bases (MTN's mobile subscriber base historically exceeding 70 million and Airtel exceeding 60 million) and unstructured supplementary service data (USSD) infrastructure. However, because they are barred from credit creation, their operational profitability relies on treasury yields on statutory float investments and transaction fees from digital airtime, bill payments, and cash-in/cash-out (CICO) agent transactions. Smaller, non-telco PSBs without cellular distribution rails face structural revenue deficits, driving consolidation and white-label infrastructure partnerships.

#### B. Switching and Processing: Anti-Preferencing Enforcement
Switching remains concentrated among legacy national switches and scaled infrastructure providers:
- **NIBSS** (the central industry-owned utility);
- **Interswitch Limited** (Verve / Quickteller rails);
- **Unified Payment Services Limited (UPSL)**;
- **eTranzact International Plc**.

The CBN’s structural firewalls—preventing switches from direct acquiring—neutralized attempts by payment processors to create vertically integrated proprietary closed loops. Consequently, competition has pivoted toward processing latency, system availability (uptime SLAs), and API-driven routing for alternative rails (such as NIBSS Instant Payments [NIP], QR codes, and cardless direct-debit APIs).

#### C. Agent Networks and POS Terminals: The End of Sub-Agent Arbitrage
The agency banking space experienced hyper-growth from 2019 to 2023, surpassing an estimated 1.5 to 2.0 million POS agent points nationwide, driven primarily by Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay. However, the mandatory CAC terminal registration and tiered KYC sweeps transformed unit economics:
- Aggregators face direct liability for terminal fraud under the revised Consumer Protection and Cybercrime compliance frameworks.
- The cost to onboard an agent has escalated from nominal app downloads to comprehensive document retrieval, physical geo-verification, and tax identification mapping.
- This regulatory burden has compressed net agent interchange margins, causing independent regional super-agents to liquidate or convert into captive, exclusive distribution networks for the top three acquiring networks.

### 4. Concrete Case: The 2024 Neobank Onboarding Freeze and KYC Re-architecting

A definitive stress-test of the CBN’s supervisory posture occurred in April–May 2024, when the Central Bank directed four prominent institutions—**OPay Digital Services Limited, Moniepoint Microfinance Bank, PalmPay Limited, and Kuda Microfinance Bank**—to completely pause onboarding new customers.

**Context and Mechanics**:
- The regulatory trigger involved systemic leaks between consumer fintech wallets and unauthorized foreign exchange (FX) and peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency trading desks, which bypassed statutory transaction monitoring guidelines and National Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) reporting thresholds.
- To resume onboarding (cleared between late May and June 2024), these fintechs had to overhaul their onboarding architectures:
  1. Complete deprecation of unverified Tier 1 phone-number-only accounts;
  2. Mandatory real-time biometric validation against NIBSS and the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) databases at the moment of account creation;
  3. Physical residential address verification via third-party geo-tagging or physical agent dispatch for accounts exceeding specific daily velocity thresholds;
  4. Explicit blocking of crypto-related transaction narration and instantaneous STR (Suspicious Transaction Report) generation.

**Market Outcome**:
This operational pause halted user acquisition for weeks and imposed substantial capital expenditure on compliance technology. Crucially, it demonstrated that digital banks and payment processors cannot operate as lightweight software wrappers over commercial bank rails; they are held to identical supervisory standards as traditional tier-1 commercial deposit money banks (DMBs), solidifying high capital reserves as the primary determinant of long-term viability.

Prior falsified answers suffered from severe substantive errors and fictitious assertions regarding regulatory parameters:

1. **Refutation of Fictitious Ownership Caps and Regulatory Updates**:
   - *Prior Falsification (61c9a7ce)* claimed that an "updated 2024 guideline" imposed a *"cap of 40% agent network ownership by any single fintech"* and asserted that *"only 7 of 14 applicant PSBs met the capital threshold in a 2024/2025 licensing round"*.
   - *Evidence and Fact Check*: The CBN has **never** promulgated a "40% agent network ownership cap" for fintechs or super-agents. Agent network operations are governed under the *Regulatory Framework for Agent Banking Operations in Nigeria* (2013) and the *Supervisory Framework for Payment Service Banks* (2020), neither of which contains an ownership percentage ceiling for agent networks. Furthermore, inventing specific round statistics ("7 of 14 applicant PSBs") misrepresents the CBN’s licensing regime, which does not operate in public "rounds" like telecom spectrum auctions, but rather processes applications on an individual, rolling basis through an Approval-in-Principle (AIP) phase followed by Final Licensing.

2. **Omission of the Core PSB Profitability Failure Mode**:
   - Prior analyses overlooked the structural regulatory constraint that governs PSB viability: the **lending prohibition**. Under Section 4.2 of the *Supervisory Framework for Payment Service Banks*, PSBs are expressly forbidden from granting consumer or commercial loans, advances, or guarantees. 
   - By ignoring this failure mode, previous assessments failed to capture why PSBs have not disrupted consumer lending and why their revenue models remain hypersensitive to monetary policy rate (MPR) cycles and CBN treasury yields. When money-market yields compress, PSBs are exposed to structural margin collapse unless they sustain massive, low-cost transaction velocity across their agent rails.

### Executive Summary: The Structural Reset of Nigerian Payments

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)—under Governor Olayemi Cardoso—has transitioned Nigerian fintech regulation from a permissive, growth-subsidized regime into an institutionalized, stability-first supervisory framework. The era of regulatory arbitrage, rapid unverified wallet onboarding, and unrestricted vertical stacking has ended. 

Instead, the CBN's regulatory regime is re-engineering market competition and redirecting innovation across three primary pillars:
1. **Payment Service Banks (PSBs):** Strict balance-sheet ring-fencing (prohibitions on credit intermediation and foreign exchange trading) confines telco-backed and specialized PSBs to transaction-fee economics and sovereign debt yields, preserving credit creation for commercial banks while forcing PSBs to compete on distribution efficiency and rural reach.
2. **Switching and Processing Infrastructure:** High capital barriers (minimum paid-up capital of ₦2 billion plus ₦2 billion escrow), mandatory corporate segregation under Payment Service Holding Companies (PSHC), and explicit cross-market concentration caps (limiting institutions holding >25% of consumer issuing to 15% of merchant acquiring) are dismantling closed-loop monopolies and forcing structural unbundling.
3. **Agent Networks and Merchant Acquiring:** The enforcement of single-principal agent exclusivity (ending multi-terminal "multi-homing"), daily cash-out velocity limits (₦1.2 million per agent), terminal geo-fencing, and mandatory Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) formalization have converted informal retail cash points into an exclusive, highly defensible corporate franchise layer.

The net effect on **competition** is a structural bifurcation: forced contestability at the merchant acquiring layer, coupled with high regulatory moats that favor heavily capitalized incumbents and bank-fintech holding companies over early-stage entrants. The net effect on **innovation** is a decisive pivot away from front-end customer acquisition and consumer wallet proliferation toward "compliance-as-infrastructure"—specifically automated Anti-Money Laundering (AML) monitoring, biometric identity verification, domestic data localization, and ISO 20022 interoperability.

### 1. Payment Service Banks (PSBs): The Balance-Sheet Boundary

Payment Service Banks—introduced under the CBN’s regulatory framework to accelerate financial inclusion in unbanked rural corridors—operate under deliberate structural asymmetries designed to prevent non-bank disintermediation of traditional deposit money banks (DMBs) (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2020b).

```
                      +-------------------------------------------------------+
                      |         Payment Service Bank (PSB) Architecture       |
                      +-------------------------------------------------------+
                                                  |
                     +----------------------------+---------------------------+
                     |                                                        |
                     v                                                        v
        Permitted Activities                                     Statutory Prohibitions
  ---------------------------------                       -----------------------------------
  • High-volume, low-value deposits                       • Direct retail/corporate lending
  • P2P transfers & bill payments                         • Foreign exchange (FX) trading/holding
  • Debit & prepaid card issuance                         • Underwriting insurance
  • Min. 25% rural agent deployment                       • Holding open FX risk positions
  • 75% deposits in Gov securities/CBN                    • Cross-subsidizing unhedged credit
```

#### A. Prudential Asymmetries and Revenue Models
Under the CBN's *Supervisory Framework for Payment Service Banks* (CBN, 2020b), PSBs—including MTN’s MoMo PSB, Airtel’s SmartCash PSB, 9PSB, and Hope PSB—must maintain a minimum paid-up capital of ₦5 billion. However, their charter carries rigid operational boundaries:
* **Lending Prohibition:** PSBs are barred from advancing consumer loans, credit cards, or corporate facilities from their balance sheets.
* **Liquid Asset Deployment:** At least 75% of total deposit liabilities must be invested in zero-risk Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) treasury bills, sovereign bonds, or eligible liquid deposits at the CBN.
* **Foreign Exchange Restrictions:** PSBs cannot maintain open foreign exchange (FX) trading positions or accept foreign currency deposits.

#### B. Competitive and Innovative Consequences
* **Yield-Constrained Unit Economics:** Because PSBs cannot monetize low-cost deposits through high-margin lending spreads (net interest margins), they cannot cross-subsidize customer acquisition. They are forced to operate strictly on micro-transaction fees, utility commission splits, and sovereign debt yields.
* **Rural Distribution Mandates:** The statutory requirement that at least 25% of PSB physical agent points be located in rural, underserved corridors forces operators like MoMo PSB and SmartCash PSB to focus their balance sheets on low-connectivity, cash-dominated regional economies. 
* **Innovation Vector:** Barred from credit, PSB innovation has focused on **offline rails and network resilience**—such as optimized USSD string caching, encrypted interactive voice response (IVR) flows, and agent float rebalancing algorithms tailored for areas with unstable cellular connectivity.

### 2. Switching Companies: Structural Unbundling and Concentration Caps

Switching and processing companies form the core clearing and transaction-routing infrastructure of Nigeria's National Financial Switch. The CBN's heightened supervision has targeted systemic risk and vertical market foreclosure.

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                    CBN Payments Licensing Framework                                     |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| License Tier                       | Minimum Capital Floor    | Permissible Operational Scope           |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Switching & Processing             | ₦2,000,000,000           | Transaction switching, clearing, routing|
|                                    | (+ ₦2,000,000,000 Escrow)| Prohibited: Holding customer float/MMO  |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Mobile Money Operator (MMO)        | ₦2,000,000,000           | E-money issuance, pool accounts, wallets|
|                                    | (+ ₦2,000,000,000 Escrow)| Prohibited: Inter-bank switching        |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Payment Solution Services (PSS)    | ₦250,000,000 aggregate   | Bundled license: PSSP, PTSP, Super-Agent|
| • PSSP (Payment Gateway)           | ₦100,000,000             | Gateway integration, payment aggregation|
| • PTSP (Terminal Management)       | ₦100,000,000             | POS terminal deployment and maintenance |
| • Super-Agent (Agent Management)   | ₦50,000,000              | Sub-agent monitoring and cash liquidity |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Payment Service Bank (PSB)         | ₦5,000,000,000           | Low-value deposits, payment transfers   |
|                                    |                          | Prohibited: Credit extension, FX trading|
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
```

#### A. Prohibition of Vertical License Commingling
Under the licensing architecture established by Circular PSM/DIR/GEN/CIR/01/022 (CBN, 2020a), the CBN strictly prohibits a single legal entity from holding both a Switching license and a Mobile Money Operator (MMO) license. 
* Entities seeking to operate across both layers must establish a Payment Service Holding Company (PSHC) structure with legally separated corporate governance, firewalled balance sheets, and independent risk management (Techpoint Africa, 2026).
* The enforcement of this boundary was illustrated when the CBN imposed administrative penalties on unauthorized wallet functionality operated by pure-play switches (e.g., sanctioning synthetic balance-holding products), compelling firms to either partner with licensed deposit-taking institutions or acquire regulated microfinance bank (MFB) subsidiaries (Business Insider Africa, 2024; Tech in Naija, 2026).

#### B. Market Structure Concentration Caps (June 2026 Circular)
On 15 June 2026, the CBN Payments System Supervision Department issued Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, establishing cross-market concentration limits to prevent two-sided market foreclosure (Launch Base Africa, 2026; TechCabal, 2026):
* **The 25% / 15% Cross-Market Ceiling:** Any regulated institution—evaluated at the consolidated group level—holding **more than 25% of consumer issuing** (digital wallets, customer accounts, debit cards) is legally barred from holding **more than 15% of merchant acquiring** (POS terminals, online checkout gateways, settlement aggregation), and vice versa.
* **Compliance and Divestment:** Groups exceeding these thresholds were given a mandatory restructuring and compliance deadline of 31 December 2026 (Vanguard, 2026).
* **Competitive Impact:** This directly forces the unbundling of vertically integrated platforms (such as Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay). By restricting a single entity from capturing both interchange yields on the issuing leg and merchant discount rates (MDR) on the acquiring leg, the CBN opens merchant acceptance rails to mid-tier acquirers, challenger gateways, and tier-1 commercial bank subsidiaries (e.g., Access Bank's Hydrogen, GTCO's Squad).

#### C. Data Localization and Automated AML Surveillance
* **Domestic Data Hosting:** Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004 mandates that all transaction data generated within Nigeria must be localized and stored on domestic infrastructure by 1 January 2027, accelerating demand for Tier-III and Tier-IV data centers in Lagos and Abuja while raising infrastructure overheads for cloud-native entrants (Launch Base Africa, 2026; PwC Nigeria, 2026).
* **Automated AML/CFT Monitoring:** Under Circular BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/019/002, issued in March 2026, all payment processors and switching entities must maintain real-time automated transaction surveillance, behavior-based anomaly detection, and automated Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) filings with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) (Techpoint Africa, 2026).

### 3. Agent Banking and POS Networks: From Kiosk Arbitrage to Corporate Franchises

Agent banking expanded rapidly between 2020 and 2024, deploying over 5.5 million POS terminals by late 2024 (NIBSS, 2024) to compensate for branch closures and currency shortages. However, regulatory concerns regarding untracked cash aggregation, black-market FX routing, and fraud vulnerabilities triggered comprehensive supervisory interventions.

```
       Pre-2024 Agent Environment                          November 2026 Supervised Regime
  +------------------------------------+              +------------------------------------+
  | • Informal multi-homing (3-5 POS)  |              | • Single-principal exclusivity     |
  | • Unregistered individual kiosks   |  ==========> | • Mandatory CAC business legal entity|
  | • Unlimited cash-out velocity      |              | • ₦1.2m agent daily cash-out cap   |
  | • Roaming, untracked terminals     |              | • 70m geo-fenced terminal radius   |
  +------------------------------------+              +------------------------------------+
```

#### A. Single-Principal Exclusivity
Under the CBN’s revised *Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria* (enforced from 1 April 2026), retail POS agents are prohibited from maintaining multi-homing relationships across competing principals (Central Bank of Nigeria, 2025; Legal 500, 2026):
* **The Exclusive Principal Rule:** Every agent must operate under a single principal institution (a bank, MFB, PSB, MMO, or licensed super-agent) at any given time. Transactions must settle through a dedicated, monitored agent wallet linked exclusively to that principal.
* **Competitive Dynamics:** Multi-terminal kiosks—where operators swapped between Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay terminals to hedge against network downtime—have been declared non-compliant. Consequently, network principals compete aggressively on **backend uptime, settlement latency, and agent retention incentives**, as an agent tied to an unstable platform faces complete revenue loss during network outages (The Condía, 2026).

#### B. Velocity Capping, Geo-Fencing, and Corporate Registration
* **Daily Cash Velocity Caps:** Under Section 8 of the Agent Banking Guidelines, customer withdrawals are capped at ₦100,000 per day (₦500,000 per week), while an individual agent’s cumulative cash-out volume is capped at ₦1.2 million per day (Central Bank of Nigeria, 2025; EFInA, 2025). This eliminates large-scale informal cash hoarding and currency arbitrage.
* **Spatial Geo-Fencing:** Following initial implementation at a 10-meter perimeter, the CBN relaxed the terminal geo-fencing radius to 70 meters from registered business coordinates, enforced from 1 August 2026 (Legal 500, 2026). POS terminals operating outside their verified geographic coordinates are subject to automated remote deactivation via certified Payment Terminal Service Aggregators (PTSAs: NIBSS and Unified Payment Services Ltd).
* **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) Mandate:** Under Section 863(1) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA 2020), all retail POS operators must register as formal legal business entities with the CAC (Corporate Affairs Commission, 2024). This requirement pruned marginal, part-time operators from the market, driving independent kiosks into formal aggregator franchise networks.

### 4. Systemic Supervision and the Statutory Horizon (Bill SB.959)

On 10 November 2026, the Nigerian Senate passed Bill SB.959 at third reading, amending the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020 to explicitly codify CBN supervisory authority over non-bank financial technology firms (Vanguard, 2026; Lawyard, 2026):
* **Systemically Important Institutions (SII) Designation:** The legislation empowers the CBN to designate large payment platforms, switching companies, and digital neo-banks as SIIs based on transaction volumes, balance-sheet float, and systemic interconnectedness.
* **Prudential Oversight:** Designated non-bank fintechs will face bank-equivalent supervisory measures, including mandatory stress-testing, comprehensive technology-risk audits, heightened corporate governance disclosures, and direct supervisory audit interfaces.
* **Legislative Status:** As of mid-November 2026, Bill SB.959 awaits concurrence from the House of Representatives and presidential assent; while not yet statutory law, it establishes a clear forward signal that scaled fintechs will be regulated as systemically critical public utilities.

### 5. Synthesis: How Competition and Innovation Have Changed

#### A. The Realignment of Competition

| Competitive Vector | Permissive Era (2018–2023) | Supervised Regime (November 2026) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Market Structure** | Vertically integrated super-apps capturing both issuing and acquiring | Forced unbundling via 25%/15% concentration caps and holding company firewalls |
| **Entry Barriers** | Modest capital thresholds, venture-subsidized growth, rapid API integrations | High capital moats (₦2B–₦5B), escrow requirements, domestic data hosting, and continuous RegTech audits |
| **Agent Networks** | Shared, multi-homed agent kiosks operating across multiple aggregators | Exclusive, single-principal agent franchises competing on uptime and SLA reliability |
| **Bank-Fintech Balance** | Rapid fintech customer acquisition via lightweight phone-number onboarding | Regulatory symmetry (mandatory BVN/NIN for all tiers) enabling commercial banks to reassert acquiring strength |
| **Industry Consolidation** | Proliferation of specialized seed-stage consumer wallets | Aggressive M&A: fintechs acquiring licensed MFBs; weaker firms exiting or becoming B2B providers |

#### B. The Trajectory of Innovation

Supervisory tightening has not halted technological innovation in Nigerian payments; rather, it has redirected engineering resources away from growth-hacking and frictionless signups toward **governance, infrastructure resilience, and enterprise integration**:

1. **Compliance-as-Infrastructure (RegTech):** Engineering talent and venture capital have shifted into automated compliance tooling. The primary product battlegrounds are real-time AML surveillance engines, algorithmic transaction velocity controls, and biometric liveness verification integrated directly with the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) and NIBSS databases.
2. **Open Banking and Interoperability:** Following the release of the CBN Operational Guidelines for Open Banking (Circular PSM/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/043), payment innovation has moved toward standardized API aggregation, consent-management frameworks, and structured B2B corporate treasury integrations (Central Bank of Nigeria, 2023a; BusinessDay, 2026).
3. **ISO 20022 and the National Payment Stack:** Migration to the ISO 20022 messaging standard under the National Payment Stack has transformed transaction metadata routing, enabling richer commercial invoicing, dispute automation, and straight-through reconciliation across diverse payment switches.
4. **Offline and Multi-Channel Reliability:** With single-principal exclusivity placing the entire burden of terminal availability on the host institution, providers are innovating in dynamic cellular SIM fallback, USSD backchannels, and store-and-forward batch authorization models to safeguard agent operational uptime.

Historical regulatory precedent indicates that systemic stability concerns could prompt phased compliance extensions.
* **Impact on Rural Financial Inclusion (Contested / Moderate Uncertainty):** Industry bodies—including the Association of Mobile Money and Bank Agents of Nigeria (AMMBAN)—have argued that strict daily withdrawal caps (₦1.2 million per agent), CAC registration overheads, and geo-fencing requirements disproportionately strain marginal rural agents, risking localized cash-desertification. Conversely, the CBN and public advocates maintain that formalization eliminates predatory cash surcharges, curbs illicit financial flows, and builds a sustainable, traceable financial foundation (EFInA, 2025; Vanguard, 2026).
* **Cloud Infrastructure Capacity (Moderate Uncertainty):** Full compliance with the 1 January 2027 data localization mandate depends on the commercial availability and pricing of domestic Tier-III/IV data center colocation space in Nigeria, which could impose higher operational cost burdens on mid-tier switching and processing licensees (PwC Nigeria, 2026).

### Executive Summary

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has fundamentally transformed the Nigerian payments ecosystem from a period of hyper-growth, regulatory arbitrage, and frictionless customer acquisition into a mature, compliance-driven regime defined by structural unbundling, capital ring-fencing, and systemic oversight. Guided by Governor Olayemi Cardoso, the CBN's regulatory interventions in 2025 and 2026 focus on three primary pillars:
1. **Payment Service Banks (PSBs)** operating under balance-sheet restrictions that prevent credit intermediation and foreign-currency exposure.
2. **Switching and Processing Companies** subjected to strict activity firewalls, local data-residency mandates, and structural cross-market concentration caps.
3. **Agent Banking Networks** constrained by single-principal exclusivity, mandatory Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) business registration, terminal geo-fencing, and hard cash-out limits.

Rather than extinguishing competition or halting technological progress, this supervisory posture has redirected innovation. Front-end "super-app" growth hacking and low-KYC wallet onboarding have given way to back-end compliance engineering—such as automated Anti-Money Laundering (AML) monitoring, biometric identity pipelines, ISO 20022 National Payment Stack integration, and enterprise B2B infrastructure. However, high fixed compliance costs have raised entry barriers, consolidating the market around well-capitalized incumbents and commercial banks while placing the last-mile agent economy under structural strain.

### 1. The 2025–2026 Supervisory Architecture

```
                                  +-------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |         Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Core            |

                                  +-------------------------------------------------------+
                                                              |

| • 25%/15% Cross-Market Cap        |               | • 75% Sovereign Reserve Requirement|               | • Daily Cash-Out Cap: ₦1.2 Million|
| • Prohibited from Consumer Wallet |               | • Prohibited: Direct Credit & FX  |               | • Geo-Fenced 70m Terminal Radius  |

+-----------------------------------+               +-----------------------------------+               +-----------------------------------+
```

#### A. Structural Licensing Tiers and Group Ring-Fencing
Under the CBN’s payments licensing framework established under its December 2020 circular (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2020a) and supervised under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, licensing categories enforce strict capital floors and functional separation:
* **Switching and Processing** (Minimum Share Capital: ₦2.0 billion plus ₦2.0 billion refundable escrow): Authorized to route and clear inter-bank transactions and operate payment gateways, but strictly barred from directly issuing customer-facing wallets or holding customer deposits (Lawzana, 2026).
* **Mobile Money Operators (MMO)** (Minimum Share Capital: ₦2.0 billion): Authorized to issue electronic money wallets and manage pooled customer accounts (Lawzana, 2026).
* **Payment Solution Services (PSS)** (Aggregate Capital: ₦250 million): Encompassing Payment Solution Service Providers (PSSP, ₦100 million), Payment Terminal Service Providers (PTSP, ₦100 million), and Super-Agents (₦50 million) (Lawzana, 2026).
* **Payment Service Banks (PSB)** (Minimum Share Capital: ₦5.0 billion): Authorized to accept retail deposits and offer payments, but governed by strict balance-sheet asymmetries (CBN, 2020b).

To curb regulatory arbitrage resulting from multi-licence holding companies, the CBN exposed ring-fencing rules requiring each regulated subsidiary within a group to maintain independent governance, capital, liquidity, and risk-management architectures (TechCabal, 2026). Groups can no longer cross-subsidize operations or commingle data and capital across separate payment, lending, and deposit-taking entities without dedicated capitalization for each license tier.

#### B. The June 2026 Market-Structure Concentration Caps
On June 15, 2026, the CBN’s Payments System Supervision Department issued Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, introducing structural anti-monopoly caps across the value chain (Launch Base Africa, 2026):
* **The 25%/15% Cross-Market Limit:** Any licensed payment institution (or group of related entities evaluated under common control) holding **more than 25% of the consumer issuing market** (cards, wallets, and accounts) is restricted to a **maximum of 15% of the merchant acquiring market** (POS terminals, payment gateways, and merchant collection), and vice versa (Launch Base Africa, 2026).
* **Compliance Deadlines:** Institutions breaching these thresholds must restructure or execute asset divestments by **December 31, 2026** (Launch Base Africa, 2026).
* **Data Localisation & Beneficial Ownership:** All payment transaction data generated within Nigeria must be stored and processed on domestic data infrastructure by **January 1, 2027**, accompanied by mandatory disclosure of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs) (Launch Base Africa, 2026).

#### C. Agent Banking Overhaul and Velocity Restrictions
Following the *Circular and Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria* issued on October 6, 2025, regulatory enforcement reached full implementation in 2026 (CBN, 2025; CryptoCompass, 2026):
* **Single-Principal Exclusivity (Effective April 1, 2026):** Point-of-Sale (POS) agents are restricted to serving a single principal institution (bank, MMO, PSB, or super-agent) at a time, dismantling the informal multi-terminal model where agents operated competing devices side by side (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **Transaction & Cash-Out Limits:** Individual customer cash-out and cash-in operations are capped at ₦100,000 per day and ₦500,000 per week, while total daily cash-out volume for an individual agent is capped at ₦1.2 million (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **Geo-Fencing and Routing:** POS terminals must be registered with licensed Payment Terminal Service Aggregators—Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) or Unified Payment Services—and geo-fenced to their registered business address within a permitted spatial radius (widened from 10 meters to 70 meters by a May 29, 2026 circular, with enforcement from August 1, 2026) (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **CAC Registration Mandate:** Under Section 863(1) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA 2020), all POS operators and agent points must formally register as legal business entities with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) (CryptoCompass, 2026).

#### D. Automated AML Surveillance and Legislative Framework
* **Automated AML Baseline Standards (Circular BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/019/002, March 10, 2026):** Mandates real-time transaction monitoring, automated Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) filing with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU), and BVN/NIN-linked customer risk profiling across all supervised financial institutions (MemberCheck, 2026). Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) were granted 18 months and Other Financial Institutions (OFIs)/fintechs 24 months to reach full technical compliance (Nigerian Eye, 2026).
* **Systemically Important Institutions (SII) Legislative Backstop:** On November 10, 2026, the Nigerian Senate passed Bill SB.959, amending BOFIA 2020 to empower the CBN to designate systemically important fintechs as SIIs (Vanguard, 2026). Designated entities will face enhanced supervisory access, mandatory stress testing, and bank-like operational resilience frameworks (Vanguard, 2026).

### 2. Structural Impacts on Market Competition

```
       Hyper-Growth Era (2018–2023)                         Supervisory Era (2024–2026)
  +-------------------------------------+             +-------------------------------------+
  | • Integrated super-app monopolies   |             | • Forced issuing/acquiring split    |
  | • Frictionless phone-number KYC     |  ========>  | • Mandatory biometric NIN/BVN gates |
  | • Multi-homed informal POS kiosks   |             | • Single-principal agent exclusivity|
  | • Light-touch compliance overhead   |             | • High capital floors & RegTech moats|
  +-------------------------------------+             +-------------------------------------+
```

#### A. Forced Vertical Separation and Merchant Acquirer Opening
The 25%/15% market-structure caps directly target vertically integrated operators—such as Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay—that historically captured interchange and processing margins across both ends of a transaction (Launch Base Africa, 2026). By forcing groups to unbundle or limit market share on one side of the ledger by December 31, 2026, the CBN has broken closed-loop routing advantages. 

This structural unbundling creates market opportunities for mid-tier acquirers, independent payment solution service providers (PSSPs), and commercial bank subsidiaries (such as Guaranty Trust Holding Company's Squad/HabariPay and Access Bank's Hydrogen) to capture merchant acquiring volume that market leaders are legally constrained from absorbing (Launch Base Africa, 2026).

#### B. Consolidation at the Top and Squeeze on Early-Stage Entrants
While the market-structure caps promote contestability at the merchant acquiring layer, the overall supervisory regime raises fixed operational overheads:
* **Capital Moats:** Licensing capital floors (₦5.0 billion for PSBs; ₦2.0 billion for switches and MMOs), paired with refundable escrow deposits and onshore data localization infrastructure requirements (effective January 1, 2027), favor heavily capitalized players (Lawzana, 2026; Launch Base Africa, 2026).
* **M&A over Greenfield Entry:** Early-stage startups face prohibitive capital and compliance hurdles. Consequently, market entry has shifted toward acquiring existing licensed charters. For example, Paystack acquired Ladder Microfinance Bank, and Flutterwave secured a microfinance banking charter following its acquisition of open-banking startup Mono (Tech in Naija, 2026).
* **Bank-Fintech Convergence:** Traditional commercial banks, undergoing their own recapitalization exercise mandated by the CBN in March 2024, have re-asserted authority over corporate collections and transaction switching, treating fintechs as specialized software distribution channels rather than autonomous parallel banking systems.

#### C. Agent Network Dynamics: From Multi-Homing to Franchise Competition
The single-principal agent mandate has transformed agency banking from a shared, multi-tenant distribution model into an exclusive franchise system (CryptoCompass, 2026):
* **Shift in Uptime Burden:** Because agents can no longer switch to a secondary terminal during network outages, principals must compete for agent loyalty based on backend switch uptime, rapid settlement clearance, and commission structures (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **Market Bifurcation:** Scaled operators with robust technical infrastructure (e.g., Moniepoint, OPay) have captured agent market share, while smaller super-agents struggling with compliance costs and network instability lose agent coverage (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **Informal Network Pruning:** Mandatory CAC business incorporation and identity checks have pruned low-margin, informal sub-agents, consolidating terminal distribution under professional merchant networks (CryptoCompass, 2026).

### 3. Transformation of Payments Innovation

#### A. Pivot from Growth Hacking to RegTech and Compliance Engineering
Following the April–May 2024 supervisory onboarding freezes imposed on major digital platforms over illicit FX and cryptocurrency peer-to-peer (P2P) leakages (Media Talk Africa, 2024), engineering priorities shifted from viral customer acquisition toward compliance infrastructure:
* **Automated Biometric Pipelines:** Product development is centered on real-time NIN and BVN validation, facial liveness verification, and physical address geo-tagging during customer onboarding (Media Talk Africa, 2024).
* **Transaction Monitoring Analytics:** Switching operators and payment providers invest heavily in graph analytics, velocity-checking models, and real-time AML engines capable of detecting structured cash pooling and automated suspicious transaction patterns prior to clearing (MemberCheck, 2026).
* **Standards-Based Rails:** Migration to ISO 20022 messaging standards under the National Payment Stack (launched in November 2025) has modernized payment metadata payload handling across clearing switches (Techpoint Africa, 2026).

#### B. Embedded Finance and the Open Banking Horizon
* **API-Driven Distribution:** Because securing direct PSB or switching licenses is capital-intensive, early-stage innovators build embedded-finance products—such as inventory management tools, B2B merchant credit analytics, and supply-chain payout APIs—leveraging the infrastructure of fully licensed bank or PSB partners (Applied Worldwide, 2026).
* **Staggered Open Banking Execution:** While the CBN issued the *Operational Guidelines for Open Banking in Nigeria* in March 2023, nationwide production API rollouts remain in phased implementation as of late 2026 (FlyingEze, 2026). Permissioned data-sharing, account aggregation, and consent management are being tested within the CBN’s Regulatory Sandbox cohorts, delaying wide-scale API-driven retail disintermediation (FlyingEze, 2026).

#### A. The Financial Inclusion vs. Systemic Integrity Trade-off
The CBN's regulatory reset represents a deliberate policy trade-off: prioritizing systemic stability, AML traceability, and anti-monopoly controls over frictionless growth. However, this posture introduces operational frictions at the financial inclusion frontier:
* **Agent Infrastructure Strain:** Enforcing single-principal exclusivity alongside the ₦1.2 million daily agent cash-out limit restricts liquidity distribution in rural regions lacking traditional bank branches (CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **KYC Friction for Last-Mile Users:** Strict biometric BVN/NIN validation requirements reduce identity fraud but create onboarding friction for unbanked populations lacking formal identity documentation (CryptoCompass, 2026).

The business being supervised is increasingly a lending business, not a payments business.** OPay's own SEC filings show first-half 2026 revenue of $467.1 million, up 136.5 per cent, with net income of $90.9 million — and lending, at $236.1 million, had overtaken payments as its largest revenue line; Nigeria supplied 89.5 per cent of revenue (TechCabal, 2026). In 2025 the company made a $72.5 million profit on $536.3 million in revenue as new loans grew 285 per cent to $938.3 million (TechCabal, 2026). This reframes what the CBN's tightening is actually disciplining. The January 2026 upgrades of OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, PalmPay and Paga to national licences, and the ring-fencing rules that stop groups from cross-subsidising across licences, bite hardest precisely because these firms used microfinance bank licences to move from transaction fees into lending and deposits. Innovation is therefore shifting from payments features into credit products built on banking-style licences — which is why the CBN's supervision of them is converging on bank supervision, and why the June 2026 market-structure caps and the proposed Systemically Important Institution designation are aimed at firms whose economics are already bank-like.

**4. The open institutional question for 2027 is who polices competition: the CBN or the FCCPC.** At the 4 March 2026 public hearing on Bill SB.959, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) backed stronger oversight but stressed the importance of clearly defining regulators' responsibilities to avoid overlapping functions, and called for effective coordination between the CBN and the FCCPC to ensure the new framework promotes fair competition and protects consumers (The Cabal, 2026). This fault line is the direct answer to the competition half of the question. The June 2026 market-share caps are simultaneously prudential supervision and competition policy: if the CBN enforces them as stability rules, they cap dominance; if no competition authority tests whether they entrench incumbents, the same caps become a moat. The verified answers treat the caps as CBN policy; the missing piece is that Nigeria's competition regulator has publicly asked for a defined role in exactly this framework, and that jurisdictional question is unresolved as of November 2026.

**Bottom line.** The rulebook the verified answers describe is real, but the November 2026 evidence shows the tightening works through three channels the rulebook alone does not capture: recurring multi-agency fines that rise with scale, a cross-border regulatory veto over the sector's flagship listing, and a lending-led business model that makes bank-style supervision the binding constraint. Competition is therefore being reshaped less by any single CBN circular than by the combined cost of fines, the closure of the IPO exit, and an unresolved CBN–FCCPC boundary over who decides what counts as dominance.

**Uncertainty note.** The N994 million fine figures are as reported from OPay's audited financial statements (ThisDay, 2026, reporting disclosures sighted by InsideBusinessNG); I have not independently inspected the statements. The attribution of the IPO inquiry to a Chinese regulator is Bloomberg's reporting, not OPay's statement, which named no jurisdiction. The IPO terms and revenue figures are from OPay's SEC filings as reported by TechCabal (2026).

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tighter licensing and supervision is changing Nigerian payments through three mechanisms that earlier analysis has underplayed: enforcement is now priced into fintech valuations, the regulator itself has entered the switching layer with a public rail, and supervision is being calibrated in public — with the costs falling on specific business models rather than evenly across the market. The result is not simply "more compliance"; it is a redistribution of who can compete, on what infrastructure, and at whose expense.

## 1. Enforcement now has a price tag — and a capital-markets consequence

The clearest evidence that supervision has teeth arrived in November 2026, when OPay Digital Services' audited financial statements disclosed roughly ₦946 million in regulatory penalties incurred between 2023 and 2025 (reported as nearly ₦1 billion), imposed by the CBN, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria and the Corporate Affairs Commission (ThisDay, 2026). The breakdown is instructive about what the CBN is actually punishing: ₦26 million in 2023 and ₦113.7 million in 2024 for anti-money-laundering and terrorism-financing breaches, ₦197 million for violations of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020, and — the largest single item — ₦464 million paid to the CBN in 2025 for breaching the Framework for Mobile Money Services in Nigeria 2021. The NDPC added a ₦125 million fine under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

Two implications follow. First, the fines escalated over time rather than deterring after the first sanction, which suggests the CBN's earlier penalties were treated as a cost of doing business — and that the 2025 fine, nearly half the three-year total, marks a genuine escalation. Second, compliance risk is now being repriced by investors, not just regulators: OPay had planned to raise about $304 million on the New York Stock Exchange at a valuation of about $4 billion, but on 30 October 2026 it terminated the offering a day after signing the underwriting agreement, following a regulatory inquiry in an undisclosed foreign jurisdiction (ThisDay, 2026). The Nigerian fines and the foreign inquiry have not been established to be connected, but the sequence shows that a fintech's governance record is now a fundraising variable. For competition, this matters: the giants can absorb nine-figure fines, but a failed IPO reprices the whole sector's cost of capital, and it advantages firms whose compliance record is clean enough to raise money over firms whose growth was bought with regulatory forbearance.

## 2. The switching layer: the regulator has built its own rail

The most consequential change for switching companies is one the CBN did not impose by circular but by construction. The Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) has rolled out the National Payment Stack (NPS), a sovereign, ISO 20022-compliant infrastructure designed to succeed the 15-year-old NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP) system. By August 2026 it had processed 26.55 million transactions worth ₦1.4 trillion across 48 participating financial institutions, and by 25 September 2026 it had passed 100 million successful transactions (Lagos Business News, 2026). The NPS is built for API-based integration, cross-border compatibility, smart risk scoring, end-to-end traceability and real-time monitoring.

This reframes competition among switching and processing companies. Private switches previously competed on connectivity and uptime; now they compete alongside a public utility rail that the regulator itself operates through NIBSS, with fraud monitoring and identity capabilities built in. The NPS also changes what "innovation" means for a switching company: the defensible ground shifts from owning a proprietary pipe to building products on top of a shared, standardised rail — richer ISO 20022 data, faster settlement, lower integration cost. The early leaderboard is also telling: FirstBank led participating institutions in transaction volume and Fidelity Bank in transaction value (Lagos Business News, 2026). On the new rail, incumbent banks — not fintechs — are setting the pace, which reverses the last decade's pattern in which fintechs owned the growth channels and banks followed.

The same logic applies at the terminal layer. All POS transactions must now route through the two licensed Payment Terminal Service Aggregators, NIBSS and Unified Payment Services Limited, with automatic failover between them (CryptoCompass, 2026). Dual routing is a resilience measure, but it also concentrates visibility: every terminal transaction is observable by the aggregators, which is the technical precondition for the caps, geo-fencing and AML automation the CBN is enforcing elsewhere.

## 3. Agent networks: exclusivity shifts the uptime burden to the principal

The revised Regulatory Framework for Agent Banking, issued in October 2025 and enforced in full for principal exclusivity on 1 April 2026, requires every POS agent to operate under a single principal institution at a time; an agent with a Moniepoint terminal may no longer keep an OPay or PalmPay device as backup (CryptoCompass, 2026). Earlier answers correctly note the concentration risk this creates. What they miss is the mechanism: multi-homing was never primarily about regulatory arbitrage for agents — it was insurance against fragile switching infrastructure. When one issuer's switch timed out or a fintech's settlement rail lagged, the agent switched terminals and kept cash flowing. By outlawing the backup terminal while mandating Corporate Affairs Commission registration, the CBN has shifted the entire uptime burden onto the principal's backend. Competition among principals therefore stops being about who recruits the most agents and becomes about whose backend fails least — a contest the best-capitalised firms with the most reliable switching infrastructure win, and a further reason the agent market consolidates around them.

The geo-fencing episode shows supervision being calibrated rather than simply tightened. The CBN originally required terminals to operate within a 10-metre radius of their registered address, but consumer GPS chips in dense markets routinely drift more than 25 metres, threatening millions of false-positive declines across 5.56 million deployed terminals. In a circular of 29 May 2026 the CBN expanded the radius to 70 metres and moved the enforcement deadline to 1 August 2026 (CryptoCompass, 2026). The compromise saved plaza merchants and petrol stations but still eliminated an entire category of mobile commerce: roaming market collectors, daily ajo (thrift) savings agents who walk stall to stall, and dispatch riders can no longer process payments beyond 70 metres of their registered coordinates unless they obtain corporate fleet exemptions or switch to pure transfers. Innovation in last-mile collection is therefore not merely discouraged; for the roaming model it is now legally impossible on hardware POS.

The unit economics complete the squeeze. A ₦10,000–₦15,000 CAC registration hurdle, five-year AML record-keeping, 72-hour dispute-resolution timelines, a ₦1.2 million daily agent cash-out cap and per-customer withdrawal limits of ₦100,000 daily and ₦500,000 weekly mean standalone "umbrella agents" whose business is trading cash for a ₦100–₦200 fee are exiting or folding into pharmacies, supermarkets and petrol stations, where terminals serve goods checkout rather than pure cash arbitrage (CryptoCompass, 2026). The agent network is being converted from an informal cash-distribution system into a network of formal micro-branches attached to real retail businesses — more traceable, but with fewer, larger nodes.

## 4. Competition: the closed loop is being broken at group level

The market-structure caps in Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004 of 15 June 2026 — no institution with more than 25% of consumer issuing may hold more than 15% of merchant acquiring, and vice versa, with compliance due 31 December 2026 — apply at the consolidated group level (CryptoCompass, 2026). That detail is decisive. The winning playbook of Moniepoint, OPay and PalmPay was closed-loop vertical integration: distribute tens of millions of consumer debit cards, deploy millions of POS terminals, and settle card-on-own-terminal transactions internally with near-zero interbank friction and about 99% uptime. A group-level cap means a holding company cannot evade it by putting cards in a microfinance subsidiary and terminals in a switching or super-agent entity. The giants must now choose a primary lane — issuing or acquiring — and shed, throttle or divest the other side, which is the first time regulation has directly attacked the unit economics of the closed loop rather than its licensing perimeter.

The same circular bundles three further mandates — mandatory payment-data localisation with full compliance by 1 January 2027, Ultimate Beneficial Ownership disclosures, and systemic-oversight protocols (CryptoCompass, 2026). Localisation is a fixed-cost shock: every payment record, BVN lookup, card token, fraud model and analytics pipeline generated in Nigeria must be hosted domestically. Large firms can fund an onshore cloud migration; smaller mobile money operators cannot, and will merge or surrender share. Compliance cost is therefore not merely a moat — it is a consolidation mechanism with a dated deadline.

## 5. Innovation is being redirected into infrastructure the regulator can see

The pattern across all of this is consistent: innovation that depends on opacity — informal agents, multi-homing, cross-licence subsidy, offshore data — is being closed off, while innovation that increases traceability is being subsidised by the regulator's own infrastructure. The NPS rewards API-based products, richer transaction data and real-time risk scoring; the automated-AML standards reward AI-driven monitoring; the sandbox's second cohort covers virtual assets and stablecoins. What is being starved is product innovation at the distribution edge: roaming collection, informal cash-out, and the low-KYC onboarding that powered the fintech boom.

Whether this trade is worth it turns on three dated tests. The 31 December 2026 market-share deadline will show whether the giants actually shed volume or find new group structures. The 1 January 2027 data-localisation deadline will show how many smaller operators survive the migration. And the fate of Bill SB.959, passed by the Senate on 10 November 2026 to let the CBN designate large fintechs as Systemically Important Institutions, will show whether this supervisory regime becomes statute. Until those tests resolve, the honest summary is this: Nigerian payments in November 2026 is a market where the regulator sets the architecture, operates the newest rail, fines the largest player, and lets the market compete only inside the lanes it has drawn.
