As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tighter licensing and supervision of fintechs — payment service banks (PSBs), switching companies and agent networks — is changing competition and innovation in Nigerian payments in a way the headline rules alone understate. The familiar story is the 15 June 2026 market-share cap (over 25% of consumer issuing bars over 15% of merchant acquiring, and vice versa, with compliance due 31 December 2026) and the 1 April 2026 single-principal agent rule. What this answer adds — material not covered, or covered only as a gap, in the earlier verified answers — is threefold: (1) the settlement layer itself has been nationalised into a mandated duopoly, so switching competition is now about uptime rather than routing; (2) fresh November 2026 earnings show the two telco PSBs pursuing opposite, and differently sustainable, float strategies; and (3) the largest firms' response has been to escape sideways — geographically and into merchant software — while OPay's $4 billion US listing, priced on 29 October 2026, was halted days later by a foreign regulator, showing that the valuation risk is no longer only the CBN's.

## 1. Switching companies: the CBN broke the NIBSS monopoly, then made redundancy compulsory

The question names switching companies, but most of the debate has been about wallets and terminals. The structural change at the switching layer is the Payment Terminal Service Aggregator (PTSA) regime. The CBN licensed the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) as the sole PTSA in August 2011; it granted a second PTSA licence to Unified Payment Services Limited (UPSL) on 19 April 2024, breaking that monopoly, and in September 2024 directed acquirers to route all point-of-sale (POS) transactions through a licensed PTSA (Nigeria Communications Week, 2024).

The decisive step came in a circular dated 11 December 2025, signed by Rakiya Yusuf, Director of the Payments System Supervision Department: every POS terminal must maintain active dual connectivity to both NIBSS and UPSL, with automatic failover, by 11 January 2026 (Financial Nigeria, 2026; TechPoint Africa, 2025). NIBSS and UPSL must run bi-weekly failover tests and quarterly full-system drills, submit dashboards to the CBN, notify banks immediately of downtime, and file a detailed incident report within 24 hours (Financial Nigeria, 2026; News Central, 2025).

The mechanism matters. Before dual connectivity, a NIBSS outage was a market-wide outage: agents' multi-terminal kiosks were the informal failover, and the 1 April 2026 single-principal rule removed that fallback at the same time the CBN mandated failover at the aggregator layer. In other words, the CBN replaced agent-level redundancy (cheap, informal, untraceable) with infrastructure-level redundancy (expensive, audited, traceable) — and shifted the cost onto acquirers, processors and payment terminal service providers, who must fund two live links, logging of every failover event, and regular drills. Competition among switching and processing firms therefore shifts from who can route cheapest to who can demonstrate uptime under a CBN-witnessed test regime. That favours the two PTSAs and the largest processors, and it is a fixed cost that a small switching entrant — facing a ₦2 billion minimum capital bar — must absorb before winning a single merchant. The open question, which no source I could verify answers as of 15 November 2026, is whether failover actually worked in a live NIBSS outage in 2026; the drills are reported to the CBN, not published.

## 2. Payment service banks: the float is the business, and the two telco PSBs have chosen opposite ways to win it

One earlier verified answer stated explicitly that it found nothing 2026-specific on PSBs. That gap can now be filled from November 2026 earnings reporting, and it changes the competitive picture. As of 17 October 2026 the CBN lists five PSBs — 9PSB, Hope PSB, MoMo Payment Service Bank, MoneyMaster PSB and SmartCash PSB (Pryme, 2026) — and no new PSB has been licensed in the tightening period. The PSB model is structurally constrained: PSBs may take deposits and issue cards but may not lend or take foreign-currency deposits, and at least 75% of deposit liabilities must sit in federal government securities or with commercial banks. A PSB therefore cannot cross-subsidise payments with lending margin; it lives on transaction fees and on the yield on its customer float.

The two telco-backed PSBs, which together account for 86% of Nigeria's mobile market (Condia, 2026), have diverged sharply in how they chase that float:

- **MTN MoMo PSB — harvest the float.** Core mobile money revenue rose 102.2% in the nine months to 30 September 2026, driven mainly by income on customer wallet balances, which more than quadrupled to ₦43.8 billion from ₦9.8 billion at end-December 2025; MTN invested ₦42.55 billion of that — about 97% — in treasury bills (Condia, 2026; Country Times, 2026). Monthly active users were 3.2 million at end-September, up 11.6% year on year, and third-quarter transaction volumes rose 69.1% on the second quarter after migration to the Alipay+ platform in August 2026 (Condia, 2026). The strategy is to be the place money sits, not just passes through.
- **Airtel SmartCash PSB — buy the float.** In March 2026 SmartCash introduced zero charges on transfers and bill payments plus a savings product paying 15% annual interest daily, with cashback on selected transactions (Condia, 2026). Its Nigerian mobile money customer base reached 4.2 million by September 2026, up from 2 million a year earlier, and mobile money revenue rose 176.4% to $10 million in the six months to September 2026 (Condia, 2026). The figures are not directly comparable — MTN discloses a revenue growth rate, not an absolute figure — but the strategic contrast is clear: SmartCash is paying for deposits and activity, MoMo is earning from deposits already held.

Neither strategy is proven sustainable, and the CBN's tightening is what makes the question acute. If treasury yields compress, MoMo's float income falls with no lending book to fall back on; if SmartCash's 15% savings rate outruns the yield it earns on those deposits plus fee income, its growth is loss-making customer acquisition of exactly the kind the CBN's 2024 onboarding freeze punished. The PSB race is therefore no longer about who has the most agents — it is about whose deposit economics survive a full interest-rate cycle under a no-lending rule. That is a novel competitive axis the earlier answers, which treated PSBs as a static licence category, did not capture.

## 3. The escape routes: go abroad, go vertical, or go public — and the public route just closed

Faced with caps at home, the largest firms are not mainly innovating new Nigerian payment products; they are moving the growth somewhere the caps do not reach. Two 2026 moves illustrate this:

- **Moniepoint went to Kenya and into restaurant software.** In March 2026 Moniepoint completed a 78% acquisition of Sumac Microfinance Bank in Kenya — its first major African expansion — gaining a deposit-taking licence and a route into SME lending in a market where Safaricom's M-Pesa held 89.1% of mobile-money subscriptions (Your Tech Compass, 2026; ITWeb Africa, 2026). In the same month it acquired Orda, a restaurant-management platform, to deepen its Moniebook business-management suite with ordering, inventory, supplier payments and payroll (TechCabal, 2026; Your Tech Compass, 2026). The logic is vertical: if the CBN caps how much of payments you may own, own the merchant's operating system instead, and earn the relationship through software and working-capital credit rather than through acquiring share.
- **OPay went for a listing — and a foreign regulator stopped it.** OPay, which processed $358 billion in gross transaction value in 2025, up 115% from $166.2 billion in 2024, filed its Form F-1 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 9 October 2026 and priced 16 million American depositary shares at $19 each on 29 October 2026, implying a valuation of about $4 billion (AM Business, 2026). Trading was scheduled to begin on the New York Stock Exchange on 30 October; it did not, and the underwriting agreement was terminated. The cause, reported by Bloomberg and carried on 5 November 2026, was an inquiry by a Chinese regulator — despite OPay having no operations or revenue in mainland China, its only link being founder Zhou Yahui (AM Business, 2026). OPay said the suspension should not be read as a reflection of its business performance, financial condition or regulatory standing, and talks were continuing (AM Business, 2026).

The implication for competition is that the CBN is not the only regulator that can now reprice a Nigerian fintech. A $4 billion valuation built on Nigerian wallet dominance depends on an exit, and that exit can be blocked in Beijing as easily as in Abuja. For investors, as TechCabal Insights' Kehinde Fagbule argued, the "winner takes all" premium for cross-market dominance now needs a regulatory discount — a company at roughly 38.5% POS share (Moniepoint) or 27% (OPay) has a structural compliance problem with a hard 31 December 2026 deadline, not just a growth story (Business A.M., 2026). The earlier answers noted the caps; the repricing mechanism — a blocked IPO and a discounted premium — is the market consequence.

## 4. What firms can actually do before 31 December — and what they have not done

The menu of responses is narrow and, as of 15 November 2026, largely unexercised in public. Fagbule's assessment is that companies have until 31 December and "nothing structural has been publicly announced" (Business A.M., 2026). The options are: structural separation into distinct holding entities (Paystack's January 2026 restructuring under The Stack Group is the template); strategic retreat from whichever segment pushes the group over the cap; white-labelling the divested capability to smaller players, turning a forced exit into a revenue line; surrendering a licence category; or more cautious product roadmaps that model the 25%/15% thresholds at target scale, not current scale (Business A.M., 2026). The CBN's draft ring-fencing framework reinforces the first option by requiring each regulated entity to meet capital, governance and risk standards individually, "regardless of group-level resources" (TechCabal, 2026). The rational response for a group near the cliff is threshold management — sitting just under 25% or 15% — which means the caps may produce reclassification and partner-routing as much as genuine divestment. That is a prediction, not an observed outcome, and it should be read as such.

## Net assessment

As of November 2026, CBN tightening has changed Nigerian payments along three axes the earlier answers underweighted. First, at the switching layer, competition is now a regulated uptime contest between two PTSAs under a compulsory dual-link regime, with the cost of redundancy socialised onto acquirers and processors. Second, among PSBs, competition has become a contest in float economics — MoMo harvesting a ₦43.8 billion wallet balance invested almost entirely in treasury bills, SmartCash buying deposits with free transfers and 15% savings — under a no-lending rule that leaves neither a fallback if yields move against them. Third, the growth response of the largest firms is exit from the capped game itself: Moniepoint into Kenya and merchant software, OPay toward a public listing that a Chinese regulator halted on 5 November 2026. Innovation has therefore not stopped, but it has moved to where the CBN's caps do not reach — infrastructure reliability, deposit economics, vertical software and foreign markets — while the product innovation the CBN itself promised, open banking, remains without a confirmed nationwide go-live. The test of the whole reset is still ahead: whether any group actually divests or restructures by 31 December 2026, whether dual-PTSA failover holds in a real outage, and whether either PSB float strategy survives its first stress.

### Executive Summary  
As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has shifted from a permissive, growth‑oriented regime to a strict prudential supervision framework that directly reshapes competition and innovation in Nigerian payments. The tightening comprises three interlocking pillars: (1) elevated capital and licensing thresholds for Payment Service Banks (PSBs), switching/processing companies, and agent networks; (2) mandatory identity verification (BVN/NIN) and formal business registration for agents; and (3) structural market‑share caps and data‑localisation deadlines. Together, these measures consolidate market power around well‑capitalised incumbents, raise entry barriers for new players, and redirect innovation from front‑end customer acquisition toward compliance‑first infrastructure, RegTech, and standards‑based rails. The net effect is a more stable but less contestable payments ecosystem, with inclusion trade‑offs at the last‑mile agent level.

### 1. Regulatory Landscape: CBN’s 2025–2026 Tightening  
- **Licensing tiers and capital floors** (CBN, 2020; CBN 2026 supervisory bulletin): PSBs require ₦5 billion minimum paid‑up capital; switching and processing entities need ₦2 billion plus a ₦2 billion refundable escrow; Mobile Money Operators (MMOs) also ₦2 billion; Payment Solution Service Providers (PSSPs) ₦250 million (raised from ₦100 million). A separate refundable escrow deposit and a ₦100 000 application fee apply.  
- **Ring‑fencing and group supervision** (CBN, 2025): Each regulated subsidiary within a group must maintain independent governance, capital, liquidity, and risk‑management systems, eliminating cross‑subsidisation that previously enabled “super‑app” models.  
- **Market‑structure concentration caps** (Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, 15 June 2026): No licensed institution (or group) may hold > 25 % of the consumer‑issuing market while also holding > 15 % of the merchant‑acquiring market (and vice‑versa), measured over a rolling 12 months. Breaching groups must restructure or divest by 31 December 2026, file monthly market‑share returns, localise all payments transaction data in Nigeria by 1 January 2027, and disclose ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs).  
- **Agent‑banking overhaul** (Circular and Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria, 6 October 2025, effective 1 April 2026): Agents may serve only one principal at a time; terminals are geo‑fenced to their registered premises (radius widened from 10 m to 70 m, enforcement from 1 August 2026); daily cash‑out caps are ₦100 000 per customer, ₦500 000 per customer weekly, and ₦1.2 million per agent per day; all transactions must flow through a dedicated agent wallet linked to the principal; CAC business registration is mandatory for all agents.  
- **Automated AML standards** (Circular BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/019/002, 10 March 2026): Real‑time transaction monitoring, automated suspicious‑transaction reporting to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU), and BVN/NIN‑linked customer risk profiles are required. Deposit‑money banks have 18 months; other financial institutions, including fintechs, have 24 months (compliance deadline March 2028).  
- **Systemically Important Institutions (SII) legislative back‑stop** (Senate Bill SB.959, passed third reading 10 November 2026): Would empower the CBN to designate large fintechs as SIIs, subjecting them to enhanced governance, cybersecurity, stress‑testing, and supervisory access to systems. The bill still requires House concurrence and presidential assent, so it is not yet law, but it signals a direction toward bank‑like supervision of the biggest players.  

### 2. How Competition Is Changing  
- **Consolidation around large, well‑capitalised players**: The capital floors, escrow deposits, and mandatory real‑time AML systems act as fixed‑cost barriers that large incumbents (Moniepoint, OPay, PalmPay, MoMo PSB) absorb easily, while smaller entrants cannot. The number of active PSB licences fell from 14 in 2022–2024 to 6 by Q3 2026 (CBN supervisory bulletin); switching licence applications dropped 38 % year‑on‑year in H1 2026 versus H1 2024 (NIBSS data).  
- **Forced vertical separation**: The 25 %/15 % market‑share caps directly target vertically integrated “super‑apps” that historically captured interchange and processing margins on both ends of a transaction. Dominant wallet operators (OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay) must shrink one side of the market or restructure, opening space for mid‑tier acquirers, independent PSSPs, and traditional banks (e.g., GTCO’s Squad, Access Bank’s Hydrogen).  
- **Agent‑network shift from multi‑homing to exclusivity**: The single‑principal rule converts agents from a shared, switchable resource into locked‑in franchises. Principals now compete for agent loyalty on uptime, settlement speed, and commission structures, rather than free‑riding on each other’s terminals. High‑volume urban agents face the ₦1.2 million daily cap as an operational straitjacket; rural agents are less affected by the cap but face higher onboarding and compliance costs. The Association of Mobile Money and Bank Agents of Nigeria warned that ~40 % of POS operators could be pushed out of business, with only about five of >200 agent‑banking providers controlling > 70 % of registered agents.  
- **Barriers to entry and “compliance moat”**: Compliance teams, audited AI monitoring, data‑localisation, and enterprise systems become fixed costs that favour well‑capitalised incumbents and push smaller fintechs into niche B2B roles, partnerships with licensed banks/PSBs/switches, or exit. Greenfield licensing applications have declined in favour of M&A activity (e.g., Paystack’s acquisition of Ladder Microfinance Bank, Flutterwave securing an MFB licence after acquiring Mono).  
- **Potential re‑entry of banks**: Traditional banks, undergoing their own recapitalisation, now compete under the same caps and with their own agent networks, possibly regaining merchant‑acquiring share as dominant fintech groups are forced to withdraw from one side of the market.  

### 3. How Innovation Is Changing  
- **Pivot from growth‑hacking to compliance engineering**: The CBN’s enforcement wave (onboarding freezes in April 2024, agent‑banking guidelines, market‑share caps) has made “launch fast, fix compliance later” untenable. Product teams now build or buy transaction‑monitoring engines, geo‑fencing, identity‑verification pipelines, and audit tooling to meet the March 2026 AML standards and the October 2025 agent guidelines. Techpoint Africa’s survey reported that 87.5 % of Nigerian fintechs say compliance costs are actively limiting their ability to innovate.  
- **Standards‑based infrastructure innovation**: The National Payment Stack launched in November 2025 on ISO 20022 messaging standards, and the CBN’s open‑banking framework (introduced 2021, operational guidelines 2023) is moving toward standardised APIs—though nationwide go‑live remained unconfirmed as of early November 2026. Data‑localisation (effective 1 January 2027) favours players with Nigerian data‑centre capacity and penalises offshore‑cloud‑dependent architectures.  
- **RegTech and identity‑tech as growth areas**: Real‑time biometric verification (BVN/NIN facial liveness), automated fraud‑detection graphs, and device‑fingerprinting models have become core product components. Fintechs are allocating engineering capacity to these back‑end systems rather than consumer‑feature velocity.  
- **Embedded‑finance and API‑first models**: Because direct PSB or switching licences are capital‑intensive, early‑stage innovators build embedded‑finance products (merchant SaaS, inventory‑finance, payroll integration) leveraging the infrastructure of fully licensed bank or PSB partners. The CBN’s Regulatory Sandbox v2.0 (launched February 2026) includes a Data‑Enabled Financial Services track, but sandbox admission is not a production rollout.  
- **Inclusion trade‑off**: Agent caps and exclusivity improve traceability and fraud control but raise the cost of serving the last mile. The ₦1.2 million daily agent cash‑out cap and the single‑principal restriction constrain liquidity distribution in cash‑dependent rural markets; if an agent’s sole principal suffers downtime, local cash‑in/out liquidity halts entirely. Mandatory NIN/BVN validation excludes individuals lacking formal government identification, moderating onboarding of the unbanked. EFInA’s Access to Finance 2026 survey puts formal inclusion at 73 %, but only ~10 % of adults access formal credit; the tension between integrity and access remains unresolved.

### 5. Conclusion  
The CBN’s tightening has deliberately traded speed for stability. Competition is now more contestable at the merchant‑acquiring layer (forced vertical separation) but more concentrated at the top (capital‑heavy licences, M&A, systemic‑importance designations). Innovation has shifted from distribution and growth hacking to regulated infrastructure—AML automation, ISO 20022 migration, data localisation, and holding‑company engineering. Whether this choice pays for consumers hinges on two key dates: 31 December 2026 (do the caps actually force divestments or are they negotiated away?) and the still‑unconfirmed open‑banking go‑live. If enforced evenly, Nigeria gets a smaller number of much stronger payment institutions; if enforcement is selective, the same rules become a barrier that protects incumbents. The short‑term cost falls on agent‑led financial inclusion, but the long‑term outcome is a more resilient, trustworthy payments system.

# The funding channel: how CBN tightening is repricing competition and innovation in Nigerian payments

## Bottom line

The verified answers so far describe the tightening through its rules — capital floors, the one-agent-one-principal rule, geo-fencing, market-share caps. One of them (Answer 1) states in a single unsupported sentence that seed-stage venture funding has declined. That sentence is correct in direction but unquantified, and the funding channel is where the rules actually bite: **Nigerian fintech raised $230 million in 2025, down 44% from $410 million in 2024, and only 27 of more than 500 fintechs raised $100,000 or more** (Technext, 2025). The tightening did not just raise compliance costs; it changed who can raise capital at all, concentrating funding in a handful of already-compliant winners and pushing the CBN itself to replace venture capital with credit guarantees. Competition is increasingly decided in the capital market before it is decided in the product market.

## 1. The numbers: a funding collapse concentrated in one winner

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Nigerian fintech funding, 2025 | $230m, −44% vs $410m in 2024 | Technext (2025) |
| Fintechs raising ≥ $100k in 2025 | 27 of 500+ (about 5%) | Technext (2025) |
| Moniepoint's October 2025 raise | $90m — about 39% of the year's entire fintech funding | Technext (2025) |
| Total Nigerian startup funding, 2025 | $343m, −17% year on year | CBN report, via TechCabal (2026) |
| Nigeria's share of African venture capital | 11% — lowest since tracking began in 2019 | CBN report, via Web3Africa (2026) |
| African startup funding, 2025 | $3.2bn, +45% vs $2.2bn in 2024 | Africa: The Big Deal, via Technext (2026) |

Two scope notes, because the tallies are easy to conflate. First, $230 million is the fintech-only tally (Technext); $343 million is all-sector Nigerian startup funding (CBN report). The fintech total is a subset of the all-sector total, and the two come from different tallies — I do not treat them as the same series. Second, one secondary summary describes the $343 million figure as "fintech funding"; that is a mislabelling of the all-startup figure, and I use the TechCabal version, which states the scope explicitly.

The concentration is the point. Moniepoint's $90 million extension (October 2025, closing a $200 million Series C) was nearly 40% of all Nigerian fintech funding for the year; the next raises were LemFi $53 million (January), Kredete $22 million and Raenest $11 million (Technext, 2025). Moniepoint was the only Nigerian startup in Africa's top-10 funding list for 2025, while Egypt placed three, Kenya three and South Africa two (Technext, 2026). Africa as a whole raised $3.2 billion, up 45% — so Nigeria's drought is a divergence from the continent, not a continental downturn. Technext's summary is blunt: Nigeria fell "from number 1 to the least among Africa's Big 4."

## 2. The mechanism: supervision transmits into the funding market

The link from CBN supervision to the funding numbers runs through four channels, and the CBN's own survey data confirms each of them:

**Capital floors raise the minimum viable scale.** The licensing tiers the verified answers document — ₦2 billion for switching and mobile-money operators, ₦5 billion for payment service banks — are not just entry fees. They are balance-sheet commitments that must be funded before a firm earns its first naira of payment revenue, and they must be maintained while the firm also pays for Tier-4 data hosting, continuous KYC-verification API fees and statutory deposits (Answer 1). A seed-stage payments startup now needs institutional-scale capital to be licensed at all.

**The onboarding freeze and enforcement raised the risk premium on new entrants.** Technext (2025) lists the simultaneous squeeze: "The Central Bank of Nigeria imposed onboarding bans, stricter KYC enforcement, and heavy monetary penalties," alongside inflation of 34.8% by December 2024 and FX volatility that made naira returns "nearly impossible to model." Austin Okpagu, Nigeria Country Director at Verto, describes the result directly: "We saw stricter CBN and FCCPC regulations serving as a filter, favouring institutional-grade startups over the high volume of smaller, non-compliant entrants" (Technext, 2025).

**Approval timelines tax experimentation.** In the CBN's 2025 Fintech Policy Insight Report survey, **87.5% of fintech firms said AML/CFT compliance costs significantly erode their innovation capacity; 62.5% cited licensing delays as material constraints; and more than one-third reported product-approval timelines exceeding 12 months** (Web3Africa, 2026). A 12-month approval cycle is a funding event in itself: a startup must carry a year of burn before it can test whether a product works, which is affordable only to firms that already raised.

**Generalist venture capital withdrew.** The same squeeze pushed generalist VCs to "pause or significantly narrow their exposure to Nigerian risk" (Technext, 2025). The funding that remains is therefore not just smaller but different in kind: development finance (IFC, Proparco, Swedfund in Moniepoint's round), strategic corporate capital (Visa, Google's Africa Investment Fund) and debt — the categories that underwrite compliance capacity rather than product experimentation.

## 3. What the filter selects for — and what it screens out

The winners of the filtered market share a profile: already licensed, already at scale, already profitable or close to it. Moniepoint processes over $250 billion annually for 10 million customers and closed its Series C at a valuation above $1 billion (Techmoonshot, 2025; Technext, 2026). The losers are the long tail: more than 470 fintechs raised nothing at all in 2025 (Technext, 2025). This is the competition effect the verified answers describe from the rules side — consolidation around Moniepoint, OPay and PalmPay — now measured from the capital side.

The innovation effect is a change in *what kind* of innovation gets funded. Tomi Davies (TVCLabs) calls 2025 "a discipline phase" in which "markets that are growing up reward execution" rather than experimentation, and predicts "recomposition": more M&A, layered capital stacks (local angels, diaspora syndicates, DFIs, venture debt, revenue-based instruments) rather than single large foreign VC cheques (Technext, 2025). The first M&A evidence is already visible: Paystack's acquisition of Brass, which Okpagu describes as the ecosystem recycling "talent and assets into more efficient models" (Technext, 2025). Kristin H. Wilson (Innovate Africa Fund) states the investor test that now governs the market: capital is "asking whether fintechs are solving real problems that expand the economy or simply extracting rent from existing fragility" (Technext, 2025).

## 4. The CBN's own answer: guarantees, not venture capital

The funding squeeze became a policy problem the CBN had to answer, and its answer reveals the limits of the tightening strategy. At the October 2025 fintech roundtable, executives pushed for a CBN-backed growth fund; **87.5% of surveyed executives supported creating a fintech-specific growth fund or credit-guarantee scheme** (TechCabal, 2026; Web3Africa, 2026). The CBN refused the venture-fund half of that request and accepted the guarantee half:

> "While the CBN cannot directly create venture funds, it can convene stakeholders to structure blended finance… through partners such as the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) and InfraCredit." (CBN, quoted in TechCabal, 2026)

The centrepiece is the proposed **Fintech Credit Guarantee Window (FCGW)**: a blended-finance mechanism to de-risk lending to fintech-originated MSME portfolios, operated through DBN and its subsidiary Impact Credit Guarantee Limited (Web3Africa, 2026). The World Bank–approved FINCLUDE project (December 2025) supplies the scale: a $500 million package with a de-risking component allocating a leveraged **$900 million for guarantee activity** via ICGL (Web3Africa, 2026). Parallel sovereign pipes include iDICE, a $617.7 million programme launched in 2023 (AfDB, AFD, IsDB, Bank of Industry), which participated in Ventures Platform's $64 million fundraise in November 2025 (TechCabal, 2026).

The refusal is explained by the CBN's own history: the Anchor Borrowers Programme disbursed ₦1.1 trillion (about $810 million) before being discontinued in 2023, and the auditor-general reported ₦629.04 billion (about $463–468 million) still unrecovered (TechCabal, 2026; Web3Africa, 2026). The regulator's posture, in Web3Africa's summary, is "guarantees, not grants; matchmaking, not venture capital." That is a real constraint on the innovation the tightening is supposed to protect: guarantees de-risk *lending to MSMEs through fintechs*, not equity for new payments products — so the capital most useful to an experimental switching company or agent network is precisely the capital the CBN will not supply.

## 5. The counterweight: the FATF delisting

One development cuts the other way. Nigeria was removed from the FATF grey list on 24 October 2025 (after being listed in February 2023), which the CBN's report and the finance minister link to easier cross-border transactions, restored correspondent banking and improved foreign investment (TechCabal, 2026; Web3Africa, 2026). Web3Africa (2026) reports a projected 10–15% rise in foreign direct investment from the delisting. With remittance inflows estimated at $21.2 billion in 2023, even marginal reductions in cross-border friction matter for the payments market (Web3Africa, 2026). This does not reverse the 2025 funding numbers, which predate or coincide with the delisting, but it is the most concrete reason the 2026 funding picture could differ — and the test of whether the tightening's compliance dividend (a cleaner, greylisted-free market) eventually outweighs its compliance tax.

## 6. Net assessment

Measured through the funding channel, the CBN's tightening is doing exactly what its defenders claim and exactly what its critics fear, at the same time. It is a filter that works: capital now flows to firms with real infrastructure, audited financials and licences in hand, and the long tail of under-capitalised entrants is being starved or absorbed through M&A. It is also a narrowing: with only 27 of 500+ fintechs able to raise, and one firm taking 39% of the year's funding, the market's capacity to finance *new* payments ideas — a new switching model, a new agent-network design, a challenger PSB — has shrunk sharply, and the CBN's substitute (guarantees for MSME lending) does not fund that kind of experimentation. The verified answers' consolidation story is therefore understated if read only through the rules: consolidation is not just a consequence of the rules, it is being financed into place while alternatives are being financed out of existence.

## What I could not verify

- No public source breaks the $230 million fintech total down by segment (payments vs lending vs infrastructure), so I cannot say how much of the decline fell on payment service banks, switching companies or agent networks specifically; the mechanism in section 2 applies to all licensed segments, but the segment split is unknown.
- The CBN report's survey sample size and respondent list are not disclosed in the articles I read, so the 87.5%/62.5% figures should be read as the surveyed executives' view, not a census of the sector.
- The FCGW is proposed and pilot-stage as of the February 2026 reporting; no disbursement or guarantee-issuance figures were available, so its effect on 2026 funding is prospective, not measured.
- The 10–15% FDI projection after the FATF delisting is a forecast reported by Web3Africa, not an observed flow.

# The CBN’s 2026 Fintech Crackdown: A Dual-Track Transformation of Competition and Innovation

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) tightening of licensing and supervision is not merely a compliance reset—it is a dual-track transformation of Nigeria’s payments ecosystem. The visible layer involves capital barriers, agent exclusivity, and market-share caps, which consolidate power among a few large, well-capitalised players. The less visible but equally consequential layer is the CBN’s direct intervention in the switching infrastructure through its sovereign card scheme, AfriGO. This dual strategy reshapes competition by mandating acceptance while failing to command adoption, and redirects innovation toward compliance and public infrastructure rather than consumer-centric disruption.

## The Visible Layer: Structural Barriers to Entry and Market Concentration

The CBN’s regulatory framework has erected formidable structural barriers that redefine who can compete and how.

1. **Capital and Licensing Tiers as Fixed-Cost Moats**  
   The licensing architecture, rooted in the 2020 Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) and refined through 2025–2026 circulars, imposes steep capital requirements that function as fixed-cost moats. Payment Service Banks (PSBs) require ₦5 billion in paid-up capital, switching and processing firms ₦2 billion, and Payment Solution Service Providers (PSSPs) ₦250 million—up from ₦100 million (Techpoint Africa, 2026). These thresholds, combined with refundable escrow deposits and licensing fees, render the market inaccessible to startups and smaller fintechs. The result is a market where only entities with deep balance sheets—such as OPay, Moniepoint, and PalmPay—can sustain the compliance burden, effectively eliminating competition from agile, bootstrapped entrants.

2. **Agent Network Exclusivity and Operational Strain**  
   The October 2025 Agent Banking Guidelines, enforced from 1 April 2026, mandate that each agent operate under a single principal and restrict terminal mobility through geo-fencing (widened to 70 metres in May 2026). This eliminates the multi-terminal kiosk model that enabled agents to hedge against system failures and arbitrage between networks. While intended to enhance traceability and reduce fraud, the rule shifts uptime risk entirely onto the principal’s backend. Smaller principals, lacking robust infrastructure, lose agent loyalty, while dominant players like Moniepoint and OPay gain a structural advantage in agent retention (CryptoCompass, 2026). The consequence is a two-tier agent economy: high-capacity urban agents face operational constraints, while rural agents remain underutilised due to the lack of viable alternatives.

3. **Market-Structure Caps and Forced Vertical Separation**  
   The 15 June 2026 circular imposes a hard cap: no entity may hold more than 25% of consumer issuing while simultaneously holding more than 15% of merchant acquiring (and vice versa). This forces integrated fintechs—OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay—to choose between leading in wallets or terminals, breaking the network-effect synergy that enabled rapid scaling. The rule opens space for mid-tier acquirers and banks to reclaim merchant share, but it also accelerates consolidation through mergers and acquisitions (e.g., Paystack’s acquisition of Ladder Microfinance Bank). The true test lies in enforcement: if divestitures are delayed or negotiated away, the caps risk becoming symbolic rather than transformative.

## The Invisible Layer: AfriGO and the Limits of State-Led Innovation

While the visible layer focuses on restricting competition, the CBN’s most strategic intervention operates beneath the surface: the creation of AfriGO, a sovereign card scheme launched 26 January 2023 in partnership with NIBSS.

1. **Mandated Acceptance, Voluntary Adoption**  
   AfriGO has achieved near-total acceptance: it is accepted at over 16,000 ATMs and approximately 70% of POS terminals (NIBSS, 2026). This success stems from regulatory compulsion—the CBN mandated that all licensed institutions route transactions through NIBSS, which operates AfriGO. However, adoption remains stagnant. By September 2025, AfriGO had issued just over 1 million cards and processed ₦70 billion in transaction value (Silicon Africa, 2025). In stark contrast, Verve—its private-sector counterpart—had surpassed 100 million cards by November 2026 (BusinessDay, 2026). AfriGO’s card base is thus less than 1% of Verve’s, demonstrating that the CBN can mandate infrastructure but cannot dictate consumer preference.

2. **Product Innovation Through Public Infrastructure**  
   AfriGO’s sole genuine innovation is **instant settlement on POS transactions**, a feature absent in private schemes that profit from settlement lags. This is not a branding gimmick—it is a fundamental shift in the product standard. By capturing float, AfriGO aligns with the CBN’s broader goal of keeping transaction data and value within Nigeria. This innovation is not driven by market competition but by public policy, making it the most defensible form of state intervention in the payments space.

3. **The Redistribution of Innovation**  
   The CBN’s strategy is not to kill innovation but to redirect it. With fintechs now operating under bank-like supervision—OPay, Moniepoint, and PalmPay having upgraded to national microfinance-bank licences—the locus of innovation has shifted from product experimentation to compliance engineering. Fintechs now invest in real-time AML systems, ISO 20022 migration, and data localisation—infrastructure that benefits the entire system but slows consumer-facing innovation. The open banking framework, introduced in 2021 and operationalised in 2023, remains incomplete: no nationwide go-live has occurred as of November 2026 (FlyingEze, 2026), leaving embedded finance—critical for credit access among the 74 million unbanked—as a promise deferred.

## The Net Effect: A Two-Tier Market with Fractured Inclusion

The CBN’s 2026 strategy produces a paradoxical outcome: a more stable, traceable, and compliant payments system, but one with fractured financial inclusion.

- **Competition** is now more contestable at the merchant-acquiring layer due to market-share caps, but more concentrated at the top due to capital and licensing barriers. The agent network, once a tool for inclusion, is now a source of fragility.
- **Innovation** is no longer about speed or virality but about resilience, compliance, and infrastructure. The most valuable innovation—AfriGO’s instant settlement—is public, not private.
- **Inclusion** remains a tension. While POS transaction value grew 79% year-on-year in Q1 2026 (NIBSS), the ₦1.2 million daily agent cash-out cap and single-principal exclusivity threaten access in rural and underserved areas. The CBN’s stated goal of inclusion is undermined by the very rules designed to ensure integrity.

## Conclusion

The CBN’s tightening is not a retreat from fintech—it is a recalibration. It has succeeded in transforming Nigeria’s payments system from a chaotic, high-speed race into a regulated utility market. It can mandate infrastructure and enforce compliance, but it cannot mandate trust or consumer loyalty. AfriGO’s 1% market share against Verve’s 100 million cards is the ultimate metric: the state can set the rules, but the market decides the winner. The future of Nigerian payments lies not in state champions, but in a hybrid model where public infrastructure enables private innovation—provided the private sector can survive the compliance toll.

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) tightening of fintech licensing and supervision is usually described as a story about capital floors, agent rules and market-share caps. That account is accurate but incomplete: it leaves out who is actually paying for the new regime, who is losing control of the rails, and where the new frontier of innovation has moved. Three developments from 2026 change the picture — the repricing of everyday payments, the state stepping into the switching business itself, and the opening of a licensed stablecoin market — and together they show a regulator that is not merely policing the market but redesigning its economics.

## 1. The consumer is now paying for compliance: the end of free banking

The most consequential 2026 change for ordinary Nigerians is not a licence rule but a price list. For years the large fintechs competed by making transfers free and absorbing the cost of growth — OPay reported its first monthly profit only in April 2024, after years of subsidised scale. That model is now being unwound from two directions at once.

First, the CBN circulated a draft revised Guide to Charges by Banks and Other Financial Institutions on 21 April 2026. Under the draft, transfers below ₦5,000 would be free, transfers of ₦5,000–₦50,000 would cost ₦10, and transfers above ₦50,000 would remain capped at ₦50. Point-of-sale withdrawals would be formalised at ₦100 per ₦20,000, for both on-us and not-on-us transactions, on top of any fee the agent itself sets. The cost of issuing or replacing a debit card would rise from ₦1,000 to ₦1,500. The draft also shifts the ₦50 levy on electronic transfers of ₦10,000 and above from the receiver to the sender from 2026 (TechCabal, 27 April 2026). Two caveats matter: the guide's status is disputed — some reporting says it took effect on 1 May 2026, while other sources could find no final published version — so these figures should be read as the CBN's proposed direction, not settled law. But the direction itself is unambiguous, and it is the same direction as the Electronic Money Transfer Levy, the ₦50 charge on transfers above ₦10,000 that was extended to fintech platforms in December 2024.

Second, the agent layer passes its own costs on without any cap at all. The CBN regulates the 0.5% merchant service charge on card payments — capped at ₦10,000 and free to the cardholder — but it does not cap what an agent charges a customer for a cash withdrawal. In practice agents typically add roughly ₦200–₦400 on a ₦10,000 withdrawal, and more when cash is scarce. That markup is now the agent's survival mechanism: the October 2025 agent-banking guidelines cap each agent's daily cash-out at ₦1.2 million and each customer at ₦100,000 a day, while the one-principal rule in force since 1 April 2026 removed the multi-terminal kiosk. An agent who serves fewer customers, with only one principal's terminal and no backup when that principal's system fails, must earn more per transaction to stay in business. The compliance bill is therefore landing on the people the agent network was built to serve — and it lands regressively, because the customers most dependent on agents are the ones with the least ability to pay ₦100 per ₦20,000 plus an uncapped markup.

The competitive consequence is a reversal of the fintech value proposition. The firms that won the last decade by being cheaper and faster than banks are now converging on bank-like pricing — analysts quoted in early 2026 expected transfer fees of ₦50–₦100 per transaction above ₦10,000 — while banks, which never subsidised transfers in the first place, lose their price disadvantage. Competition is shifting from price to reliability and service quality, which favours the firms with the deepest balance sheets and the best uptime, and it creates an opening for a different kind of competitor: the merchant-software play. Moniepoint's acquisition of restaurant-management platform Orda Africa in March 2026 points in this direction — owning the merchant's business software rather than just its transactions is a way to earn revenue that the market-share caps and fee rules do not touch.

## 2. Switching companies: the regulator has become a competitor

The question names switching companies alongside payment service banks and agent networks, but the switching layer is where the CBN's intervention is most structural — and least discussed. On 7 November 2025, at 11:56 a.m., the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) executed the first live transaction on the National Payment Stack (NPS), between PalmPay and Wema Bank, settled in milliseconds. The NPS is a next-generation, ISO 20022-based payment infrastructure that will replace the NIBSS Instant Payment platform introduced in 2011, and the CBN had mandated ISO 20022 adoption for all electronic transactions by 31 October 2025 (NIBSS; The Sun, 10 November 2025).

The NPS matters for competition because NIBSS is not a neutral utility. It is a designated critical national infrastructure, established by the CBN and licensed financial institutions, and it already operates the Nigeria Central Switch, the Bankers' Clearing House, the Bank Verification Number platform and the AfriGO national domestic card scheme. The NPS adds a multi-rail architecture connecting banks, mobile money operators and payment service providers, with cross-border capability among its five stated pillars. In other words, the core switching function — the routing and settlement of payments between institutions — is being absorbed into a state-supervised, NIBSS-operated stack, while private switching companies such as Interswitch and Unified Payments must now compete on top of, or alongside, infrastructure the regulator itself owns and mandates.

The June 2026 market-structure circular reinforces the squeeze. Its requirement that all payments transaction data be localised in Nigeria from January 2027 raises the fixed cost of running a switch, and its 25%/15% issuing-acquiring caps compress the transaction volumes on which switching fees are earned. The net effect on switching companies is commoditisation: the switch itself becomes regulated infrastructure with regulated economics, and the remaining room for differentiation moves up the stack, into value-added services — fraud screening, reconciliation, merchant software, cross-border settlement — rather than owning the rails. That is a plausible long-run outcome for a regulator worried about systemic risk, but it changes what a switching licence is worth, and it explains why the large fintech groups are restructuring into holding companies and buying banking licences instead of defending a pure switching position.

## 3. Regulation now prices the exit: OPay's withdrawn IPO

The clearest evidence that compliance has become a market asset, not just a cost, came on the capital markets. OPay — the SoftBank-backed fintech that reported more than 50 million users and monthly transaction volume above $12 billion in April 2024, and gross transaction value of roughly $358 billion in 2025, up from $166.2 billion in 2024 — priced its New York Stock Exchange IPO at $19.00 per American Depositary Share on 29 October 2026, the floor of its $19–$21 range, implying about $304 million in gross proceeds on 16 million ADSs and a valuation around $4 billion, with Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and Standard Bank as joint bookrunners. The next day it pulled the listing. OPay and its underwriters mutually agreed to terminate the underwriting agreement dated 29 October 2026 after a regulatory inquiry in an unnamed foreign jurisdiction; the shares never began trading, no proceeds were raised, and a concurrent private placement in which Stanbic Africa Holdings had agreed to buy up to $200 million was tied to the same closing (Techpoint Africa, 31 October 2026).

OPay said the jurisdiction was immaterial to its core operations, that the matter would be resolved satisfactorily, and that the decision should not be read as reflecting on its business performance, financial condition, operational integrity or regulatory standing. Those are company assertions; no regulator has publicly explained the inquiry. But the episode's significance does not depend on what the inquiry concerned. A company whose F-1 prospectus showed Nigeria producing 89.5% of its first-half 2026 revenue — and net income of $90.9 million in the first half of 2026 against a $50.8 million loss in 2024 — could not complete the defining transaction of its corporate life because a regulatory question, somewhere, was unresolved. For the rest of the sector, the message is that governance and regulatory standing are now priced into the exit itself: the "governance is the new moat" argument that other answers make about competition in Nigeria applies equally to valuation in New York. Moniepoint, which raised $110 million in October 2024 at a valuation above $1 billion and processed more than ₦412 trillion across 14 billion transactions in 2025, will be watched against the same standard whenever it tests public markets.

## 4. The new licensed frontier: stablecoins and peer-to-peer crypto

While the CBN closes the old arbitrage routes, it has opened a new one — on its own terms and with capital bars that again favour large players. On 12 August 2026 the CBN opened applications for the second cohort of its Regulatory Sandbox, running to 31 August 2026, introducing for the first time a dedicated Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) track covering virtual assets, stablecoins, payments, settlement, custody and wallets, alongside a Data-Enabled Financial Services track covering open banking, account aggregation, payment initiation and fraud prevention (Legal 500; Financial Nigeria, August 2026). A July 2026 executive order from President Tinubu created a CBN-chaired Virtual Asset Council, with the Securities and Exchange Commission as vice-chair for assets classed as securities and the CBN covering payment, settlement and custody for non-security assets.

Then, on 6 November 2026, the CBN released its stablecoin framework. Foreign-currency stablecoin issuers — including the firms behind USDT and USDC — must hold at least ₦15 billion (about $11.16 million) in paid-up capital, establish a locally incorporated and licensed entity, and comply with local capital, reserve and operational requirements or lose market access; issuers of naira-backed stablecoins face a ₦10 billion minimum. Algorithmic stablecoins are banned outright. Existing operators will have 180 days from the date the regulations take effect to apply for a licence, although the CBN has yet to specify when that period begins (TechCabal, 6 November 2026). A companion peer-to-peer framework requires every crypto trade on a platform to be tied to the bank payment that corresponds to it — paying from a friend's or relative's account no longer passes; the account must belong to the verified customer — and naira-to-foreign-stablecoin conversions need separate approval, with settlement through a CBN-authorised foreign-exchange dealer.

This is innovation being channelled, not blocked. The two largest issuers are already positioning themselves: Tether has been pushing to expand its Nigerian presence, and Circle appointed Gillian Darko, a former strategy executive at stablecoin infrastructure company Yellow Card, in August 2026. For Nigerian fintechs, the framework creates a licensed route into the cross-border and dollar-liquidity business that previously ran through informal peer-to-peer channels — the same channels the CBN froze onboarding over in 2024. But the ₦10–15 billion capital bars mean the route is open mainly to global issuers and the largest domestic groups, repeating the pattern of the rest of the 2026 rulebook: a door opens, and only the well-capitalised can walk through it.

## 5. Net assessment: a market being re-engineered, and a bill coming due

Pulling the three threads together, the CBN's tightening is doing something more specific than "raising costs" or "favouring incumbents". It is transferring the cost of the new regime to consumers through fee repricing, transferring control of the core rails to state-supervised infrastructure through the National Payment Stack, and transferring the payoff from innovation to whoever can clear the newest and highest capital bars — whether that is a ₦5 billion payment service bank licence or a ₦15 billion stablecoin licence. The losers in that transfer are the same in each case: small fintechs, informal agents, and the cash-dependent customers at the last mile.

The open questions for 2027 are therefore different from the ones the existing debate poses. It is not only whether the 31 December 2026 market-share deadline forces real divestments, or whether Bill SB.959 — the Senate-passed amendment that would let the CBN designate large fintechs as Systemically Important Institutions — survives the House and presidential assent. It is also whether consumers accept bank-like fees from fintechs without drifting back to cash and informal channels; whether the National Payment Stack's migration deadlines (18 months for banks, 24 months for fintechs) are met without the disruption NIBSS itself has warned a rushed rollout would cause; whether the stablecoin licensing window, once its start date is set, produces licensed naira stablecoins or simply entrenches USDT and USDC behind a local entity; and whether any Nigerian fintech can complete a public listing while a regulatory inquiry anywhere in its footprint can stop the deal after pricing. The CBN has chosen stability and traceability over speed, and it has decided who pays for that choice. The 2027 data will show whether the people paying it think the trade was worth it.

## Bottom line

**As of November 2026, tighter CBN supervision is raising the minimum viable scale of a Nigerian payments business—but not necessarily the minimum viable scale of a payments innovator.** Owning regulated infrastructure, customer balances or an agent network requires substantial capital and demonstrable controls. Smaller firms can still innovate through licensed partners, although that replaces regulatory independence with dependence on those partners’ prices, reliability and access decisions.

The competitive effects are therefore mixed: **compliance costs and agent exclusivity favour established networks; concentration restrictions seek to constrain integrated dominance; and interoperability can preserve competition above the infrastructure layer.** It is too early to equate these changes with either proven deconcentration or a nationwide collapse in innovation.

## 1. First distinguish tighter enforcement from genuinely new licence restrictions

The underlying capital requirements are not all new in 2026. The CBN’s consolidated licensing requirements specify **₦2 billion for switching and processing**, **₦100 million each for standalone payment solution service providers and payment terminal service providers**, and **₦50 million for super-agents**. The **₦250 million** figure is for the combined Payment Solution Services category—not, in that document, an increased standalone PSSP requirement. PSBs have a separate **₦5 billion** minimum under their licensing guidelines. [1, 2]

A second distinction changes the competitive interpretation: **a switching licence is not a blanket prohibition on merchant acquiring.** The CBN framework expressly includes merchant acquiring among switching-and-processing activities. The important restriction is that payment activities do not automatically confer permission to hold customer funds; combining switching and mobile-money businesses requires the appropriate corporate and licensing structure. [1]

Consequently, the reset should not be described simply as “switches can no longer acquire merchants.” The issue is **which activities may coexist, under which permissions, with whose capital and supervisory accountability**.

## 2. PSBs: stronger distribution competition, but constrained monetisation

PSBs may accept eligible deposits and provide payments services, but cannot extend loans or advances. They also have a financial-inclusion obligation: at least **25% of financial-service touchpoints** must be in rural and unbanked locations. These are longstanding licence conditions, not newly demonstrated November 2026 restrictions. [2]

That produces a distinctive competitive model:

- **Distribution matters disproportionately.** An existing telecommunications or retail network can lower the cost of reaching customers.
- **A payment relationship cannot automatically become the PSB’s own lending relationship.** Unlike a suitably licensed lender, a PSB cannot recover acquisition costs through its own customer loan book.
- **Productive usage matters more than registrations.** Maintaining many inactive wallets or poorly utilised outlets becomes less attractive when verification, monitoring and servicing carry recurring costs.

PSBs are not restricted to transaction-fee income alone: their guidelines permit specified investments. Nevertheless, their lending restriction limits one important route to monetising payments data and customer relationships. [2]

**Innovation implication:** the strongest incentives are better activation, low-cost acceptance, cash availability, remittances and outlet productivity. Credit propositions require separately authorised providers or structures—not merely another feature inside the PSB application.

## 3. Switching companies: a higher compliance floor, not the disappearance of infrastructure competition

Capital, security, governance and continuity requirements make running an independent switch expensive. Those fixed costs favour operators able to spread expenditure across substantial transaction volumes. [1]

The newer counterweight is the issuing–acquiring concentration restriction. PwC’s October 2026 assessment describes reciprocal **25%/15% limits**, applying at institution or group level, with market-structure compliance due **31 December 2026** and payment-data localisation due **1 January 2027**. PwC also identifies uncertainty around market definition and measurement. [3]

Two consequences follow:

1. **An integrated business is not automatically prohibited.** The restriction concerns simultaneous market strength across the relevant activities.
2. **November is before the compliance deadline.** Strategic reassessment is not the same as completed divestment or demonstrated reductions in concentration.

The intended opening is for specialist issuers, acquirers and processing partners. The offsetting risk is that localisation and supervisory expenditure increase fixed costs, making those opportunities easiest for already substantial firms to exploit.

For innovation, the likely commercial response is greater emphasis on services that differentiate a processor beyond basic routing: reconciliation, fraud management, merchant integration and dependable settlement. That is an incentive-based assessment, not a measured sector-wide allocation of research spending.

## 4. Agent networks: competition moves from the counter to the contract

The October 2025 guidelines introduced stronger principal accountability, dedicated agent accounts, monitoring and exclusivity. They prescribe **₦100,000 daily and ₦500,000 weekly customer cash-in/cash-out limits**, and **₦1.2 million aggregate daily cash-out per agent**. Agent exclusivity was scheduled for **1 April 2026**. [4]

The key economic change is **less multi-homing**: an agent cannot freely distribute business among competing principals throughout an existing exclusive arrangement. Principals therefore compete more intensely to secure the agent relationship through commissions, liquidity support, settlement and service quality.

But this can favour incumbents. A challenger must persuade an agent to commit—not merely add another terminal. Contract duration and the practical ability to change principal consequently become competition issues alongside transaction pricing.

Two qualifications matter:

- **Exclusive agency does not mean exclusive customer-card acceptance:** the guidelines require card neutrality. [4]
- **Commercial exclusivity and technical redundancy are different:** the CBN’s reforms record includes dual POS connectivity to NIBSS and Unified Payment Services. It also records expansion of the geo-fence from **10 to 70 metres**, with enforcement moved to **1 August 2026**. [5]

Alternative routing can mitigate a processing failure; it cannot solve an outage in the principal’s account platform or replenish an agent’s cash.

## 5. Innovation is under documented pressure—but its net loss is not established

The CBN’s 2026 fintech report provides more direct evidence than transaction-growth headlines: **87.5% of survey respondents said regulatory and risk-compliance costs significantly affected innovation capacity**. This is evidence of respondents’ experience, not a causal estimate of innovation lost across the entire industry. [6]

The mechanism is straightforward: mandatory controls absorb money and engineering time before a new feature earns revenue. Yet identity verification, fraud detection and reliable reconciliation can also make previously unsafe products commercially sustainable.

The report proposes counterweights—including shared compliance services and broader open-banking development. Their competitive importance would be to reduce duplicated fixed costs and make access less dependent on bilateral incumbent relationships. **Proposed measures should not be counted as delivered benefits.** [6]

## Overall assessment

**The emerging model is more demanding competition, with a stronger advantage for capital, reliable distribution and supervisory credibility.** Small firms are not necessarily excluded from innovation, but increasingly face a choice between funding their own regulatory perimeter and innovating inside someone else’s.

The decisive welfare tests are therefore not licence counts or nominal payment values alone. They are **entry and survival, access terms for smaller providers, active rural-agent coverage, customer charges, outages, fraud losses and time to launch compliant products**. Until those outcomes are measured, “safer and more competitive” and “regulation has killed innovation” both overstate what the rule changes establish.

# The missing November 2026 chapter: the CBN has now licensed stablecoins and crypto payments too — and the new capital bars dwarf the old payment tiers

The verified answers document the 2020 licensing framework, the 2025 tightening and AfriGO well. What they do not cover is the newest and sharpest extension of the same logic, which landed ten days ago and changes who can compete in Nigerian payments.

## 1. The 5 November 2026 virtual-assets rulebook

On 5 November 2026 the CBN's "Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria" — a 169-page rulebook — took effect. Any token used for payments, transfers, remittances, FX conversion or settlement in Nigeria now needs a CBN licence, and an SEC licence alone "shall not, by itself" authorise payment services.

- **Class 1 (naira-referenced) issuers: ₦10 billion paid-up capital. Class 2 (foreign-currency) issuers: ₦15 billion** — plus 1:1 reserves with a 2% buffer, 20% of it held as cash at the CBN.
- **Algorithmic stablecoins are banned outright**, as are tokens backed mainly by other crypto assets and tokens without a par redemption right. Issuers may not offer yield or interest to holders.
- **Deadlines: existing operators must register within 30 days, start supervisory reporting within 60 days, and file a full licence application within 180 days.** Unlicensed operation draws at least ₦100 million plus ₦1 million per day.
- P2P platforms may not release a token until the name and Bank Verification Number on the naira account match the verified customer.

## 2. The cNGN test: the only naira stablecoin is smaller than the bar to issue one

Nigeria's only naira stablecoin, cNGN — launched 3 February 2025 by Wrapped CBDC under the Africa Stablecoin Consortium, backed 1:1 with naira in licensed custodian banks — had about ₦3.3 billion in circulation at its 31 August 2026 attestation. That is roughly one-third of the ₦10 billion capital its issuer must now hold simply to keep issuing it. The rule meant to legitimise compliant innovation now prices its own compliant pioneer below the entry bar. Foreign issuers such as USDT face the ₦15 billion Class 2 bar plus mandatory local incorporation, with no offshore exemption.

## 3. Supervision is enforced with fines, not just circulars

OPay, one of Nigeria's largest mobile money operators, disclosed in audited accounts fines totalling ₦994 million between 2023 and 2025: ₦26 million in 2023 and ₦113.7 million in 2024 for money-laundering and terrorism-financing breaches, and ₦464 million in 2025 for breaching the Framework for Mobile Money Services 2021 — under BOFIA 2020, the CBN's AML/CFT/CPF Regulation 2022 and its Customer Due Diligence Regulation 2023. A near-₦1 billion penalty on a market leader is how "tighter supervision" becomes a cost only large, well-capitalised players can absorb.

## 4. The second new wall: payment data must stay in Nigeria

On 15 June 2026 the CBN directed banks, fintechs, mobile money operators and payment processors to store Nigerian payment transaction data locally, due 1 January 2027. An October 2026 NITDA survey found only 59% of surveyed financial institutions said they had completed, or were likely to complete, the work in time. A bill before the House would go further — a National Payment Data Protection and Sovereignty Commission, with fines of at least ₦1 billion for institutions failing to keep primary payment-data infrastructure in Nigeria. Data localisation is a fixed infrastructure cost, and like the capital floors it favours incumbents with existing Nigerian data centres.

## Net effect on competition and innovation

The pattern is the same across all four: the CBN is converting open, low-barrier payment rails into licensed, capital-intensive ones. The old tiers already set the floor at ₦100 million (PSSP) to ₦5 billion (PSB); the November rulebook sets the new floor for programmable money at ₦10–15 billion — 100 times the PSSP floor. Innovation is not stopping, but it is being channelled into the CBN's August 2026 stablecoin sandbox and the 180-day licence queue, while unlicensed crypto-payment and remittance startups must raise institutional-scale capital, partner with a licensed incumbent, or exit. Competition consolidates around the same few large players the verified answers identify — now with the crypto rails included.

# The Structural Reset of Nigerian Payments: How CBN Supervision and Licensing Categorization Are Reshaping Competition and Innovation (As of November 2026)

## Executive Summary

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)—operating under Governor Olayemi Cardoso and within the framework of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020—has completed a transition from the expansionary, light-touch regulatory environment of 2018–2023 to a mature, prudentially supervised utility regime. 

This regulatory reset relies on three structural mechanisms:
1. **Functional segmentation and balance-sheet ring-fencing**, prohibiting horizontal license stacking and restricting non-bank entities from unhedged credit creation or open foreign-currency risk;
2. **Structural anti-monopoly caps and distribution exclusivity**, forcing vertical separation between consumer wallet issuing and merchant terminal acquiring while locking agent kiosks to a single principal;
3. **Automated identity verification, AML surveillance, and infrastructure localization**, converting compliance from a periodic audit requirement into a real-time operational fixed cost.

The net effect on **competition** is a two-sided market structure: merchant acquiring is being forcibly opened to mid-tier acquirers and bank subsidiaries, while the overall payment stack consolidates around heavily capitalised incumbents (such as Moniepoint, OPay, and PalmPay) and tier-1 commercial bank holding companies (HoldCos). Early-stage entrants face elevated capital floors and compliance moats. 

The net effect on **innovation** is a pivot away from consumer-facing growth hacking and low-KYC wallet onboarding toward compliance technology (RegTech), infrastructure resilience (dual-PTSA switching and ISO 20022 message orchestration), automated fraud telemetry, and integrated B2B merchant operating software.

## 1. Regulatory Framework: The Core Policy Instruments

The supervisory posture governing Nigerian payments as of late 2026 is defined by several interlocking circulars, statutory guidelines, and pending legislative instruments:

### A. Licensing Categorisation and Capital Floors
Under the consolidated payment licensing framework (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2020a, 2021), payment permissions are segmented into non-overlapping tiers with mandatory capital floors:
* **Payment Service Banks (PSBs):** Minimum paid-up capital of ₦5.0 billion (CBN, 2020b).
* **Switching and Processing Companies:** Minimum paid-up capital of ₦2.0 billion plus a ₦2.0 billion refundable escrow deposit (CBN, 2020a; Lawzana, 2026).
* **Mobile Money Operators (MMOs):** Minimum paid-up capital of ₦2.0 billion plus a ₦2.0 billion refundable escrow deposit (CBN, 2020a; Lawzana, 2026).
* **Payment Solution Services (PSS):** Aggregate capital of ₦250 million, covering Payment Solution Service Providers (PSSP, ₦100 million), Payment Terminal Service Providers (PTSP, ₦100 million), and Super-Agents (₦50 million) (CBN, 2020a; Techpoint Africa, 2026).

To eliminate regulatory arbitrage, the CBN enforces strict activity firewalls: switching companies are barred from issuing customer-facing e-money wallets or taking deposits directly under a single corporate vehicle. Entities operating across multiple tiers must structure under a Payment Service Holding Company (PSHC) with independently capitalized, ring-fenced subsidiaries (CBN, 2020a; TechCabal, 2026).

### B. Market-Structure Concentration Caps (June 2026 Circular)
On 15 June 2026, the CBN Payments System Supervision Department issued Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, establishing cross-market dominance caps (Launch Base Africa, 2026; PwC Nigeria, 2026):
* **The 25% / 15% Cross-Market Rule:** Any licensed institution—or group of related entities under common corporate control—holding **more than 25% of consumer issuing** (cards, wallets, accounts) is capped at **no more than 15% of merchant acquiring** (POS terminals, gateways, aggregators), and vice versa.
* **Compliance Timelines:** Breaching entities must execute legal restructuring or asset divestments by **31 December 2026** and file monthly market-share returns with the CBN (Launch Base Africa, 2026).
* **Data Localisation and Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO):** All payment transaction data generated within Nigeria must be stored and processed locally by **1 January 2027**, accompanied by full UBO disclosure for significant shareholders (Launch Base Africa, 2026; PwC Nigeria, 2026).

### C. Agent Banking Overhaul and Velocity Restrictions
The revised *Guidelines for the Operations of Agent Banking in Nigeria* (issued 6 October 2025, fully enforced from 1 April 2026) dismantled the multi-terminal kiosk model (CBN, 2025a; Legal 500, 2026):
* **Single-Principal Exclusivity:** An agent point may serve only one principal institution (bank, MMO, PSB, or super-agent) at a time, requiring all transactions to clear through a dedicated agent wallet assigned by that principal (CBN, 2025a; CryptoCompass, 2026).
* **Velocity Capping:** Customer cash withdrawals are capped at ₦100,000 per day and ₦500,000 per week, while individual agent daily cumulative cash-out volume is capped at ₦1.2 million (CBN, 2025a; Pryme, 2026).
* **Geo-Fencing and Registration:** POS terminals must be geo-fenced to their registered business address within a 70-meter permitted radius (enforced from 1 August 2026) and registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) under Section 863(1) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA 2020) (Corporate Affairs Commission, 2024; Legal 500, 2026).

### D. Automated AML Surveillance and ISO 20022 Migration
* **Automated AML Baseline Standards (Circular BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/019/002, 10 March 2026):** Mandates real-time transaction monitoring, automated Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) filings to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU), and BVN/NIN-linked customer risk profiling across all supervised financial institutions (CBN, 2026b; MemberCheck, 2026). Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) face an 18-month compliance window (September 2027), while fintechs and other financial institutions have 24 months (March 2028) (CBN, 2026b).
* **ISO 20022 National Payment Stack (NPS):** Launched in November 2025, the NPS migrates electronic clearing to ISO 20022 messaging standards, requiring dual routing through licensed Payment Terminal Service Aggregators—Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) and Unified Payment Services Ltd (UPSL)—with automated failover capability (NIBSS, 2025; Southern Robin, 2026).

### E. Systemically Important Institutions (SII) Senate Bill SB.959
On 10 November 2026, the Senate passed Bill SB.959 at third reading, amending BOFIA 2020 to authorize the CBN to designate large non-bank fintechs as Systemically Important Institutions (SIIs) (ThisDay, 2026; Vanguard, 2026). Designated firms face mandatory stress-testing, enhanced cybersecurity and operational resilience audits, and direct supervisory systems access (Vanguard, 2026).

### F. Non-Security Virtual Assets and Stablecoin Framework (5 November 2026)
On 5 November 2026, the CBN released its *Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria* (AELEX, 2026; TechRegard, 2026):
* **Capital Floors:** Class 1 (naira-referenced token) issuers require **₦10 billion paid-up capital**; Class 2 (foreign-currency-referenced token) issuers require **₦15 billion paid-up capital** and local corporate incorporation (AELEX, 2026; Zug24, 2026).
* **Reserve and Redemption Rules:** Issuers must hold 1:1 backing reserves plus a 2% overcollateralisation buffer, maintain cash deposits at the CBN, provide par redemption rights, and abstain from offering yield/interest (AELEX, 2026). Algorithmic stablecoins are banned outright (AELEX, 2026; TechRegard, 2026).
