# Legislative and executive authority under the 2008 Falkland Islands Constitution

## Overview

The **Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008** (SI 2008/2846), whose Constitution entered into force on **1 January 2009**, combines substantial internal self-government with continuing United Kingdom sovereignty and ultimate Crown authority.

In broad terms:

- The **Legislative Assembly** enacts most domestic legislation and controls local taxation and appropriations, subject to the Constitution.
- The **Falkland Islands Government** administers local public services, while elected legislators participate in central executive policymaking through the **Executive Council**.
- Formal executive authority remains vested in **the Crown** and is exercised locally by the **Governor**, rather than by a locally elected prime minister or cabinet.
- On most domestic matters, the Governor must consult the Executive Council and ordinarily act on its advice.
- The Governor has expressly defined special responsibilities for **external affairs and defence**, and for **internal security, including the police**, together with other powers conferred by particular constitutional provisions.
- The United Kingdom retains important reserve controls: instructions to the Governor through a Secretary of State, disallowance of local laws, and the preserved power of the Crown in Council to legislate for the Islands.

All section references below are to the Constitution contained in the 2008 Order as made.

## 1. Legislative authority

### The Legislative Assembly’s domestic lawmaking power

The Constitution assigns the Islands’ ordinary lawmaking function to a legislature consisting of **the Crown and the Legislative Assembly**. Subject to the Constitution, the legislature may make laws for the **“peace, order and good government of the Falkland Islands.”** This is a broad domestic power covering matters such as local public services, regulation, taxation and public finance, but it cannot be used to override the Constitution, its fundamental-rights protections, or its allocation of reserved responsibilities (s. 39; United Kingdom, 2008).

The Legislative Assembly consists of:

- **Eight elected members**; and
- Two ***ex officio* members**, namely the **Chief Executive** and the **Financial Secretary**, who are **not entitled to vote** in the Assembly (s. 27(1)–(2)).

The Assembly has its own **Speaker**; the Governor is not its ordinary presiding officer. Consequently, elected members control the Assembly’s voting business even though senior appointed officials participate in its proceedings.

The Assembly’s legislative power is accompanied by financial-constitutional controls. In particular, measures imposing or increasing taxation, charging money on public funds, or authorising expenditure are subject to the Constitution’s requirements concerning governmental recommendation and appropriation. The result is that the Assembly authorises public revenue and expenditure, but within rules intended to coordinate spending proposals with the administration’s financial responsibilities.

### Crown and United Kingdom controls over legislation

Local legislative competence is extensive, but it is not sovereign or legally unlimited.

| Control | Constitutional effect |
|---|---|
| **Assent by the Governor** | A bill passed by the Assembly must be presented to the Governor. Acts in the monarch’s name, and the Constitution provides for assent, refusal of assent, or reservation of a bill for the monarch’s pleasure, subject to the applicable constitutional provisions and instructions (s. 41). |
| **Disallowance** | A local law that has received assent may subsequently be disallowed by the Crown acting through a **Secretary of State**. Disallowance is therefore a continuing UK reserve safeguard, not merely a historical survival (s. 42). |
| **Crown-in-Council legislation** | The Order expressly preserves the Crown’s power, acting in Council, to make laws for the Falkland Islands. The creation of the Legislative Assembly did not transfer ultimate constituent authority to the Islands (s. 43). |
| **Constitutional supremacy** | Because the Assembly’s power is expressly “subject to” the Constitution, it cannot use an ordinary local law to abolish the Governor’s constitutional functions, extinguish the reserved Crown powers, or remove the Constitution’s rights protections. |

These mechanisms do **not** mean that every routine local bill must first be drafted or approved in London. The ordinary sequence is local Assembly legislation followed by gubernatorial assent. Disallowance and legislation by Order in Council stand above that process as reserve powers.

## 2. Executive authority

### Formal authority: the Crown and the Governor

Section 55 vests the executive authority of the Falkland Islands in **the Crown**. Subject to the Constitution, that authority is exercised on the Crown’s behalf by the **Governor**, either directly or through officers subordinate to the Governor.

The Governor is appointed by the monarch and is not elected by, or constitutionally responsible to, the Legislative Assembly in the manner of a prime minister. The Governor may also receive instructions from the Crown transmitted through a UK **Secretary of State**. Thus, the Constitution does not establish a Westminster-style local cabinet in which elected ministers collectively possess the whole executive power.

### Local administration and the Executive Council

Local administration is nevertheless substantial. The **Falkland Islands Government**, headed administratively by the **Chief Executive**, operates government departments and delivers domestic public services.

The central constitutional link between elected representatives and executive policymaking is the **Executive Council**. Under section 57(1), it comprises:

- **Three elected members of the Legislative Assembly**, chosen from the elected membership; and
- Two ***ex officio* members**, the **Chief Executive** and the **Financial Secretary**.

The Governor presides over the Council’s proceedings. The Council provides high-level policy advice, but its elected members do not thereby become an independent sovereign cabinet.

### The normal rule for domestic business

Sections 64 and 65 establish the ordinary decision-making rule:

1. The Governor must **consult the Executive Council** when exercising executive functions, unless the case falls within a constitutional exception.
2. After consultation, the Governor must generally **act in accordance with the Council’s advice**.
3. Departures from that advice are governed by specific constitutional grounds and procedures, not by an unrestricted personal discretion.

For an ordinary domestic-policy matter, the practical chain is therefore:

**local administration and elected policy input → Executive Council consideration and advice → action by the Governor, normally in accordance with that advice.**

This arrangement gives elected representatives meaningful participation in domestic government while leaving formal executive authority with the Crown.

## 3. Powers reserved to, or specially exercised by, the Governor

It is important to distinguish the Governor’s two expressly designated **special-responsibility fields** from other powers that the Constitution assigns to the Governor under separate provisions.

### A. External affairs and defence — section 66

The Governor has special responsibility for **the conduct of external affairs and defence**. These matters remain within the Crown/United Kingdom framework, and the Governor exercises the relevant functions subject to the Constitution and applicable instructions received through a Secretary of State.

Accordingly:

- The Falkland Islands do not possess an independent foreign policy or separate sovereignty in international relations.
- Defence is not an ordinary domestic portfolio controlled by the Legislative Assembly or by the elected members of the Executive Council.
- Local representatives may express and advance local interests, but that does not transfer ultimate responsibility for external relations or defence from the Crown/UK structure.

### B. Internal security, including the police — section 67

The Governor also has special responsibility for **internal security, including the police**. Policing and internal security therefore have a distinct constitutional status; they are not simply ordinary departmental matters subject to unrestricted direction by elected politicians.

These two provisions—sections 66 and 67—are the Constitution’s express list of gubernatorial special-responsibility fields. **The civil service and the administration of justice should not be added to that list.** Public-service appointments and discipline are dealt with through their own constitutional provisions and safeguards, while courts and judicial authority are addressed separately in the judicature chapter. In particular, judicial independence means that the Governor’s executive office does not entail personal control over court decisions or a reserved executive portfolio called “the administration of justice.”

### C. Consultation exceptions and action contrary to Executive Council advice

Section 64 recognises circumstances in which the ordinary consultation requirement does not apply or is qualified. These include, for example:

- Functions that the Constitution expressly makes exercisable in the Governor’s discretion, on particular advice, or under instructions from the Crown;
- Matters falling within the Governor’s special responsibilities under sections 66 or 67;
- Matters judged too unimportant to require Executive Council advice; and
- Exceptionally urgent cases in which consultation cannot occur before action is required.

In an urgent case, the constitutional safeguard is subsequent communication to the Executive Council of the measures taken and the reasons for them.

Section 65 separately regulates action **against** Executive Council advice. Depending on the circumstances, such action may rest on instructions from the Crown through a Secretary of State, the Governor’s section 66 or 67 responsibilities, or the constitutional test concerning the interests of **public order, public faith or good government**. The provision also imposes reporting and, where applicable, Secretary-of-State-approval requirements.

The legal consequence is twofold:

- Executive Council advice is not absolutely binding in every field; but
- The Governor cannot lawfully disregard it merely because of a personal preference on an ordinary domestic issue.

### D. Other functions are governed provision by provision

The Governor also has functions concerning such matters as the legislative process, prorogation and dissolution, public offices, and prerogative acts. These are not all exercised under one uniform rule. Some require consultation or advice from a specified body; others are subject to instructions or to a personal constitutional judgement. They should therefore be distinguished from the narrow, expressly stated special responsibilities in sections 66 and 67.

## 4. The resulting division of authority

| Institutional sphere | Principal authority |
|---|---|
| **Elected island sphere** | Ordinary domestic legislation through the Legislative Assembly; local taxation and appropriation subject to constitutional procedures; scrutiny of government business; and elected participation in Executive Council policy advice. |
| **Local administrative sphere** | Administration of departments and delivery of public services through the Falkland Islands Government, headed administratively by the Chief Executive. |
| **Governor/Crown sphere** | Formal executive authority; assent functions; special responsibility for external affairs, defence, internal security and the police; and constitutionally regulated exceptions to ordinary Executive Council control. |
| **United Kingdom reserve sphere** | Appointment and instruction of the Governor through Crown institutions; action by a Secretary of State, including disallowance of local laws; preserved Crown-in-Council legislative power; and ultimate responsibility arising from the Islands’ status as a UK Overseas Territory. |

The Constitution therefore creates neither complete independence nor day-to-day direct administration of every local matter by the United Kingdom. It establishes **locally democratic domestic lawmaking and administration within a Crown executive structure, with narrowly identified gubernatorial special responsibilities and broader UK constitutional reserve powers**.

### The Constitutional Framework

The Falkland Islands Constitution is a predominantly codified constitution documented primarily within the **Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008**. It was made on **5 November 2008** by Queen Elizabeth II in a meeting of the Privy Council at Buckingham Palace, laid before Parliament on **12 November 2008**, and came into force on **1 January 2009**, replacing the 1985 Constitution. The new Constitution did four things the old one did not: it **modernised the chapter on fundamental rights and freedoms** of the individual; it **embedded self-determination in the main body** of the Constitution (rather than leaving it as an implication); it **created an elected Legislative Assembly** to replace the Legislative Council; and it **better defined the role of the Executive Council and reduced the powers of the Governor**. It also provided for finance, the public service, the administration of justice, and a **Complaints Commissioner** (the islands' ombudsman). The structure is: Chapter I (ss. 1-22) Protection of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms of the Individual; Chapter II (ss. 23-25) The Governor; Chapter III (ss. 26-36) The Legislature; Chapter IV (ss. 37-55) Powers and Procedures of the Legislative Assembly; Chapter V (ss. 56-67) The Executive; with further chapters on finance, the public service, and the administration of justice.

### Legislative Authority: The Legislative Assembly

Chapter III creates the **Legislative Assembly**, which replaced the Legislative Council that had existed since the 19th century. Section 26(2) lays out its composition: **eight members elected by universal adult suffrage**, the **Speaker**, and two ***ex officio*** members - the **Chief Executive** and the **Director of Finance**. (The eight elected members are returned from two constituencies: five from Stanley and three from Camp.) Chapter IV (ss. 37-55) gives the Assembly the power to make laws (s. 37), and describes the sittings, voting, quorum, and the role and election of the Speaker. There are **no political parties** in the Falklands: all eight elected members sit as independents, and the Assembly functions by consensus rather than by party discipline. The Assembly's functions are to propose new laws and national policy, **approve finance** (the budget), and **hold the executive to account**. The Governor has the power to **dissolve the Legislative Assembly at any time**, and to give **Royal Assent** to any law passed by the Assembly (s. 55 is the Governor's reserved power in relation to legislation: the Governor may withhold assent or reserve a bill for the Secretary of State's consideration).

### Executive Authority: The Governor and the Executive Council

Chapter V vests executive authority in the Crown: **s. 56(1) - "The executive authority of the Falkland Islands is vested in Her Majesty"** - and s. 56(2) provides that it "shall be exercised on behalf of Her Majesty by the Governor, either directly or through officers subordinate to him or her." The Governor is appointed by the Crown through the Secretary of State (Chapter II, ss. 23-25), and exercises the duties of head of state in the monarch's absence. The Governor **normally acts only on the advice of the Executive Council** (s. 57): three of the elected members of the Legislative Assembly, elected annually by the Assembly to serve on the Council, and two *ex officio* members (the Chief Executive and the Director of Finance), with the Governor as presiding officer. Critically, **only the elected members of the Legislative Assembly serving on the Executive Council have a vote** to progress a change in law or policy; the Governor, the Chief Executive, and the Director of Finance do not vote. Government policy and its execution are primarily decided by the three elected Executive Council members. The **Chief Executive** is the head of the Civil Service and runs the administration day to day. The Constitution permits the Governor to act **without consulting the Executive Council** and even **against its advice** (ss. 66-67) - but in both cases the Governor **must immediately inform the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs**, who can overrule the Governor's actions. This is the constitutional safety valve: the Governor's reserve powers exist, but they are exercised under London's supervision, not independently.

### The Powers Reserved to the Governor

The Governor's reserved responsibilities are **foreign affairs, defence, and internal security**. Section 25 describes the Governor's role in defence and internal security, giving the Governor great authority in such matters (excluding issues relating to policing) **on the advice of the Commander of the British Forces** South Atlantic Islands at Mount Pleasant Complex. The Governor is also **Commander-in-Chief of the Falkland Islands Defence Force** (the islands' own volunteer defence force). In practice, this means: the United Kingdom is responsible for the islands' defence (through the British Forces South Atlantic Islands, based at Mount Pleasant), for their foreign affairs (the islands have no foreign policy of their own; the Governor acts as the channel to London), and for internal security in the narrow sense of defence-related security - while **policing is a local matter**, run by the Royal Falkland Islands Police under the island government. Everything else - fisheries (the islands' main revenue source), taxation, education, health, infrastructure, immigration, and the civil service - is the responsibility of the island government, through the Legislative Assembly and the Executive Council. The Governor also serves as **His Majesty's Commissioner for South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands**, which have no settled population and no elected government, and are administered directly by the Commissioner. The division is therefore: **the islands govern themselves in all domestic matters; London governs defence, foreign affairs, and internal security; and the Governor is the person in whom both meet** - presiding over the Executive Council, giving Royal Assent to laws, and acting as the Crown's representative and the channel to the Secretary of State.

### Self-Determination in the Constitution

The 2008 Constitution's most politically significant feature is that it **embeds self-determination in the main body of the Constitution**. Chapter I (ss. 1-22), on the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of the individual, is worded broadly from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, but with a much greater emphasis on the right of self-determination. The preamble (the "Whereas" clauses) states: "all peoples have the right to self-determination and by virtue of that right they freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development and may, for their own ends, freely dispose of their natural wealth and resources," and that "the realisation of the right of self-determination must be promoted and respected in conformity with the provisions of the Charter of the United Nations." This is why the Constitution matters to the sovereignty dispute: it is the legal instrument by which the islanders' right to determine their own political status is written into the law that governs them - and it is the basis on which the islanders voted in the **2013 referendum** (99.8% to remain a British Overseas Territory, 92% turnout). Argentina rejects the Constitution's premise (it regards the islanders as an implanted population, not a people) - but the Constitution itself is the islands' governing law, and it is the framework within which the island government and the United Kingdom divide authority.

The Constitution **reduced the Governor's powers** relative to 1985, created the elected Assembly, and **embedded self-determination** in its main body (Chapter I and the preamble). The Chief Executive heads the Civil Service; the Governor is also Commissioner for South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

# What this answer adds

Earlier answers cover the core division (Assembly, Executive Council, assent, disallowance, the Governor's reserved legislative power) in detail. This answer adds the parts none of them develops: the **money side of the division** (Chapter VI, Finance, ss. 74–81), the **judiciary's appointment and removal machinery** (Chapter VIII, ss. 88–90), and the **Complaints Commissioner** (Chapter IX, ss. 95–96) — plus corrections of section numbers and procedures that earlier answers state wrongly, checked against the text of the Order itself.

# Short answer

The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008 (SI 2008/2846, made 5 November 2008, in force 1 January 2009) gives the islands internal self-government while the Crown keeps sovereignty. The elected Legislative Assembly makes domestic law and controls the purse; the Governor, acting normally on the advice of the Executive Council, runs the executive; and the Governor and the Crown retain defence, external affairs, internal security, justice, audit and senior appointments, plus the powers to refuse assent, to legislate over the Assembly's head, to disallow local laws, and to legislate for the territory by Order in Council. The division is completed by two mechanisms earlier answers do not examine: a finance chapter that makes public money spendable only on the Assembly's authority while putting audit in the Governor's hands, and independent oversight bodies (the Public Accounts Committee, the courts, and the Complaints Commissioner) that neither the Assembly nor the Governor controls (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/made).

# 1. The core division, in brief

Executive authority is vested in Her Majesty and exercised on her behalf by the Governor (s. 56). The Governor must normally consult the Executive Council — three elected Assembly members plus the Chief Executive and the Director of Finance as non-voting ex officio members (s. 57) — and accept its advice (s. 66(1)). The Governor may act against that advice where, in his or her judgement, good governance requires it, or where the advice would affect external affairs, defence, internal security including the police, administration of justice, audit, or public-service appointments, discipline and management (s. 67(1)–(2)); the Governor must then forthwith report the matter and the Council's views to a Secretary of State (s. 67(3)), and any Council member may have their dissent minuted (s. 67(4)). On defence and internal security (other than the police) the Governor must consult the Commander British Forces and act in accordance with that advice (s. 25). Laws are made by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Legislative Assembly (s. 37); a Bill becomes law only on the Governor's assent, which the Governor may grant, refuse or reserve (s. 52); an assented Ordinance may be disallowed by Her Majesty through a Secretary of State (s. 54); and if the Assembly fails to pass a Bill or carry a motion the Governor considers necessary, the Governor may declare it to have effect as if passed — but only after informing the Executive Council and only on prior instructions from a Secretary of State (s. 55). Above all this, section 11 of the Order itself reserves to Her Majesty full power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of the Islands, including laws amending the Order or the Constitution (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made). The Governor normally acts only on Executive Council advice, and only the elected members of the Council vote on policy (Politics of the Falkland Islands, 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_Falkland_Islands).

# 2. The money side: Chapter VI, Finance (ss. 74–81)

This is where the legislative–executive division bites hardest in practice, because it decides who may spend public money.

- **One fund, one gate.** All government revenues go into a single Consolidated Fund (s. 74). No money may be withdrawn from it except to meet expenditure charged on the Fund by the Constitution or another law, or where an appropriation Ordinance authorises it (s. 75).
- **The Assembly holds the purse; the executive proposes.** The Director of Finance must prepare estimates of revenue and expenditure and lay them before the Legislative Assembly before or within thirty days of the start of each financial year, and the heads of expenditure go into an appropriation Bill (s. 76). The Assembly therefore authorises spending; the executive cannot spend without it. Supplementary estimates and supplementary appropriation Bills cover shortfalls or overspends (s. 76(3)).
- **A narrow executive safety valve.** If the appropriation Ordinance is not in operation at the start of the financial year, the Director of Finance — not the Governor, and not the Assembly — may authorise withdrawals to carry on government services, but only for up to four months or until the Ordinance comes into operation (s. 77). Similarly, the Director of Finance may advance money from a Contingencies Fund for an urgent and unforeseen need, but a supplementary estimate and appropriation Bill must then be laid before the Assembly as soon as possible to replace the advance (s. 78). Debt charges are a charge on the Consolidated Fund, so creditors are paid regardless of the annual appropriation (s. 79).
- **Audit is the Governor's, but the auditor is independent.** The Governor, acting in his or her discretion, must arrange the audit of the public accounts, the courts, and all government authorities and statutory bodies, and auditors have access to all relevant books and records (s. 80(1)). Audit reports go to the Governor, who must publish them and lay them before the Assembly and the Public Accounts Committee (s. 80(2)); and anyone conducting an audit is not subject to the direction or control of any other person or authority (s. 80(3)). So the Governor commissions the audit, but neither the Governor nor the elected executive can direct its findings.
- **The Public Accounts Committee is a hybrid check.** It has three members appointed by the Governor after consultation with the elected Assembly members (from people who are not Assembly members) and two elected Assembly members (s. 81(1)); the Director of Finance and the chair and deputy chair of the Assembly's Standing Finance Committee are disqualified from membership (s. 81(1)). It examines all public accounts and audit reports laid before the Assembly, may summon any person and require answers and information, and is not subject to the direction or control of any other person or authority (s. 81(5)–(6), (9)). It reports to the Assembly, keeping the Governor closely informed, at least annually, and publishes its reports (s. 81(7)). The reasoning chain is therefore: the executive proposes spending, the Assembly authorises it, the Governor's auditors check it, and a committee neither side controls scrutinises it in public (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made; Politics of the Falkland Islands, 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_Falkland_Islands).

# 3. The judiciary: appointed by the Governor, removable only through London (ss. 88–90)

The administration of justice is a reserved matter (s. 67(2)(d)), and the appointment machinery shows why it is insulated from both the Assembly and the local executive.

- The Chief Justice, the President of the Court of Appeal and the Justices of Appeal are appointed by the Governor **in pursuance of instructions given by Her Majesty through a Secretary of State** (s. 88(1)) — so the Governor does not choose them freely; London instructs. The Senior Magistrate, by contrast, is appointed by the Governor acting in his or her discretion (s. 88(4)).
- Removal is deliberately hard: a judge or the Senior Magistrate may be removed only for inability or misbehaviour (s. 90(3)), and only after the Governor appoints a tribunal of persons who hold or have held high judicial office, the tribunal advises referral, and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council advises Her Majesty that the judge ought to be removed (s. 90(4)–(5)). The Governor may suspend a judge while the question is investigated (s. 90(7)). Neither the Assembly nor the Executive Council has any part in appointing or removing judges (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made).

# 4. The Complaints Commissioner: an ombudsman outside both branches (ss. 95–96)

Chapter IX creates a further check on the executive that no earlier answer develops. The Governor, acting in his or her discretion, may appoint a Complaints Commissioner to investigate complaints of maladministration in the government of the Islands, or other matters prescribed by Ordinance (s. 95(1)). No Assembly member and no public officer may be appointed (s. 95(2)), and the Governor may remove a Commissioner only for inability or misbehaviour (s. 95(3)(d)). In investigating a complaint, the Commissioner "shall not be subject to the direction or control of any other person or authority" (s. 96(2)). The Commissioner is therefore appointed by the Governor but answers to neither the Governor nor the elected government in the conduct of investigations — a small, independent check on the executive's day-to-day administration (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made).

# 5. Corrections to earlier answers, verified against the Order's text

Reading the Order itself corrects four points on which earlier answers disagree:

- **The Crown's reserved law-making power is section 11 of the Order, not section 10, 12 or 13.** Section 11 reserves to Her Majesty "full power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of the Falkland Islands including … laws amending this Order or the Schedule" (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/made). Answers citing sections 10, 12 or 13 of the Order for this power are wrong.
- **The Governor's reserved legislative power (s. 55) has no subject-matter limit.** Section 55(1) applies whenever the Governor considers it necessary that "any Bill introduced or any motion proposed" should have effect and the Assembly fails to pass or carry it; it does not confine the power to defence, external affairs or internal security, as one earlier answer states. Its hedges are procedural, not topical: the Governor must inform the Executive Council and hear its views (s. 55(2)), must have prior instructions from a Secretary of State (s. 55(3)), and an objecting Assembly member may submit written reasons within fourteen days, which the Governor must forward to a Secretary of State (s. 55(4)); declarations about motions (not Bills) may be revoked by a Secretary of State (s. 55(5)) (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made).
- **Acting against Executive Council advice requires reporting, not prior approval.** Section 67(3) requires the Governor who acts against advice to "forthwith" report the matter and the Council's views to a Secretary of State. There is no requirement of prior approval before acting against advice — the prior-approval/instructions requirement belongs to the s. 55 reserved legislative power, not to s. 67 (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made).
- **The ex officio officers are the Chief Executive and the Director of Finance.** Section 57(1) names those two offices; "Financial Secretary" is the pre-2008 title — section 6(4) of the Order itself provides that the person holding the office of Financial Secretary immediately before the appointed day holds the office of Director of Finance under the new Constitution (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/made; Politics of the Falkland Islands, 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_Falkland_Islands).
- **There is no Judicial and Legal Services Commission in the Constitution.** The full text of the Schedule contains no such body; judicial appointments run through s. 88 as described above. An earlier answer's claim that appointments are made on the advice of such a commission is unsupported by the Constitution's text (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/schedule/made).

# 6. What the division amounts to

The Constitution does not separate powers into clean boxes. The Governor sits in both branches: part of the Legislature (no Bill becomes law without his or her assent, s. 52), chair of the Executive Council, appointer of senior officers and judges, commissioner of audits, and appointer of the Complaints Commissioner. What keeps this from being gubernatorial rule is that each reserve power is routed through a different check: the Assembly authorises all spending (ss. 74–76); the Governor's audit is independent and published (s. 80); the Public Accounts Committee, the courts and the Complaints Commissioner are all expressly beyond anyone's direction or control (ss. 80(3), 81(9), 96(2)); acting against elected advice must be reported to London (s. 67(3)); and legislating over the Assembly's head needs London's prior instructions (s. 55(3)). The ultimate backstop is section 11 of the Order: the Crown can legislate for the Islands, including amending the Constitution itself, without the Assembly (The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008, SI 2008/2846, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/made).

**The 2008 Constitution provides substantial local self-government, but not a sovereign separation from the United Kingdom.** Elected island institutions ordinarily determine domestic policy; the UK retains responsibility for defence and foreign relations, alongside ultimate legislative authority. The Governor participates in island government while also exercising Crown powers and receiving instructions through a UK Secretary of State. ([gov.fk](https://www.gov.fk/assembly/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2026/04/Political-System-Guidebook-3.pdf))

### Legislative authority

The elected **Legislative Assembly** makes local laws and approves budgets. Under **section 37**, lawmaking formally belongs to the Governor acting with the Assembly’s advice and consent. ([gov.fk](https://www.gov.fk/assembly/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2026/04/Political-System-Guidebook-3.pdf))

The principal retained controls are:

- **Assent — s. 52:** The Governor may assent, refuse assent, or reserve a Bill for the Crown. Constitution-inconsistent Bills must be reserved; before refusing assent, the Governor must explain why and allow members to submit views to London.
- **Disallowance — s. 54:** The Crown, through a Secretary of State, may annul an assented Ordinance after allowing Assembly reconsideration.
- **Reserved legislation — s. 55:** The Governor may deem an introduced Bill or qualifying motion passed after Assembly failure, but must hear Executive Council views and obtain **prior Secretary of State instructions**. There is no urgency exemption from that requirement.
- **Constitutional change — Order, s. 11:** The Crown reserves legislative power, including amendment of the Constitution. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/pdfs/uksi_20082846_en.pdf))

Separately, **Westminster retains power to legislate for the Islands**; UK Orders in Council can also alter territorial laws and constitutions. Local legislative autonomy therefore does not exclude overriding UK legislation. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-9706/))

### Executive authority and the Governor’s reservations

Executive authority is exercised for the Crown by the Governor. The **Executive Council** is the local executive decision-making body: three annually elected Assembly members hold its votes; the Chief Executive and finance officer are non-voting. The Governor chairs but is not a Council member. The civil service implements policy under the Chief Executive. ([gov.fk](https://www.gov.fk/assembly/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2026/04/Political-System-Guidebook-3.pdf))

**Section 66 normally requires consultation and acceptance of Council advice. Section 67 permits overriding it for good governance or where advice affects external affairs, defence, internal security—including police—justice, audit, or public-service appointments, discipline and management.** The Governor must immediately report the matter and Council views to London; members may minute dissent. Under **s. 25**, military advice binds the Governor on defence and internal security, excluding police. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2846/pdfs/uksi_20082846_en.pdf))

The crucial distinction is thus **ordinary locally directed government versus retained constitutional intervention powers**—not complete gubernatorial control of every domestic matter touching a reserved subject. ([gov.fk](https://www.gov.fk/assembly/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2026/04/Political-System-Guidebook-3.pdf))

# Analytical Review of the 2008 Falkland Islands Constitution: Authority Distribution and Reserved Gubernatorial Powers

The 2008 constitutional architecture of the Falkland Islands is defined by **The Falkland Islands Constitution Order 2008** (Statutory Instrument 2008 No. 2846, enacted via the British Settlements Acts 1887 and 1945, entering into force on January 1, 2009) (United Kingdom, 2008).
